The third major TAM suffix does not encode the aspect of an event, but rather its mood: irrealis mood applies to unreal or hypothetical events and states. The irrealis suffix is - na ‘ irr ’, which has the phonological ly conditioned allomorph - nda ‘ irr ’ ( sec:4.2 ).

The irrealis mood can be applied to verbs referring to events thought of as occurring in any temporal frame. Examples ex:verbs:33 and ex:verbs:34 are both translated in English as occurring in the future. As a time frame that is perforce hypothetical or not (yet) real, the future is almost always encoded in Ulwa with irrealis verb forms. Note that aspect -- perfective or imperfective -- is not specified by the irrealis suffix, as suggested by the multiple translations in ex:verbs:33 and ex:verbs:34.

Gambri mï umbe apa maytana.\\
Gambri mï umbe apa ma=ita- na \\
[name] 3sg.subj tomorrow house 3sg.obj= build- irr \\
(a) ‘Gambri will build the house tomorrow.’\\
(b) ‘Gambri will be building the house tomorrow.’ [elicited]

Nungol ndï wambana nduwananda.\\
nungol ndï wambana ndï=wana- nda \\
child 3pl fish 3 pl =cook- irr \\
(a) ‘The children will cook the fish.’\\
(b) ‘The children will be cooking the fish.’ [elicited]

The irrealis suffix can express a number of modal distinctions, such as deontic (‘should’, ‘must’), abilitative (‘can’, ‘could’), and optative (‘would that’) moods, as illustrated by ex:verbs:35.

Gambri mï (tap) apa maytana.\\
Gambri mï (tap) apa ma=ita- na \\
[name] 3sg.subj (maybe) house 3sg.obj= build- irr \\
(a) ‘Gambri should build the house.’\\
(b) ‘Gambri can build the house.’\\
(c) ‘Would that Gambri were building the house!’ [elicited]

The epistemic adverb tap ‘maybe’ is often possible in these sentences, but it is not necessary for conveying irrealis mood ( sec:8.2.4 ). Note, however, that tap ‘maybe’ cannot be used when the speaker wishes to convey that the action will necessarily happen (i.e., ‘will’, ‘must’). Thus, sentence ex:verbs:35 (with tap ‘maybe’ included), cannot mean *‘Gambri will build the house’ or *‘Gambri must build the house’.

When used in reference to past time, the irrealis mood indicates potential (i.e., ability) or lack thereof ex:verbs:36.

Ndï ango luwa miniya mana.\\
ndï ango luwa min=iya ma- na \\
3 pl neg place 3 du =toward go- irr \\
`They could not go to them.’ (Literally ‘They nowhere could go to them.’) [ulwa001_18:34]

When used in reference to past time, the irrealis mood can also indicate a counterfactual statement, as in ex:verbs:37.

Awal maka nungol ndul li mana.\\
awal maka nungol ndï=ul li ma- na \\
yesterday thus child 3 pl =with down go- irr \\
`[He] would have gone down with [his] children yesterday.’ [ulwa014_33:22]

Sentence ex:verbs:37 is proven to be counterfactual by the speaker’s immediately following sentence ex:verbs:38, which shows that this intended action of the man going with his children was unrealized.

Ticha ngala mbiye em i stap. \\
ticha ngala mbï-i-e em i stap\\
teacher pl.prox here-go. pfv-dep 3 sg pred stay\\
`But these teachers came, so he stayed.’ ( ticha, em, i, stap = TP) [ulwa014_33:26]

In some multiclausal construction s, the irrealis form of a verb may be best translated by an English infinitive, showing purpose or intention, as in ex:verbs:39 and ex:verbs:40.

Wa me ndul landa.\\
wa ma=i ndï=ul la- nda \\
village 3 sg.obj =go. pfv 3 pl =with eat- irr \\
`[They] went home to eat with them.’ [ulwa002_05:56]

Malimap matï yawa mananda.\\
ma=alima-p ma=tï yawa ma=na- nda \\
3 sg.obj =beat- pfv 3sg.obj =take uncle 3 sg.obj =give- irr \\
`[We] beat it [= sago starch] to give to [our] uncle.’ [ulwa014_00:15]

Sentences such as ex:verbs:39 and ex:verbs:40 are analyzed as consisting of two full clauses, so there is actually nothing akin syntactic ally to the English infinitive. The absence of dependent marker dependent marking ( sec:12.2.1 ) on the first clauses of examples ex:verbs:39 and ex:verbs:40 suggests that the clauses containing these purpose -denoting irrealis verbs are actually independent sentences, without any sentences dependent upon them. Thus, the irrealis suffix can be considered here a means of imbuing a desiderative or intentive meaning to the verb. Thus, ex:verbs:39 could be translated ‘[They] went home; [they] wanted to eat with them’; and ex:verbs:40 could be translated ‘[We] beat it; [we] intended to give it to [our] uncle’.

summary: The irrealis suffix in Ulwa is -na, with the phonologically conditioned allomorph -nda, and it marks mood rather than aspect. It is used for unreal or hypothetical situations across time frames, especially future events, but also for deontic, abilitative, optative, and past potential or counterfactual meanings; in some multiclausal constructions, it adds a purpose or intention reading, though these are analyzed as independent clauses rather than true infinitives.

The three basic TAM markings in Ulwa account for much of the suffix al verbal morphology of all declarative and interrogative sentences. In imperative sentences, however, verbs in Ulwa may receive the imperative suffix -n ‘ imp ’. For the syntax and function of imperative clauses in Ulwa, see sec:13.2.

tab:4.11 presents a sample of Ulwa verbs to illustrate their imperative forms, shown along with the irrealis forms for comparison.

The form [-n] found in imperative verbs may be related historically to the irrealis suffix -na ‘ irr ’. At any rate, there is indeed something kindred between irrealis and imperative forms, since, in irregular verb s that exhibit different stem s in the irrealis mood, the imperative ending will affix to the irrealis verb stem, never to the perfective / imperfective stem. Thus, for example, the imperative of ‘eat’ is [lan] (cf. la-nda ‘eat [ irr ]’) and not †[aman] (cf. ama-p ‘eat [ pfv ]’) and the imperative of ‘let’ is [lakan] (cf. laka-na ‘let [ irr ]’) and not †[kan] (cf. ka ‘let [ ipfv/pfv ]’). Furthermore, there is a semantic similarity between the two suffix es, since, among other things, the irrealis suffix can encode deontic mood (i.e., ‘must’), which, when expressed in an utterance, is not unlike issuing an imperative.

verb|)
imperative|)
summary: Ulwa declarative and interrogative clauses are largely marked by the language’s three basic TAM suffixes, but imperative verbs may additionally take the imperative suffix **-n**. This suffix may be historically related to the irrealis suffix **-na**, and the two are also linked syntactically and semantically: in irregular verbs, the imperative attaches to the irrealis stem rather than the perfective/imperfective stem, and the irrealis can sometimes express deontic meaning (“must”), which is similar to an imperative.

perfective|(
verb|(

As detailed in sections sec:4.4 -- sec:4.7, an inflect ed verb in Ulwa typically has exactly one TAM suffix (which may be null suffix null in certain imperfective verb forms). There are circumstances, however, in which perfective verbs may be marked twice -- that is, they take the form: [ stem ]-[ pfv ]-[ pfv ]. In such instances, the second perfective marker adopts the vowel from the verb stem, preventing the otherwise impossible sequence †[pp]. Thus, for example, verbs with [a]-final stem s have the form [ stem ]-[p]-[ap], and verbs with [o]-final stem s have the form [ stem ]-[p]-[op] (although there seems to be some variation allowed).

The semantic effect of this double perfective is often one of signaling that an action is all-the-more over-and-done-with. Since a single perfective marker typically signals that the event is viewed as whole and completed, this double marking could be seen as superfluous. Indeed, it may be that -- as speakers use different TAM suffix es ever more interchangeably, perhaps as the result of grammatical attrition -- the extra perfective marking is simply redundant (see sec:15 for structural changes due to grammatical attrition ). There are instances, however, in which the double perfective functions something like the pluperfect category of some European languages, showing that an event is not only viewed as a completed whole, but that is has been completed before the time of some other event in the more-recent past. These usages can often be translated with the English auxiliary ‘had’ plus the past participle, as in examples ex:verbs:41 through ex:verbs:45.

nï ma=p-e Madang p-e ndï=lo- p-op \\
1 sg 3 sg.obj =be -dep [place] be -dep 3 pl =cut- pfv-pfv \\
`I had made them when I was there in Madang.’ [ulwa014_11:34]

ndï-nji inga ma=ul lo- p-op -e\\
3 pl-poss affine 3 sg.obj =with go- pfv-pfv-dep \\
`[They] had gone with their in-law.’ [ulwa035_03:33]

Asika lïmndï ndïlpïpe ngala luke asi tï nap ndala une. \\
asi-ka lïmndï ndï=lï- p-ïp -e ngala luke asi tï na-p ndï=ala uni-e\\

`After [they] had sat and watched them, these people also took seats, cheering them on.’ [ulwa032_36:45]

The double perfective can, similarly, provide the sense of ‘already’, and is translated accordingly in ex:verbs:46.

Numbu ala nungunupop.\\
numbu ala nungun-u- p-op \\
post pl.dist break-put- pfv-pfv \\
`Those posts have already broken.’ [ulwa042_05:18]

It is also possible for the word ta ‘already’ to appear within a clause exhibiting such a construction ex:verbs:47. In example ex:verbs:47, however, it may be that the form /nip/ has been reanalyzed as monomorphemic, a new verb ‘die’, derived from the perfective form of the verb ni- ‘die’ (cf. the pluractional version of this verb, nipinpu- ‘die. pl ’, sec:4.3 ).

Nïnji wot yena mï ta nipop.\\
nï-nji wot yena mï ta ni- p-op \\
1sg-poss younger woman 3sg.subj already die- pfv-pfv \\
`My younger sister has already died.’ [ulwa027_00:33]

Sentences ex:verbs:46 and ex:verbs:47 also illustrate the fact that the vowel s in the second perfective suffix do not always match the final vowel of the verb stem. Indeed, there is variability within certain verb forms. For example, there are attested forms such as lï-p-ap ‘put- pfv-pfv ’ alongside lï-p-ïp ‘put- pfv-pfv ’, as seen in ex:verbs:45. It may be that some of these putative second perfective forms are actually reduced forms of the past locative verb wap ‘be. pst ’ ( sec:10.4 ). Indeed, it is possible that they have all derived historically from wap ‘be. pst ’, which is often pronounced [wɔp]: thus, it may be that first the /w/ was lost; then, when following non-low vowel s, the vowel [ɔ] was colored to [o], and when following the low vowel, it was colored to [a]. There are no attested (double) perfective forms with the vowel s [e] or [u] (i.e., †[-ep] and †[-up] are not found as perfective suffix es). Sentences ex:verbs:48 and ex:verbs:49 further exemplify the form [-op], following the stem -final vowel s /i/ and /u/, respectively.

Ane nda ine nda nipop.\\
ane anda i-n-e anda n i -p- op \\
sun sg.dist come- pfv-dep sg.dist die- pfv-pfv \\
`That [woman] died the day before yesterday.’ [ulwa037_36:02]

John maweka i Mongima ul ngalan upop.\\
John maweka i Mongima ul ngala=n u -p- op \\
[name] also go. pfv [name] with pl.prox=obl put- pfv-pfv \\

`John had also gone and planted these with Mongima.’ [ulwa014_55:24]

In many instances, as in ex:verbs:50 and ex:verbs:51, it is not clear whether the inclusion of a double perfective should be taken to convey any sense different from that of a regular (i.e., single) perfective verb form.

An ndamapape inim nga ambip. \\
an ndï=ama- p-ap -e inim nga ambi=p\\
1 pl.excl 3 pl =eat- pfv-pfv-dep water sg.prox big= cop \\
`We were eating them [= fish], but [now] the water is high [again].’ [ulwa014_29:36]

Mï maka aw ndïn mopop.\\
mï maka aw ndï=n ma=u- p-op \\
3sg.subj thus betel.nut 3pl=obl 3sg.obj =put- pfv-pfv\\
`He had [?] planted the betel nut there.’ [ulwa014†]
summary:
Ulwa normally allows only one TAM suffix on an inflected verb, but perfective verbs can sometimes take a double perfective form, [stem]-[pfv]-[pfv]. The second perfective harmonizes with the stem vowel to avoid an illicit sequence, though there is some variation in the attested forms.  

Semantically, the double perfective often adds a sense of something being especially completed or “already” done, and in some contexts it functions like a pluperfect, referring to an event completed before another past event. In many examples, however, its meaning is not clearly different from a single perfective.

text:
Some apparent examples of double perfective marking may reflect grammatical attrition: as verbal suffix es come to be used in increasingly interchangeable ways, they lose their aspect ual force. Perhaps such seemingly redundant perfective markers are used to show that the meaning intended is truly perfective. For example, although the form i ‘go. pfv ’ is intrinsically marked for perfective aspect, speakers on occasion add what seems to be a perfective suffix -- that is, as if they were treating this form as unmarked for aspect and thus requiring a perfective suffix. Example ex:verbs:52 contains the perfective form i ‘go. pfv ’ with an unnecessary additional perfective marker -ap ‘ pfv ’, realized here as [-yap] due to glide insertion ( sec:2.5.1 ).

Li kïkal wopa nda ango mbiyap.\\
li-i kïkal wopa nda ango mbï-i- ap \\
down-go. pfv ear all sg.dist neg here-go. pfv - pfv \\
`[She] went downstream, but that deaf one did not stay here.’ [ulwa014†]

Example ex:verbs:53, on the other hand, shows how i ‘go. pfv ’ -- with the added suffix -ap ‘ pfv ’ -- can function in a double perfective construction.

Ndï lïmndï ute iyapen.\\
ndï lïmndï u=uta-e i- ap -en\\
3 pl eye 2 sg =grind- ipfv go. pfv-pfv-nmlz \\
`They were the ones who had gone and watched over you.’ [ulwa013_01:25]

Example ex:verbs:54 shows how a double perfective construction can function when i ‘go. pfv ’ is reanalyzed as lacking (intrinsic) TAM marking. In this instance, the speaker uses a perfective-marked form of the past - tense locative verb wap ‘be. pst ’ as something like an auxiliary verb. I suspect that this is a recent innovation, one influenced by grammatical attrition in the face of competing influences from the dominant language, Tok Pisin (see sec:15).

It illustrates this with forms of *i* ‘go.pfv’ that take an added perfective suffix, including cases where the sequence functions as a double perfective construction. The author also suggests that one such construction may reflect a recent innovation, possibly influenced by Tok Pisin.

perfective|(
verb|(

An interesting tug-of-war occurs when one must refer to a completed action in future time (cf. the future perfect in English, e.g., we will have eaten ). The three designations in Ulwa’s basic three-way TAM system are not mutually exclusive: that is, an event could, theoretically, be viewed both as a completed whole ( perfective aspect ) and as something not (yet) real ( irrealis mood ). Typically in Ulwa, all irrealis - mood verbs are treated the same -- that is, there are no aspect ual distinctions maintained among them ( sec:4.6 ). Thus, the sentence in ex:verbs:55 could be translated variously into English.

Nungol ndï landa.\\
nungol ndï la-nda \\
child 3 pl eat- irr \\
(a) ‘The children will eat.’ (unspecified aspect )\\
(b) ‘The children will be eating.’ ( imperfective aspect )\\
(c) ‘The children will have eaten.’ ( perfective aspect ) [elicited]

In certain multiclausal construction s, however, it may become necessary to designate the aspect of an irrealis event as being perfective. Namely, when one future event is contingent on the completion of another, this yet-to-be-completed event can be marked with a perfective suffix ex:verbs:56. Thus, in these tug-of-war scenarios between aspect and mood, aspect wins.

Anji wa koytap namndu nungol kot ma mat malnda. \\

an-nji wa ko=ita- p namndu nungol ko=tï ma ma=tï ma=lï-nda\\
1 pl.excl-poss village indf =build- pfv pig child indf =take go 3sg.obj =take 3 sg.obj =put- irr \\

`Once [we] have built a village for ourselves and gotten a pig, [we] will go and put it there.’ [ulwa014_07:07]

Such irrealis perfective constructions are especially common in multiclausal imperative s. In ex:verbs:57, the perfective verb is the suppletive form i ‘go. pfv’.

Un i anul ndul amblawalin. \\
un i an=ul ndï=ul ambla=wali-n\\
2 pl go. pfv 1 pl.excl =with 3 pl =with pl.refl =hit- imp \\
`Go and fight with us with [= against] them!’ (Literally ‘You having gone, fight with us with them!’) [ulwa002_05:19]

A verb in the first clause of such an imperative may be marked with the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’ ( sec:4.12 ). Especially when the subject of the first clause differs from that of the second, the inclusion of this suffix may be seen as necessary to convey the irrealis perfective sense of the protasis: in ex:verbs:58, the conditional suffix on the first verb, anmbi ‘come out [ pfv] ’, helps signal that the action of the following verb is contingent on the completion of the action described by this one.

Ngun anmbita una malamape una lowon.\\
ngun an-mbï-i- ta unan ma=la-ama- p -e unan lo-wo-n\\
2 du out-here-go. pfv-cond pl.incl 3 sg.obj = irr -eat- pfv-dep 1 pl.incl irr -sleep- imp \\

`Once you two have come and we’ve eaten it, let’s sleep!’ [ulwa041_01:15]

Sometimes, in the tug-of-war between perfective aspect and irrealis mood, there is a morphological tie, at least in instances in which the verb form allows some indication of irrealis mood by means other than suffix ation. This applies to verbs that have circumfix -like irrealis forms beginning with [lo-] or [la-], such as wo- ‘sleep’ and ama- ‘eat’ ( sec:4.3 ). In irrealis perfective constructions involving these verbs, the verb combines the irrealis stem with the perfective suffix.

For example, the form lowop ‘sleep [ irr/pfv ]’ combines the beginning of the irrealis form lowonda ‘sleep [ irr ]’ with the ending of the perfective form wop ‘sleep [ pfv ]’ (cf. sec:4.3 ). It is thus capable of indicating perfective aspect and irrealis mood simultaneously, as in ex:verbs:59 and ex:verbs:60.

Wa ma lowop ma siwi anglalunda mane. \\

wa ma lo-wo-p ma siwi angla-lo-nda ma-n-e\\
village go irr -sleep- pfv go grub.species await-go- irr go- ipfv-dep \\

`[He] was going to the village, and, having slept [there], was going to search for grubs.’ [ulwa038_03:51]

Maka lowop apa mot anda luke itana mane. \\

ma=ka lo-wo-p apa mot anda luke ita-na ma-n-e\\
3sg.obj =at irr -sleep- pfv house awning sg.dist too build- irr go- ipfv-dep \\

`Having slept there, I was going to build that house awning, too.’ [ulwa042_04:44]

In example ex:verbs:61, the form lowop ‘sleep [ irr/pfv ]’ occurs with some borrow ed grammar from Tok Pisin ( i no laik, literally ‘do not want’; here, roughly, ‘should’).

Un i no laik anul mbï ka lowop mana? \\

un i no laik an=ul mbï ka lo-wo-p ma-na\\
2 pl pred neg want 1 pl.excl =with here thus irr -sleep- pfv go- irr \\

`Why don’t you spend the night here with us and [then] go?’ ( i no laik = TP) [ulwa014_16:04]

In a somewhat different but related manner, the irrealis perfective form of ama- ‘eat’ seems to combine two stem s in the same form: the irrealis stem [la-] and the non- irrealis stem [ama-] occur together, along with the perfective suffix -p ‘ pfv ’, thus yielding lamap ‘eat [ irr/pfv] ’. Although elsewhere in examples containing this verb the form [la-] is glossed as the verb stem ‘eat’, in irrealis perfective constructions such as those in ex:verbs:62 and ex:verbs:63, it is glossed as ‘ irr ’, since it is the part of the verb form that is signaling its irrealis value. The vowel of /la-/ deletes before the initial vowel of /ama-/ ( sec:2.5.5 ).

Ndïlamap we un namndu atïna. \\
ndï= la-ama-p we un namndu atï-na\\
3 pl = irr -eat- pfv then 2 pl pig hit- irr \\
`Once [we] have eaten them, then you will kill pigs!’ [ulwa014_43:54]

Mol lamap mana mat mananda. \\
ma=ul la-ama-p mana ma=tï ma=na-nda\\
3 sg.obj =with irr -eat- pfv spear 3sg.obj =take 3sg.obj =give- irr \\

`Having eaten with him, [they] will give him the spear.’ [ulwa014_62:16]
summary:
The passage explains that in Ulwa’s TAM system, irrealis mood and perfective aspect can both apply to a future event, but usually irrealis verbs do not distinguish aspect. In multiclausal constructions, however, perfective marking is used when one future event depends on the completion of another, so aspect overrides mood in these cases.

It gives examples of irrealis perfective forms in future conditionals and imperatives, including special forms like *lowop* ‘sleep [irr/pfv]’ and *lamap* ‘eat [irr/pfv]’, which combine irrealis marking with perfective suffixation. These forms show that Ulwa can express both irrealis and completed aspect simultaneously when the grammar requires it.

There is a special use of imperfective verb forms that may at first seem to run counter to its typically continuous aspect ual force. Imperfective verbs may be used to signal that an action is beginning or starting. This may be referred to as inchoative aspect (or inceptive aspect ). Indeed, there is nothing technically atelic about verbs denoting the commencement of an action. That said, the inchoative imperfective verb usually does maintain the sense of uncompleted action (i.e., it encodes that an action was started but interrupted or that an action has begun but has not yet reached its conclusion, both of which actions are ongoing). Sentence ex:verbs:65 illustrates the use of the inchoative imperfective.

We mokotïp mat manane mï mame.\\
we ma=kot-p ma=tï ma=na-n-e mï ma=ama- e \\
sago 3 sg.obj =break- pfv 3sg.obj =take 3 sg.obj =give -pfv-dep 3sg.subj 3sg.obj =eat- ipfv \\

`[He] broke a piece of sago and gave it to him, and he began to eat it.’ [ulwa001_11:42]

In ex:verbs:66, it is ambiguous whether the ending [-e] on the verb sa- ‘cry’ is encoding (only) clausal dependence or (additionally) the inchoative imperfective aspect.

Mï se nï mala ndïwanawne. \\
mï sa- e nï ma=ala ndï=wana-uni-e\\
3 sg.subj cry- dep 1sg 3sg.obj= for 3 pl =feel-shout- ipfv \\
`When she started to cry, I called to them to get her.’ [ulwa032_04:28]

In ex:verbs:67, the inchoative imperfective is marked by the irregular imperfective suffix -n ‘ ipfv ’.

Tana kot ambïn wutï anmot ngalïp anankïn ala li mane.\\
tana ko=tï ambï=n wutï anmot nga=lï-p anankïn ala li ma- n -e\\
axe indf =take sg.refl=obl leg post sg.prox =put- pfv blood pl.dist down go- ipfv-dep \\

`[He] cut his shin with an axe, and blood began to run down.’ [ulwa009_00:25]

In ex:verbs:68, the inchoative imperfective is indicated by the suppletive imperfective stem of the verb u- ‘put’, without any overt suffix.

Ndï kïkal ndïwana ndïnawte inim naw.\\
ndï kïkal ndï=wana ndï=na-uta- e inim na- aw \\
3 pl ear 3 pl =feel 3 pl = detr -grind- ipfv water detr -put. ipfv \\
`They heard them [= their names] and started grinding them [= coconuts] into water.’ [ulwa018_02:14]

Likewise, in ex:verbs:69, no overt suffix is present, but the [w]-final verb stem wow- ‘sleep. ipfv ’ indicates that imperfective aspect is intended.

Mawap imba pe mï wolka nawow.\\
ma=wap imba p-e mï wolka na- wow \\
3 sg.obj =be. pst night be -dep 3 sg.subj again detr- sleep. ipfv \\
`[He] stayed the night there and again he fell asleep.’ [ulwa006_04:33]

A minor variation to inceptive or ingressive aspect may be termed resumptive aspect. This aspect can also be encoded by imperfective verb forms to signal that an action that had stopped has begun again, as in ex:verbs:70.

Mï numbu mole.\\
mï numbu ma=lo- e \\
3 sg.subj garamut 3 sg.obj =cut- ipfv \\
`He resumed making the garamut drum.’ [ulwa009_00:56]
summary: The passage explains that imperfective verb forms can have an inchoative or inceptive meaning, marking the beginning of an action rather than only ongoing or continuous action. In this use, the action is started but not yet completed, and the text illustrates that this meaning may be expressed by overt imperfective suffixes, suppletive stems, or sometimes no overt suffix at all. It also notes a related resumptive use, where imperfective forms indicate that an action that had stopped has begun again.

As detailed in sec:4.6, the irrealis suffix can express a number of modal ities, including various predictions, such as that a state or event might be or might happen. There is also, however, a verbal suffix -t ‘ spec’, which can convey a sense of epistemic possibility. It immediately follows the irrealis suffix on the verb, as seen in ex:verbs:71 and ex:verbs:72.

Nakanaka nundate.\\
na-kanaka lu-nda- t -e\\
detr- unwrap put- irr-spec-dep \\
`[It] might unwrap.’ The pronunciation [nundate] – with initial [n] – may represent influence from the Maruat-Dimiri-Yaul dialect. [ulwa014_57:24]

Mï amun wa mbi an nït mol inat.\\
mï amun wa mbï-i na=n nï=ta ma=ul i-na- t \\
3 sg.subj now village here-go. pfv talk =obl 1sg= say 3 sg.obj =with come- irr-spec \\

`He recently came here to the village and told me that he might come with her.’ [ulwa037_46:28]

Examples ex:verbs:71 and ex:verbs:72 both illustrate the sense of ‘might’ being conveyed by the speculative suffix -t ‘ spec ’, in both instances directly following an irrealis suffix. Example ex:verbs:72 further illustrates this use in indirect discourse. This must not, however, be taken to have evidentiality evidential force -- that is, the suffix is used because the reported speech is of someone who himself is speculating about whether or not he would come (not because the person reporting this information can only speculate as to whether or not the person would come). Indeed, the speaker who uttered this sentence followed it with the one given in ex:verbs:73, which does not include any speculative form. For more on indirect discourse, see sec:13.4.5.

Inim ngol mol ina nït. \\
inim nga=ul ma=ul i-na nï=ta\\
water sg.prox =with 3 sg.obj =with come- irr 1 sg =say\\
`[He] told me [he] would come with her this year.’ [ulwa037_46:32]

The speculative suffix can also be used in conjunction with the epistemic adverb tap ‘maybe’, which always comes earlier in the clause, as in ex:verbs:74.

Ngunanji yalum anda tap i wa mbïpïnate.\\
ngunan-nji yalum anda tap i wa mbï-p-na- t -e\\
1 du.incl-poss grandchild sg.dist maybe go. pfv village
here-be- irr-spec-dep \\
`Our granddaughter might come and stay here in the village.’ [ulwa014_11:10]

Sentence ex:verbs:74 also illustrates that this suffix may be followed by the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’. More examples of the speculative suffix are given in ex:verbs:75 and ex:verbs:76.

Makïnate.\\
ma=kï-na- t -e\\
3 sg.obj =say- irr-spec-dep \\
`[He] might tell him.’ [ulwa032_51:01]

Una iken malka manate.\\
unan iken ma=lï-ka ma-na- t -e\\
1 pl.incl may 3 sg.obj =put-let go- irr-spec-dep \\
`We may go follow it [= an accusation].’ ( iken < TP i ken ‘may, can’) [ulwa037_08:44]

In sentence ex:verbs:76, the force of the suffix -t ‘ spec ’ is closer to English ‘may’. Indeed, it is used alongside a Tok Pisin loanword i ken ‘may’, often used in granting permission. In sentence ex:verbs:77, -t ‘ spec ’ is used along with a different Tok Pisin loanword, here giving the sentence a speculative sense, although one with a negative flavor. The Tok Pisin word used here, nogut ‘bad’, often carries a conjunctive meaning similar to that of English ‘lest’.

Nongut mundu tï unanandat.\\
nongut mundu tï unan=na-nda- t \\
lest food take 1 pl.incl =give- irr-spec \\
`[It] might give us food.’ ( nongut < TP nogut ‘bad; lest’) [ulwa029_05:25]

The speculative suffix is indeed often used in negative irrealis clauses, typically following the negative marker ango ‘ neg ’, which tends to come early in the clause, as in sentences ex:verbs:78 through ex:verbs:85.

Ango maka anma apombam manate.\\
ango maka an-ma apombam ma-na- t -e\\
neg thus out-go middle.of.house go- irr-spec-dep \\
`[She] shouldn’t go into the middle of the house, going out like that.’ [ulwa014_35:26]

Ango apa kwan lusim manat.\\
ango apa kwa=n lusim ma-na- t \\
neg house one= obl leave go- irr-spec \\
`[They] were not going to leave out a single household.’ ( lusim = TP) [ulwa029_02:26]

Una ango luwa lundat.\\
unan ango luwa lo-nda- t \\
1 pl.incl neg place go- irr-spec \\
`We can’t go anywhere.’ [ulwa029_03:17]

Nï ango mbuka wiya inat.\\
nï ango mbï-u-ka u=iya i-na- t \\
1 sg neg here-from-let 2 sg =toward come- irr-spec \\
`I will not come to you quickly.’ [ulwa031_00:46]

Ango nokoplïndat.\\
ango nokop-lï-nda- t \\
neg hide-put- irr-spec \\
`[It] couldn’t hide [from us].’ [ulwa037_14:36]

Mï ango un apa pïnat.\\
mï ango un=n apa p-na- t \\
3 sg.subj neg 2 pl=obl house be -irr-spec\\
`It won’t last [long] in your house.’ [ulwa037_52:13]

Ango in malandate unji ametamal. \\
ango i=n ma=la-nda- t -e u-nji ametamal\\
neg hand= obl 3sg.obj =eat- irr-spec-dep 2 sg-poss spoon\\
`[You] may not eat it with [your] hand, but [must use] your spoon.’ [ulwa014_36:27]

Nï ango manat nï mbï napïna. \\
nï ango ma-na- t nï mbï na-p-na\\
1 sg neg go- irr-spec 1 sg here detr- be- irr \\
`I won’t go; I’ll stay here.’ [ulwa037_35:57]

The two clauses in ex:verbs:85 illustrate the contrast between negative irrealis clauses (here marked with speculative -t ‘ spec ’) and positive irrealis clauses (here, as usual when not needed for extra speculative force, not marked with -t ‘ spec ’). In sentence ex:verbs:86 there is also a contrast between a negative irrealis clause and a positive one. Here, the negator ango ‘ neg ’ is missing; the speculative suffix -t ‘ spec ’ alone is conveying the negative force of the first clause.

Apombam manate angani wat ando li mana.

apombam ma-na- t -e angani wat anda=u li ma-na\\
middle.of.house go- irr-spec-dep rear ladder sg.dist =from down go- irr \\

‘[She won’t] go to the middle of the house, but will go down the back ladder.’ [ulwa014_34:48]
summary: The passage explains that the speculative suffix **-t ‘spec’** follows the irrealis suffix and conveys **epistemic possibility**, roughly ‘might’ or sometimes ‘may’. It can occur in indirect discourse without evidential force, combine with the adverb **tap ‘maybe’**, and often appears in **negative irrealis clauses**, where it may follow the negator **ango** or, in some cases, alone carry a negative sense.

text:
This suffix is also commonly used in negative command s, which may use the prohibitive marker wana wanap ‘ proh ’ (see sec:13.2.4 and sec:13.3.2 for examples). The negative polarity function of the speculative marker -t ‘ spec ’ may reflect an origin as a postverbal negator (cf. Ap Ma -at ‘ neg ’). But this historical explanation is itself speculative. See sec:13.3.2 for the synchronically more common postverbal negator s in Ulwa.

Question s, which often contain words derived from the negative marker ango ‘ neg ’ ( sec:13.3 ), may also carry speculative force, employing the suffix -t ‘ spec ’ ex:verbs:87.

A un angos tïnat?!\\
a un angos tï-na- t \\
ah 2 pl what take- irr-spec \\
`Ah, what will you get?!’ [ulwa018_06:11]

speculative|)

This suffix can also be used as a device for indicating politeness, suggesting more tentativeness in the question being asked ex:verbs:88.

Unan angos natanate?\\
unan angos na-ta-na- t -e\\
1 pl.incl what detr- say- irr-spec-dep \\
`What could we talk about?’ [ulwa037_58:33]
summary:
The suffix **-t** is used in negative commands and also in questions, where it can add a speculative meaning. The text suggests that its negative polarity use may historically come from a postverbal negator, but this is only a conjecture, and in Ulwa the more common postverbal negator is **s**.

In questions, forms derived from the negative marker **ango** may take **-t** to express speculation or politeness, making the question more tentative. Examples show it functioning in both a forceful speculative question and a softer, polite one.

verb|(

Perhaps etymologically related to the speculative suffix -t ‘ spec ’ ( sec:4.11 ), the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’ is used to mark the verb in the protasis of a conditional statement. The syntax of such sentences is addressed in sec:13.5; the morphology and basic uses of this suffix are addressed in this section.

In the protasis protases of conditional statements, the suffix -ta ‘ cond ’ is affixed either to the stem of the verb (always including the vowel ) ex:verbs:89 or to the perfective form (that is, including the perfective suffix ) ex:verbs:90. Often the two forms appear to be interchangeable. I suspect that, for many speakers, an aspect ual or modal distinction that perhaps once existed is now being lost. Still, at least in some circumstances, it may be the case that the perfective version of the conditional verb is required to show a sequence of events.

Inim lopota nï mana. \\
inim lopo- ta nï ma-na\\
water rain- cond 1sg go- irr \\
`If it rains, I’ll leave.’ [elicited]

Inim lopopta nï mana. \\
inim lopo-p- ta nï ma-na\\
water rain- pfv-cond 1sg go- irr \\
`If it rains, I’ll leave.’ [elicited]

In verbs that exhibit different stem s for the irrealis mood, the conditional form is never built from the imperfective / perfective stem alone. Either it is built from this realis stem plus the perfective marker or it is built from the suppletive irrealis stem without any additional marker (cf. the discussion of imperative s in sec:4.7 ). Thus, the verb ama- ‘eat’ has as its conditional form either [amapta] (from the fully inflect ed perfective form) ex:verbs:90a or [lata] (from the irrealis stem ) ex:verbs:90b, but never †[amata] (from the imperfective / perfective stem alone).

U nïnji mundu amapta nï uwalinda. \\
u nï-nji mundu ama-p- ta nï u=wali-nda\\
2 sg 1 sg-poss food eat- pfv-cond 1 sg 2 sg =hit- irr \\
`If you eat my food, I’ll hit you.’ [elicited]

U nïnji mundu lata nï uwalinda. \\
u nï-nji mundu la- ta nï u=wali-nda\\
2 sg 1 sg-poss food eat- cond 1 sg 2 sg =hit- irr \\
`If you eat my food, I’ll hit you.’ [elicited]

I have not found any discernible difference in meaning between the alternative verb stem s in cases such as these.

Example ex:verbs:91 illustrates the conditional suffix following the suppletive perfective stem i ‘go. pfv ’.

Mï ita nï nan makïna. \\
mï i- ta nï na=n ma=kï-na\\
3 sg.subj go. pfv-cond 1 sg talk= obl 3 sg.obj =say- irr \\
`If he comes, I’ll tell him.’ [ulwa014_09:39]

The conditional suffix can also appear following the locative verb p- ‘be at’, as in ex:verbs:92 and ex:verbs:93.

Kuma lawa mapta landa. \\
kuma ala-awa ma= p-ta la-nda\\
some pl.dist-int 3 sg.obj =be- cond eat- irr \\
`When some other people are there, [they] might eat [our food].’ [ulwa033_00:18]

Ambi napta we mï lïmndï anala.\\
ambi na- p-ta we mï lïmndï an=ala\\
big detr- be -cond then 3 sg.subj eye 1pl.excl =see\\
`Once [we] had gotten big, then she saw us.’ [ulwa013_00:47]

Especially when needed to break up impossible consonant cluster s, the locative verb p- ‘be at’ may be realized phonetic ally as [pï] when preceding the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’, as in ex:verbs:94 and ex:verbs:95.

Akum pïta akumnï ndutana.\\
akum p-ta akum=nï ndï=uta-na\\
basket be -cond basket= obl 3pl =grind- irr \\
`If there is basket, [they] scoop them with the basket.’ [ulwa036_01:43]

Mawapta mï anmapïta we ande ndï wolka mol nena.

ma=wap-ta mï anma= p-ta we ande ndï wolka ma=ul na-i-na\\
3sg.obj =be. pst-cond 3sg.subj good= cop-cond then ok 3pl again 3 sg.obj= with detr -come- irr \\

`If [the sick person] has stayed there and has gotten well, then OK, they would come back with him.’ [ulwa029_10:14]

Sentence ex:verbs:95 also illustrates the use of the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’ following the suppletive locative form wap ‘be. pst ’. More examples of conditional sentence s are provided in sec:13.5.

verb|)
conditional|)
summary:
The conditional suffix **-ta** marks the verb in the protasis of conditional statements. It can attach either to the verb stem or to the perfective form, and these two patterns often seem interchangeable, though the perfective form may sometimes be required to indicate a sequence of events.

With verbs that have special irrealis stem forms, the conditional is never built from the imperfective/perfective stem alone: it is formed either from the realis stem plus **-ta** or from the suppletive irrealis stem without an added marker. The suffix also appears after locative verbs such as **p-** ‘be at’ and the suppletive form **wap** ‘be.pst’, with phonetic variation such as **pïta** when needed to avoid difficult consonant clusters.

Unlike nouns, which may be formed from other parts of speech through the addition of the derivational suffix -en ‘ nmlz ’ ( sec:3.2 ), there is no single means of deriving verbs from other parts of speech. That said, it is possible for non-verbal predication non-verbal words to serve as predicate s. This is accomplished through the use of the copular clitic =p ‘ cop ’ ( sec:10.2 ).

While most verbs are composed of simply a single free root (plus, potentially, bound morpheme bound morphology such as TAM suffix es, the detransitivizing prefix na- ‘ detr ’, or object-marker proclitic s), some can be analyzed as compound s -- that is, consisting of more than one free morpheme. The final element of such compound s (excluding any suffix es) is always a verb stem. The first element, on the other hand, may be either a noun ex:verbs:96 or another verb ex:verbs:97 (or perhaps a postposition, although this may be analyzed otherwise). Often it is not clear whether such a combination of non-bound morphemes should best be analyzed as a compound. A noun preceding a verb, for example, could simply be the object of the verb. Only when this noun-plus-verb combination permits a direct object (or an object marker ) can it be said to be a compound. Similarly, two verb stem s in succession may be separate words that are coordinate d paratactic ally. A true compound verb consisting of two verbal elements, however, should permit only one object marker (that is, the object marker should affix to the beginning of the first member of the compound ). Often, series of postposition -plus-verb-stem seem very much like compound verbs, especially when considering their phonological tendency to coalesce and reduce. However, there are few if any morphosyntactic tests to prove that such forms are true compounds.

Ndïn ndiya i iwan ndïnambïlumope.\\
ndï=n ndï=iya i iwa=n ndï= nambï-lumo -p-e\\
3 pl=obl 3 pl =toward go. pfv basket= obl 3 pl =skin-put- pfv-dep \\

`[Men] would go to them [= women] with them [= bamboo stalks], blocking them [= fish] with fish trap baskets.’ [ulwa036_02:11]

Ul wandam ma i tï u kïkal welunda.\\
u=ul wandam ma i tï u kïkal we-lo -nda\\
2 sg =with jungle go hand take 2 sg ear cut-cut- irr \\
`[They] will go to the jungle with you and box your ears with [their] hands.’ [ulwa014_00:44]

Compound verbs may contain nouns as their first element. Evidence that these forms are single (though polymorphemic) lexical items comes from the fact that they permit object marker s (preceding the entire word) and TAM suffix es (following the entire word). Examples of noun-plus-verb verbal compounds are given in ex:verbs:98, ex:verbs:99, and ex:verbs:100.

Manambuweyup kuma ndinap ndïtï wa i.

ma= nambï-we-u -p kuma ndï=ina-p ndï=tï wa i\\
3 sg.obj =skin-cut-put- pfv some 3 pl =get- pfv 3 pl =take village go. pfv \\

`[She] peeled it, got some [greens], and brought them home.’ [ulwa001_01:06]

An kaw mawutïnip.\\
an kaw ma= wutï-ni -p\\
1 pl.excl song 3 sg.obj =leg-beat- pfv \\
`We danced the song.’ [elicited]

Nï tïn manambïtwana.\\
nï tïn ma= nambït-wana \\
1 sg dog 3 sg.obj =odor-feel\\
`I smelled the dog.’ [elicited]

Note that in example ex:verbs:98 the verb is analyzed as containing not only a nominal element, but also two verbal elements. Similar constructions with ‘put’ verbs are discussed in sec:9.2.2. Additional examples of compound verbs consisting of two verb roots are given in ex:verbs:101 and ex:verbs:102. Only the final element receives TAM marking.

Ndï angos tïna nakap anwanakap.\\
ndï angos tï-na na-kï-p an= wana-kï -p\\
3 pl what take- irr detr -say- pfv 1 pl.excl =feel-say- pfv \\
`[When] they wanted to get something, [they] called us.’ [ulwa018_05:01]

Amblawanawne nay. \\
ambla= wana-uni -e na-i\\
pl.refl =feel-shout -dep detr -go. pfv \\
`Calling to each other, they went.’ [ulwa001_07:49]

Compound verbs can be even more complex, containing whole postpositional phrase s (that is, units composed of noun-plus- postposition ). Examples ex:verbs:103 and ex:verbs:104 contain the relatively prototypical noun ina ‘liver’; example ex:verbs:105, on the other hand, includes as the object of the postposition a semantic ally verb-like noun, top ‘throw’.

Nï kenmbu maynakawana.\\

summary:
The passage explains that although most verbs consist of a single free root plus possible bound morphology, some verbs are better analyzed as compounds made of more than one free morpheme. In true compound verbs, the final element is always a verb stem, while the first may be a noun, another verb, or possibly a postposition; evidence for compound status includes the ability to take only one object marker and to place TAM marking on the final element.

It also notes that many noun-plus-verb and postposition-plus-verb sequences are hard to distinguish from compounds, since they may instead be ordinary phrases or verb sequences, and there are few morphosyntactic tests to prove compound status. Several examples are given of compounds with nouns, two verbs, or postpositional elements, including forms where only the last verb receives TAM marking.

In Ulwa, words that denote properties are not particularly distinct as a class in terms of their morphosyntax. The fundamental divide among grammatical categories in Ulwa falls rather between verbs and non-verbs. When viewed within this dichotomy, adjectives resemble nouns somewhat more than they resemble verbs. For example, adjectives may receive the copular enclitic. They never receive any of the three basic TAM suffix es found on verbs. Like nouns, adjectives are not marked for person, number, gender, or case. One possible minor criterion by which adjectives may be distinguished from nouns is their placement within a noun phrase. Within NPs, adjectives follow nouns.

adjective|)
summary: In Ulwa, property-denoting words do not form a sharply distinct class; the main grammatical division is between verbs and non-verbs. Adjectives pattern more like nouns than verbs because they can take the copular enclitic but never the basic verbal TAM suffixes, and they lack person, number, gender, and case marking. They may be distinguished from nouns only slightly by their position in noun phrases, where they follow the noun.

When an adjective is neither functioning as a substantive nor serving as a predicate complement, it occurs within the limits of a noun phrase. When inside an NP, adjectives occur after the noun (the head of the NP) and before the subject marker, object marker, or any other determiner that may be found in an NP. Such adnominal adjective s never occur outside the NP (i.e., discontinuous ly). Sentences ex:adj:1 through ex:adj:4 provide examples of adjectives (in bold ) as they appear in NPs, illustrating their postnominal position, preceding determiner s.

Adjectives may also function as substantives -- that is, they may have the same formal properties as prototypical nouns. In such cases, these adjectives have the same distribution as nouns. Thus, adjectives may serve as the head s of NPs, which may themselves serve as subject ex:adj:8, direct object ex:adj:9, or object of a postposition ex:adj:10 within a clause.

One factor complicating the task of assigning words in Ulwa to the grammatical category of adjective is the fact that adjectives in NPs sometimes precede their head noun s (instead of following them). While some speakers consider this order to be ungrammatical (perhaps an influence from the word order of Tok Pisin; see sec:15), it nevertheless occurs in speech, thereby making it difficult to rely on the distributional criterion that adjectives follow nouns. This adjective-noun word order is exemplified in sentences ex:adj:11, ex:adj:12, and ex:adj:13.

The morphosyntactic similarity between nouns and adjectives also makes it difficult at times to assign certain words to one class or the other. For example, the word kalam ‘knowledge’ can have either the more nominal meaning ‘knowledge, wisdom’ or the more adjectival meaning ‘knowledgeable, knowing, wise’, and it is difficult to define one of these meanings as being the primary one. Whereas in ex:adj:14 this word carries a more noun-like meaning, in ex:adj:15 it functions more like a substantive adjective ( sec:5.3 ).

Although it does not take verbal morphology verbal TAM morphology but rather the copular enclitic (thus making it resemble nouns and adjectives rather than verbs), it seems capable of taking object arguments (thus making it resemble verbs). In each of examples ex:adj:16, ex:adj:17, and ex:adj:18, kalam ‘knowledge’ appears to have a direct object argument, including proclitic object marking in ex:adj:16 and ex:adj:17.

Another notable characteristic of the grammatical class of adjectives is its rather small size. Taking the definition (based both on semantics and on syntactic distribution) that adjectives are words that denote properties and can occur within NPs after nouns and before determiner s, then the class of adjectives is quite small, and is, perhaps, closed. The words in ex:adj:22 may come close to representing a complete list of true adjectives, at least those most commonly used in discourse. To denote most other properties that could be ascribed to nominals, Ulwa employs other grammatical strategies, such as using postpositional phrase s or verb phrase s. For example, the notion ‘fast’ may be expressed with a metaphor ical postpositional phrase apïn wat ‘on fire’, as in ex:adj:23.
summary:
Assigning words to the adjective class in Ulwa is difficult because adjectives can sometimes precede nouns in NPs, even though some speakers judge this order ungrammatical. The language also shows substantial overlap among nouns, adjectives, and verbs: words like kalam ‘knowledge/knowledgeable’ can be noun-like, adjective-like, or verb-like, while even prototypical adjectives such as tembi ‘bad’ can be used nominally or as predicate adjectives.

The adjective class itself appears quite small, perhaps closed, and mostly consists of words denoting physical properties such as size, color, temperature, and texture. For many other properties, Ulwa uses alternative grammatical strategies like postpositional phrases or verb phrases, rather than adjectives.

Various categories of pronouns are treated in the sections in this chapter. Demonstrative words, which may also function pronominally, are treated in sec:7.3. Defined in terms of discourse function, these subcategories of pronouns all consist of words that refer to something that is either identified elsewhere in the discourse or thought to be identifiable either from context or from shared knowledge of the speech act participant s. The referents of these pronominal forms are semantic ally nouns. There are distributional similarities that exist among these subgroups of pronouns (for example, their members can all serve as the head of an NP), as well as shared structural features (for example, these forms do not permit TAM suffixation).

pronoun|)
summary: This chapter treats several categories of pronouns, while demonstrative words that can also function pronominally are discussed separately in section 7.3. These forms are defined by discourse function: they refer to entities identified elsewhere in the discourse or recoverable from context or shared knowledge, and their referents are semantically nouns. They also share distributional and structural properties, such as functioning as NP heads and not allowing TAM suffixation.

personal pronoun|(
pronoun|(

The paradigm for Ulwa personal pronouns consists of three persons -- first, second, and third -- and three number s -- singular, dual, and plural. There is a clusivity distinction exhibited in first person non- singular forms. The dual forms denote exactly two referents, whereas plural number implies more than two (but can, at least for some speakers, be used to refer to exactly two referents as well, sec:9.1.2 ). The singular form, as to be expected, is used when the referent is exactly one. Pronouns do not exhibit any gender distinctions or any politeness distinctions. The forms of the personal pronouns in Ulwa are given in tab::6.1.

All (and only the) non-singular speech-act personal pronouns end in the formative /n/. The second person is marked by the vowel /u/, which occurs in each number for this person. The presence of this vowel is also felt in the first person non-singular inclusive forms; this has a certain logic to it, since these forms include the addressee(s) as a referent. The vowel /a/ is found in all first person forms, except the first person singular. Dual forms are marked by initial /ng/, present in all dual pronouns except the third person. In fact, all dual forms (except the third person ) can be analyzed as consisting of the plural equivalent of these pronouns plus word-initial /ng/. The third person dual pronoun min ‘3 du’ stands out as being formally unusual in this regard.

speech act participant

The only polysyllabic personal pronoun s (the dual and plural first person inclusive forms) are clearly derived from the combination of two other pronouns, namely a second person form ( plural or dual ) and an exclusive first person plural form -- i.e., unan ‘1 pl.incl’ < un ‘2 pl’ + an ‘ 1pl.excl’ and ngunan ‘1 du.incl’ < ngun ‘2 du’ + an ‘1 pl.excl’. If /ng/ is treated as a dual formative, /n/ as a non-singular speech act participant formative, and /a/ as an indicator of the first person, then these two pronouns could be further analyzed as /u-n-a-n/ ‘ 2-pl-1-pl’ and /ng-u-n-a-n/ ‘ du-2-pl-1-pl’, respectively. These two exclusive pronouns are perhaps younger forms, possibly calque d from one of the nearby Yuat languages, which contrast inclusive and exclusive first person forms. Indeed, proposes that a pronominal clusivity distinction is an areal feature.

Some speakers have reported an alternative 3 du pronominal form /ndin/. However, it is not well attested in my corpus. The only examples of it seem to reflect an adnominal demonstrative rather than a personal pronoun. I suspect that it is an abridged form of the dual distal demonstrative andin (cf. the form [nda] for the singular distal demonstrative anda, sec:7.3 ). The form [ndin], for example, occurs at the end of an NP in ex:pron:1.

Kambok inom ngusuwa ndin asika ndule. \\
Kambok inom ngusuwa ndin asi-ka ndï=ula-e\\
Kambuku mother poor 3 du? sit-let 3 pl =weave- ipfv \\
`Two poor women from Kambuku [village] used to sit and weave them.’ [ulwa014_42:11]

In ex:pron:2, the functional similarity between [a]ndin ‘ du.dist ’ (‘those two’) and anda ‘ sg.dist ’ (‘that’) is clear, as each form immediately follows a corresponding numeral.

wik wopa kwa nda nini ndintïna \\
wik wopa kwa anda nini ndin =tï-na\\
week all one sg.dist two 3 du?=take- irr \\
`for all of one week, or two’ ( wik = TP) [ulwa031_00:27]

Nevertheless, if there is in fact a pronominal use of ndin ‘3 du (?)’, then it most likely derives historically from this demonstrative word. A similar functional change, whereby a demonstrative has come to serve more general pronominal functions without carrying any spatial deictic meaning, can be seen in the form ala ‘ pl.dist ’ (‘those’) ( sec:7.3 ).

Each of the forms given in tab::6.1 may serve as the subject of either an intransitive or a transitive clause. Pronominal objects, on the other hand, are indicated by a paradigm of clitic s that precede a verb, postposition, or oblique marker ( tab::6.2). They are almost identical to their subject-form equivalents; the main difference occurs in the third person singular form, which is /mï/ as a subject, but /ma=/ whenever in non-subject roles.

These non-subject pronominal forms may also be used as adnominal possessor adnominal possessive pronominal forms, immediately preceding the possessum ( sec:9.1.5 ). Further information on object marker s (and non-subject pronominal forms) is provided in sec:7.2.

In casual speech, the dual and plural first person inclusive pronouns may be pronounced without the final /-n/ -- that is, [nguna] and [una] for /ngunan/ and /unan/, respectively.

summary: Ulwa personal pronouns distinguish three persons and three numbers: singular, dual, and plural, with clusivity in first-person non-singular forms. They show no gender or politeness distinctions; dual forms are marked by initial /ng/, non-singular speech-act participant forms end in /n/, and second person forms contain /u/. The text also notes that some inclusive first-person forms are transparent combinations of second-person and exclusive first-person forms, and that object/possessive pronouns are expressed by clitic forms closely related to the subject pronouns, with special allomorphy in the third singular.

possessive pronoun|(
possession|(
pronoun|(

Possessive pronominal forms are all clearly derived from the corresponding personal pronominal forms plus the word nji ‘thing’. More precisely -- the possessive pronouns correspond to the paradigm of non-subject personal pronominal forms, since the third person singular possessive form is [manji], rather than †[mïnji] (see tab::6.1 and tab::6.2 for the subject and object personal pronominal paradigms). These possessive forms do not necessarily function as subjects or objects themselves, but rather typically occur within NPs head ed by another nominal form – that is, they are typically adnominal possessor adnominal possessive pronouns. As with all pronominal forms, there is no gender distinction, whether in the third person or elsewhere.

tab::6.3 provides the forms of the possessive pronouns and possessive demonstratives in Ulwa.

All forms in tab::6.3 are transparently decomposable. There is only one minor phonological change, which affects the dual and non-third person plural forms, as well as the dual reflexive form. This is the shortening (i.e., quasi-degemination ) of the sequence nasal -plus- prenasalization. Thus, the possessive first person plural exclusive form has the underlying form /annji/, but is realized as [anji]. Similarly, second person plural /unnji/ is realized as [unji], making it homophonous with the second person singular possessive form /unji/.

Throughout this grammar, the pronominal forms are treated orthographic ally as individual words, reflecting their phonological unity. However, the glossing reflects their composite structure (i.e., object pronoun + -nji ‘ poss’ ). The possessive ending -nji ‘ poss’ is also found in full NPs, but only when they end in a determiner (i.e., an object marker or deictic ); that is, -nji ‘ poss’ cannot attach to bare nouns. Possession with full-NP possessor s is discussed further in sec:9.1.5.

Possessive pronouns do not index anything about the possessum. That is, although the possessive pronoun encodes the person and number of the possessor, it offers no information about the person or number (or gender ) of that which is possessed. Furthermore, no morphological or syntactic distinction is made in Ulwa between alienable possession alienable and inalienable possession.

Possessive forms may refer to first person ex:pron:3, second person ex:pron:4, or third person ex:pron:5 possessor s.

`Her hair is soft.’ [elicited]

Possessor s may be singular, dual, or plural, and may occur in object roles as well as subject roles. In example ex:pron:6, the possessive form refers to a third person plural possessor, here part of a direct object NP.

Ndï lïmndï ndïnji aweta mala. \\
ndï lïmndï ndï-nji aweta ma=ala\\
3pl eye 3pl-poss friend 3sg.obj= see\\
`They saw their friend.’ [elicited]

Third person possessive forms, such as the one in ex:pron:7, can have ambiguous reference, pointing either (reflexively) to an antecedent in the clause or to a third party not necessarily mentioned in the clause.

Ginam mï inim mo manji aweta ndït atalp. \\
Ginam i mï inim ma=u ma-nji i/j aweta ndï=tï ata-lï-p\\
[name] 3sg.subj water 3sg.obj =from 3sg.obj-poss friend 3pl= take up-put- pfv \\

`Ginam pulled her friends out of the water.’ [elicited]

That is, manji ‘ 3sg.obj-poss ’ in sentence ex:pron:7 can refer either to Ginam’s friends or to someone else’s (e.g., Yawat’s). To clarify that the pronoun refers to Ginam, a different form may instead be used, composed of the reflexive pronoun of the appropriate number ( sec:6.3 ) and -nji ‘ poss ’, giving the meaning ‘X’s own’, as in ex:pron:8.

Ginam mï inim mo ambïnji aweta ndït atalp. \\
Ginam i mï inim ma=u ambï-nji i/*j aweta ndï=tï ata-lï-p\\
[name] 3sg.subj water 3sg.obj =from sg.refl-poss friend 3pl =take up-put- pfv \\
`Ginam pulled her own friends out of the water.’ [elicited]

These forms are similar in function to certain pronouns found in some other languages, such as the Latin possessive reflexive pronoun suus ‘his/her/its/their own’. In addition to their use in clarifying third person antecedent s, however, the Ulwa forms may also be used with first or second person reference in order to convey the sense ‘my own’, ‘our own’, ‘your own’, and so on, as in ex:pron:9, ex:pron:10, and ex:pron:11.

Nï lïmndï ambïnji aweta mala. \\
nï lïmndï ambï-nji aweta ma=ala\\
1 sg eye sg.refl-poss friend 3sg.obj= see\\
`I saw my own friend.’ [elicited]

Min lïmndï ambinji aweta mala. \\
min lïmndï ambin-nji aweta ma=ala\\
3 du eye du.refl-poss friend 3sg.obj= see\\
`The two of them saw their own friend.’ [elicited]

Un lïmndï amblanji aweta ndala. \\
un lïmndï ambla-nji aweta ndï=ala\\
2 pl eye pl.refl-poss friend 3sg.obj= see\\
`You saw your own friends.’ [elicited]

These reflexive possessive forms are not marked for person (or gender ); they are only marked for number. They are included in tab::6.3.

It may here be noted that possessive forms need not necessarily precede nouns. Although they cannot precede verbs (without the verbs having been nominalize d), they can precede adjective s. This happens, however, only when the adjective is functioning substantively (i.e., nominally) ( sec:5.3 ), as in ex:pron:12 and ex:pron:13. This further suggests that there is little if any morphosyntactic distinction between property words (i.e., “ adjective s”) and semantic ally more prototypical nouns.

Manji anma ndï apa map. \\
ma-nji anma ndï apa ma=p\\
3 sg.obj-poss good 3pl house 3 sg.obj= be\\
`His good ones [= daughters] are in the house.’ [elicited]

Nïnji njukuta mï wandam i. \\
nï-nji njukuta mï wandam i\\
1 sg-poss small 3sg.subj jungle go. pfv \\
`My small one [= dog] went into the jungle.’ [elicited]

Finally, the possessive forms can be used substantively with an implied noun, as in ex:pron:14 and ex:pron:15.
summary:
Ulwa possessive pronouns are transparently built from the non-subject personal pronominal forms plus **-nji ‘poss’**, and they show no gender distinction. They mark the person and number of the possessor, not the possessum, do not distinguish alienable from inalienable possession, and can also have reflexive possessive forms meaning ‘X’s own,’ which are marked only for number.

The forms may function adnominally inside NPs, but they can also appear substantively or before adjectives used as nouns. A minor phonological shortening affects some dual and plural forms, and third-person possessives can be ambiguous unless the reflexive possessive form is used to specify coreference.

A reflexive pronoun generally has as an antecedent a form occurring (or implied) earlier in the same clause that has the same referent (i.e., the two words are co-indexed for reference). Reflexive pronouns are inflect ed for number, but not for person or gender. As these forms function as objects, they typically clitic ize to a following verb or postposition. The Ulwa reflexive pronouns are given in tab::6.4.

Thus, these pronouns are similar to their English translations ending in ‘-self’ or ‘-selves’, in that there is no distinction made among them for person -- whether first, second, or third -- but they are distinguished for number. These three forms are based on the same root, /amb(ï)-/. The use of reflexive pronouns is illustrated by examples ex:pron:16 through ex:pron:22.

Tambana mï ambuwalinda.\\
Tambana mï ambï =wali-nda\\
[name] 3 sg.subj sg.refl= hit- irr \\
`Tambana will hit herself.’ [elicited]

Mï ambït nïmal ndïlp. \\
mï ambï =tï nïmal ndï=lï-p\\
3 sg.subj sg.refl= take river 3 pl =put- pfv \\
`It has put itself in the rivers.’ [ulwa014_69:32]

Nï ambïnakap mol une. \\
nï ambï =nakap ma=ul uni-e\\
1 sg sg.refl =for 3 sg.obj =with shout- ipfv \\
`I was yelling at her on my own behalf.’ [ulwa032_16:56]

Ngun ambinkalamp.\\
ngun ambin =kalam=p\\
2 du du.refl= knowledge= cop \\
`You two know yourselves.’ [elicited]

Nungol ndï amblat nay. \\
nungol ndï ambla =tï na-i\\
child 3pl pl.refl =take detr- go. pfv \\
`The children brought themselves [to go along].’ [ulwa014_60:09]

Una amblakolp.\\
unan ambla =kol-p\\
1 pl.incl pl.refl =break- pfv \\
`We have broken ourselves.’ [ulwa037_31:10]

Ay ndïnkap ndïn amblan up. \\
ay ndï=nïkï-p ndï=n ambla =n u-p\\
sago 3 pl =dig- pfv 3pl=obl pl.refl=obl put- pfv \\
`[They] made [packets of] sago and left them for themselves.’ [ulwa014_49:21]

There are indications that the binding binding domain for anaphor s (i.e., reflexive pronouns) in Ulwa may be something greater than the clause -- that is, unlike in English, it is possible for the antecedent of a reflexive pronoun in Ulwa to be located in a so-called higher clause. All known examples of this occur when the matrix clause (containing the antecedent ) introduces the embedded clause (containing the reflexive pronoun ) by means of a verb of speaking (or thinking). Thus, Ulwa may be said to exhibit a sort logophoricity, since these reflexive s must be bound by an antecedent whose speech (or thought) is being reported. It should be noted, however, that there is no special logophoric pronoun in Ulwa. Examples ex:pron:23 and ex:pron:24 illustrate the use of reflexive pronouns with antecedent s in a “higher” clause.

Wangasa Wore ngala ini tï ambïnanda nate. \\
Wangasa i Wore ngala ini tï ambï i=na-nda na-ta-e\\
[name] [place] pl.prox ground take sg.refl =give- irr detr -say- dep \\
`Wangasa says that these Wore [people] will give him land.’ (Literally ‘… will give himself land’) [ulwa014_21:49]

Ambïwalinda ambul undate nakap. \\
ambï =wali-nda ambï =ul unda-t-e na-kï-p\\
sg.refl =hit- irr sg.refl =with go -spec-dep detr- say- pfv \\
`[He] thought that [the crocodile] might go around with him to kill him.’ [ulwa035_02:29]

anaphor
long-distance anaphoric reference

Example ex:pron:25 illustrates this long-distance logophoricity (or logophoric) anaphoric reference with a reflexive pronominal modifier, here used as a bare possessor, without the form -nji ‘ poss ’ ( sec:6.2 ).

Kwa mï man ambaweta kap. \\
kwa mï i ma=n ambï i=aweta kï-p\\
one 3 sg.subj 3 sg.obj=obl sg.refl =friend say- pfv \\
`Someone said that it was his friend.’ [ulwa020_00:39]

Also to be mentioned here is an interesting idiom atic use of the reflexive pronominal object marker ambla= ‘ pl.refl ’. When used with the verb asa- wali- ‘hit, kill’, this marker does not necessarily have a reflexive (or reciprocal) sense, but rather gives the entire verb the intransitive meaning ‘fight’ (as in battle). The object of fighting (the enemy) can be marked in a postpositional phrase with the postposition ul ‘with’. This can cause ambiguity not unlike what often occurs in English, since this same postpositional phrase can mark either enemies or allies. Cf. English sentences such as The English fought with the French. Sentences ex:pron:26, ex:pron:27, and ex:pron:28 exemplify this use of the verb asa- wali- ‘hit, kill’ with the reflexive pronominal object marker ambla= ‘ pl.refl ’.

Ndiya lop ndiya wa lop ndul amblasap.\\
ndï=iya lo-p ndï=iya wa lo-p ndï=ul ambla =asa-p\\
3pl =toward go- pfv 3 pl= toward village go- pfv 3 pl =with pl.refl =hit- pfv \\
`[They] went to them, went to them in the village, and fought with them [as enemies].’ [ulwa034_00:27]

Unan ndiya ma ndul amblawalinda!\\
unan ndï=iya ma ndï=ul ambla =wali-nda\\
1 pl.incl 3 pl =toward go 3 pl= with pl.refl =hit- irr \\
`Let’s go to them and fight with them [as allies]!’ [ulwa002_05:37]

Ndul ndul amblasap.\\
ndï=ul ndï=ul ambla =asa-p\\
3 pl =with 3 pl =with pl.refl =hit- pfv \\
`With them [= our allies] we fought with them [= our enemies].’ [ulwa002_03:13]

The dual and plural reflexive pronouns may, alternatively, convey a reciprocal sense (i.e., ‘each other’, ‘one another’). There may thus arise ambiguity in meaning, typically clarified through context. For example, sentence ex:pron:19 could be interpreted either as having a reflexive sense or as having a reciprocal sense (i.e., either ‘you two know each other’ or ‘you two know yourselves’). Examples of reciprocal meaning are given in sentences ex:pron:29 through ex:pron:34.

summary:
Ulwa reflexive pronouns are number-marked but not marked for person or gender, and they typically function as object clitics attached to a following verb or postposition. They normally refer back to an antecedent in the same clause, but the text notes that antecedents can also occur in a higher clause, especially in reported speech or thought contexts, giving Ulwa a kind of logophoricity without a special logophoric pronoun.

The same forms can sometimes express reciprocal meaning, especially in the dual and plural, so context is needed to distinguish readings like “the two know themselves” versus “the two know each other.” The passage also notes an idiomatic use of the plural reflexive object marker with the verb meaning ‘hit, kill,’ where it can yield the intransitive meaning ‘fight.’

Indefinite referents can be denoted by the numeral / interrogative word kwa ‘one; who?; someone’ when the referent is a human or by the phrase nji kwa ‘one thing, something’ when the referent is non-human, as illustrated by examples ex:pron:37 through ex:pron:40.

Kwa nip. \\
kwa ni-p\\
one die- pfv \\
(a) ‘Someone died.’\\
(b) ‘Who died?’ [elicited]

Nï kwa asap. \\
nï kwa asa-p\\
1sg one hit- pfv \\
`I killed someone.’ [elicited]

Nji kwa liyu.\\
nji kwa li-u\\
thing one down-put\\
`Something fell.’ [elicited]

Nï lïmndï nji kwa ala\\
nï lïmndï nji kwa ala\\
1sg eye thing one see\\
`I saw something.’ [elicited]

Sentence ex:pron:37, if given the right intonation, could be interpreted as a question, as suggested by the second translation given. This is because the form [kwa] is also used as an interrogative pronoun meaning ‘who?’ ( sec:6.5 ).

Dual and plural forms do not tend to be used for indefinite pronominal referents, at least not on their own. For non- singular indefinite referents, however, the word kuma ‘some’ may follow an NP, whether human ex:pron:41 or non-human ex:pron:42.

Ankam kuma mbin. \\
ankam kuma mbï-i-n\\
person some here-come- pfv \\
`Some people came.’ [elicited]

Ya kuma liyu. \\
ya kuma li-u\\
coconut some down-put\\
`Some coconuts fell.’ [elicited]

It is possible for subject marker s ( sec:7.1 ) to follow kuma ‘some’ ex:pron:43. Although subject marker s may also follow kwa ‘someone’, this is less common. In this way, kwa ‘someone’ seems to pattern with what are more likely true pronouns, whereas kuma ‘some’ seems to pattern more with adjective s.

Ya kuma ndï liyu.\\
ya kuma ndï li-u\\
coconut some 3 pl down-put\\
`Some coconuts fell.’ [elicited]

It should be noted as well that object marker s ( sec:7.2 ) can follow object NPs ending with kuma ‘some’, as in ex:pron:44 and ex:pron:45.

Nï lïmndï ankam kuma ndala.\\

`I saw some people.’ [elicited]

Nï ya kuma ndamap.\\

`I ate some coconuts.’ [elicited]

The interrogative form angos ‘what?’ can also be used in negative - polarity sentences (e.g., with the negator ango ‘ neg ’) to mean something along the lines of ‘whatever, whatsoever, anything’, as in examples ex:pron:46 through ex:pron:49.

1 pl.incl neg what work= obl act- irr \\
`We will not do [just] whatever [sort of] work.’ [ulwa030_02:30]

Nï ango angos ame. \\
nï ango angos ama-e\\
1 sg neg what eat- ipfv \\

The passage notes that **kwa** can also function as an interrogative ‘who?’, that subject and object markers may follow **kuma** (and less commonly **kwa**), and that **angos** ‘what?’ in negative-polarity contexts can mean ‘anything/whatever’, or ‘whatever’ in positive sentences when combined with **nji**.

The forms of the indefinite pronoun s kwa ‘one, someone’ and kuma ‘some’ ( sec:6.4 ) are the same as the forms used in asking content question s in Ulwa. The pronoun kwa ‘one, someone’ thus also means ‘who?’ (for a singular human referent), as illustrated by example ex:pron:51.

Kwa (mï) lamndu ndasap? \\
kwa (mï) lamndu ndï=asa-p\\
one (3 sg.subj) pig 3pl= hit- pfv \\
`Who killed the pigs?’ [elicited]

Similarly, the pronoun kuma ‘some’ conveys the means ‘who?’ when referring to
multiple human referents, as in ex:pron:52 and ex:pron:53.

Kuma (min) lamndu ndasap? \\
kuma (min) lamndu ndï=asa-p\\
some (3 du) pig 3pl= hit- pfv \\
`Who [= which (two) people] killed the pigs?’ [elicited]

Kuma (ndï) lamndu ndasap? \\

some (3 du) pig 3pl= hit- pfv \\
`Who [= which (three or more) people] killed the pigs?’ [elicited]

For non-human referents, the question word angos ‘what?’ is used, as in ex:pron:54, ex:pron:55, and ex:pron:56. For all interrogative pronouns, subject marker s are optional (as are object marker s).

Angos (mï) lamndu ndasap? \\
angos (mï) lamndu ndï=asa-p\\
what (3 sg.subj) pig 3pl= hit- pfv \\
`What killed the pigs?’ [elicited]

what (3 du) pig 3pl= hit- pfv \\
`What [= which (two) things] killed the pigs?’ [elicited]

angos (ndï) lamndu ndï=asa-p\\
what (3 pl) pig 3pl= hit- pfv \\
`What [= which (three or more) things] killed the pigs?’ [elicited]

wh- question

In content question s (i.e., wh- questions), the wh- word remains in situ; it is not preposed to the front of the clause as in English. Accordingly, when the ‘who’ or ‘what’ being asked about is not the grammatical subject, but rather the object of a verb, then the interrogative pronoun occurs in the typical object position (i.e., immediately before the verb), as in examples ex:pron:57 through ex:pron:60.

U lïmndï kwa mala? \\
u lïmndï kwa ma=ala\\
2 sg eye one 3sg.obj =see\\
`Whom did you see?’ [elicited]

Yata mï kuma ndasap? \\
yata mï kuma ndï=asa-p\\
man 3sg.subj some 3pl= hit- pfv \\
`Whom [= which people] did the man hit?’ [elicited]

U angos matïn? \\
u angos ma=tï-n\\
2sg what 3sg.obj= take- pfv \\
`What did you take?’ [elicited]

Nungol mï angos minanglalop? \\
nungol mï angos min=angla-lo-p\\
child 3 sg.subj what 3du =await-go- pfv \\
`What [= which two things] did the boy look for?’ [elicited]

When preceding an NP, the interrogative word ango ‘which?’ (compare angos ‘what?’) conveys the sense ‘which [NP]?’. There is no distinction made based on animacy or number or grammatical relation (i.e., whether the questioned element is a subject or an object). Significantly, whereas modifiers of NPs such as adjective s or determiner s follow their associated NPs ( sec:9.1 ), the modifying element ango ‘which?’ precedes its NP. This could serve the functional means of differentiating between ‘which [NP]?’ and ‘[NP] neg ’. Cf. ango tïn mamap ‘which dog ate it?’ vs. tïn ango mamap ‘the dog did not eat it’. Sentences ex:pron:61 through ex:pron:64 illustrate the use of ango ‘which?’.

Ango tïn (mï) mïnda mamap?\\
ango tïn (mï) mïnda ma=ama-p\\
which dog ( 3sg.subj) banana 3sg.obj =eat- pfv \\
`Which dog ate the banana?’ [elicited]

U ango mïnda (mï) mamap? \\
u ango mïnda (mï) ma=ama-p\\
2sg which banana ( 3sg.subj) 3sg.obj =eat- pfv \\
`Which banana did you eat?’ [elicited]

Ango nungolke nïnji yot matïn? \\
ango nungolke nï-nji yot ma=tï-n\\
which child 1sg-poss machete 3sg.obj= take- pfv \\
`Which child took my machete?’ [elicited]

U ango apa nditap? \\
u ango apa ndï=ita-p\\
2sg which house 3pl= build- pfv \\
`Which houses did you build?’ [elicited]

The interrogative pronoun ‘whose?’ takes the form kwanji ‘whose [ sg] ’ for singular possessor s and kumanji ‘whose [ nsg] ’ for dual or plural possessor s (no distinction is made here between the two), as may be seen in examples ex:pron:65, ex:pron:66, and ex:pron:67. These forms are transparently derived from the words kwa ‘one’ or kuma ‘some’ plus nji ‘thing’ (cf. possessive pronoun s, sec:6.2 ).

Content questions are wh-in-situ rather than wh-fronted, so the question word stays in its normal clause position, and the interrogative modifier ango ‘which?’ precedes the noun phrase regardless of animacy or grammatical relation. The language also has possessive interrogatives kwanji ‘whose [sg]’ and kumanji ‘whose [nsg],’ formed from kwa/kuma plus nji ‘thing.’

intensive pronoun|(
pronoun|(

There are two basic sets of intensive pronoun s in Ulwa. The members of one paradigm stress the fact that the referent(s) alone is/are the subject (or object). The members of the other paradigm stress the fact that the referent(s) – out of a group of potential referents -- performed the action; these are called here partitive-intensive pronoun s.

The suffix used to derive the set of (non- partitive ) intensive pronoun s is -awa ‘ int ’ (‘-self/-selves’). It may combine with any of the non-subject pronominal (or demonstrative ) forms, generating the paradigm shown in tab::6.5. Throughout this grammar, intensive pronoun s are treated orthographic ally as individual words; in the morphological glossing, however, they are broken into their composite morphemes.

The partitive-intensive pronominal suffix is -we ‘ part.int ’ (‘-self/-selves [out of multiple]’). It may combine with any of the non-subject pronominal (or demonstrative ) forms, generating the paradigm given in tab::6.6.

Ulwa has two intensive pronoun paradigms: a basic set, marked by the suffix **-awa** ‘int’, which emphasizes that the referent alone performed the action or was the subject/object, and a partitive-intensive set, marked by **-we** ‘part.int’, which emphasizes that the referent acted alone out of a larger group. Both suffixes attach to non-subject pronominal or demonstrative forms, and the grammar treats these as single words in orthography even though they are morphologically complex.  

The passage also notes that the morpheme **we** can occur independently with the meaning ‘alone,’ sometimes separated phonologically from the preceding word, including after a pronoun.

While there may also exist a full paradigm for such forms in all person s and number s, both for personal pronoun s and for demonstrative s (see sec:7.3 ), only four forms are attested in texts ex:pron:80a.

There is another set of pronominal forms, which can be used to mark the topic of a sentence. They are formed by combining a pronoun, whether personal ( sec:6.1 ) or demonstrative ( sec:7.3 ), with the topic-marking form -ambi ‘ top ’, which may derive from a strengthened form of the reflexive marker ambï= ‘ sg.refl ’ (cf. the adjective ambi ‘big’, which perhaps also derives from this intensive form). Topic-marker forms are presented in tab::6.7.

These topic-marking forms can be used to contrast one referent from another or to introduce a new referent after, say, a pause in the discourse. Some of their functions are illustrated by sentences ex:pron:85 through ex:pron:90.

`She said: “Me? I don’t know stories.”’ [ulwa014_01:20]

commiserative pronoun

Ulwa has a set of pronouns used to convey compassion toward a second person or third person referent. These affective (or commiserative) forms are transparently derived from the set of personal pronoun s plus the adjective ngusuwa ‘poor, pitiful’. Notably, the 3 sg affective pronoun derives from the object-marker pronominal form (i.e., from /ma=/), and not the subject pronominal form (i.e., not from †/mï/). There is no phonological difference between the 2 sg and 2 pl affective pronominal forms, as this historical difference has been neutralized by the place assimilation and quasi-degemination of the final /-n/ of un ‘2 pl’ before the immediately following /ng-/. All the forms may be optionally elongated by the ending [ -ta], which bears no clear semantic connection to the conditional suffix of the same form ( sec:4.12 ). The forms of the affective pronouns are shown in tab::6.8.

As an adjective, ngusuwa ‘poor’ has the same distribution to be expected of any attributive adjective (attributive) adjective in Ulwa ( sec:5.1 ): it follows the nominal head of the NP and may precede a determiner. Its use as an adjective is illustrated by sentences ex:pron:95 through ex:pron:99.

summary:
Ulwa has affective, or commiserative, pronouns used to express compassion toward second- or third-person referents. These forms are transparently derived from personal pronouns plus *ngusuwa* ‘poor, pitiful’, with the 3sg affective based on the object-marker form rather than the subject form; 2sg and 2pl have merged phonetically, and all affective pronouns may optionally take the ending *-ta*.  

The adjective *ngusuwa* behaves like a normal attributive adjective: it follows the noun and may precede a determiner. By contrast, the affective pronouns do not occur with subject or object markers or other determiners in the same phrase, and unlike the adjective, they can take *-ta*; the examples illustrate these pronominal uses.

determiner|(

I include under the heading “determiners” a number of rather different word types (including clitic s, as well as possibly affix es), that in some way indicate the definiteness or specificity of a referent, provide information that situates it in space, or identify its function within a clause. There are some syntactic commonalities among the various categories described in the following sections, although they do not necessarily constitute a single syntactic ally definable word class. One function of Ulwa determiners is to encode the number of a referent NP, which is otherwise unmarked for number. Thus, subject marker s ( sec:7.1 ), object marker s ( sec:7.2 ), and demonstrative s ( sec:7.3 ) may all be marked as singular, dual, or plural. This chapter also describes quantifiers ( sec:7.4 ) and numerals ( sec:7.5 ).

summary: The passage groups together several different kinds of “determiners,” including clitic *s* and possibly affix *es*, because they can indicate definiteness or specificity, locate a referent in space, or identify its role in a clause. It notes that these categories share some syntactic properties but may not form a single word class, and that in Ulwa they can mark number on noun phrases that are otherwise unmarked for number, including singular, dual, and plural; the chapter also covers quantifiers and numerals.
