father 3 sg.subj sharp= cop \\
`Father is angry.’ [elicited]

More commonly, however, anger is expressed by means of a verbal expression with uni- ‘shout’. In ex:clause:95, the literal expression ‘shout for [something]’ or ‘shout on account of [something]’ conveys the meaning ‘be angry about [something]’. In ex:clause:96, the literal expression ‘shout with [someone]’ conveys the meaning ‘be angry with [someone]’.

Mï ndïnap unipe.\\
mï ndï=nap uni -p-e\\
3 sg.subj 3pl =for shout- pfv-dep \\
`She was angry about them [= seeds].’ [ulwa014_12:24]

We nï mol une.\\
we nï ma=ul uni -e\\
then 1 sg 3 sg.obj =with shout- ipfv \\
`Then I got angry with her.’ [ulwa032_02:13]

See sec:5.4 for other expressions of emotional and physical states.

summary:
Ulwa normally distinguishes subject (S/A) and object (P) arguments clearly, but hunger is expressed by a special construction in which the experiencer functions as the object and ‘hunger’ is the grammatical subject, literally like “hunger hits someone.” When the experiencer is a full noun phrase, it may also appear in subject position before *mundu* ‘hunger’, while the object marker still indexes the experiencer on the verb.

The passage notes that this pattern is exceptional: other physical and emotional states such as pain, sickness, anger, and sadness are not generally expressed with this same experiencer-as-object structure. Instead, they are usually encoded by predicating a noun or adjective of the experiencer, or by other verbal expressions, such as using *uni-* ‘shout’ to express anger.

A simple sentence in Ulwa thus consists minimally of one subject and one predicate. Since subjects may be pronominal and since subject pronoun s may be omitted, it is possible for only the predicate to be overt in the clause.

The predicate consists minimally of a verb, whether transitive or intransitive. A transitive verb has an object within its phrase and may have object marker s preceding it. TAM suffix ation may appear on the verb. A predicate may contain more than one verb. There are also a number of compound verb s consisting of discontinuous elements, between which objects may occur.

The subject, too, when overt, may consist of multiple elements; these typically comprise noun phrase s. Subjects often contain subject marker s following the head of the NP. Other determiner s -- that is, in addition to subject marker s and object marker s -- are possible as well, whether as part of the subject or as part of the object in a transitive verb phrase.

In addition to the basic elements of the subject and the verb phrase (which, if transitive, also contains an object), the monoclausal sentence may contain oblique s. These typically occur between the subject and object, yielding a canonical word order of SXOV.

summary:
A simple Ulwa sentence minimally consists of a subject and a predicate, though the subject may be pronominal and omitted so that only the predicate is overt. The predicate must contain at least a verb, may include an object and TAM suffixes, and can consist of multiple or discontinuous compound verbs.  

When overt, the subject may be a multi-element noun phrase and often includes subject markers or other determiners. Monoclausal sentences may also contain obliques, which typically occur between the subject and object, giving the canonical word order SXOV.

In this chapter I examine how clauses are combined in Ulwa to form complex sentences. The combination of clauses of equal grammatical status ( coordination ) is discussed in sec:12.1. Then, in sec:12.2, I consider Ulwa’s means for showing the dependence of one clause on another ( subordination ). One special subtype of subordinate clause (the relative clause ) is investigated in sec:12.3. A very restricted form of clause chaining is discussed in sec:12.4.

complex sentence|)
summary: This chapter examines how Ulwa combines clauses to form complex sentences. It first discusses coordination of clauses with equal grammatical status, then subordination, followed by relative clauses as a special subtype of subordinate clause, and finally a very restricted form of clause chaining.

coordination|(
complex sentence|(

There is no lexical class of coordinator s or coordinating conjunction s in Ulwa -- that is, there are, generally speaking, no words equivalent to the English word and used to connect elements of equal grammatical status, whether to link words within a phrase, phrase s within a clause, or clauses within a sentence. Coordination (at all syntactic levels) is accomplished through parataxis -- coordinate elements are presented one after the other without any morphological connector, whether bound morpheme or independent word. There are, however, some possible exceptions to this generalization: speakers commonly borrow Tok Pisin conjunction s while speaking Ulwa; and there is also a rather infrequently used word ma ‘and’, which I suspect to be a recent innovation ( sec:12.1.3.)

summary: Ulwa does not have a lexical class of coordinators or coordinating conjunctions comparable to English *and*. Instead, coordination at all syntactic levels is generally expressed by parataxis, with coordinate elements simply placed in sequence without a morphological connector. The only possible exceptions are borrowed Tok Pisin conjunctions and the infrequent word *ma* ‘and’, which may be a recent innovation.

Before examining coordination between clauses, I consider how elements within phrase s may be coordinated, starting with nouns within a noun phrase. Nouns are coordinated within a noun phrase s without any overt conjunction or morphosyntactic marking to indicate conjunction. When the total number of referents among the coordinated nouns in the NP equals two, then the entire NP may receive dual subject marking or object marking. When the total number of referents is more than two, then the NP may receive plural subject marking or object marking. Examples ex:complex:1 through ex:complex:5 illustrate NPs in which two nouns are coordinated.

If a sentence contains two verbs that have different objects, then it is assumed that the coordination occurs not between two verbs within a single verb phrase but rather between two verb phrase s. However, it is not always clear whether there are two verb phrase s being coordinated within a single clause or there are two clauses being coordinated within a larger sentence. This is because it is common in Ulwa to omit subjects ( sec:11.1 ). Thus, although example ex:complex:23 is translated as though the coordination occurs within a single clause, it could alternatively be the case that there are two full clauses being coordinated, but that the subject in the second clause is omitted (i.e., ‘Alimban killed the pig and [he] cooked the meat’).

Alimban mï lamndu masap mundu nduwanap.\\
Alimban mï lamndu ma= asa -p mundu ndï= wana -p\\
[name] 3 sg.subj pig 3 sg.obj =hit- pfv food 3 pl =cook- pfv \\
`Alimban killed the pig and cooked the meat.’ [elicited]

This point leads to the focus of this section: the coordination of clauses in Ulwa. When two clauses are presented on equal grammatical footing, there is no distinction made between the two. They are presented paratactic ally, one after the other, without any dependent marker dependent marking -- that is, Ulwa employs asyndetic coordination, as illustrated by sentences ex:complex:24, ex:complex:25, and ex:complex:26.

Mangusuwa as mï nip. \\
[ma-ngusuwa asa] [mï ni-p]\\
[3 sg.obj- poor hit] [ 3sg.subj die- pfv] \\
`[They] struck the poor thing and he died.’ [ulwa037_30:42]

Nï mbïwap mokotïp. \\
[nï mbï-wap] [ma=kot-p]\\
[1 sg here-be. pst] [3 sg.obj =break- pfv] \\
`I stayed here and [I] bore her.’ [ulwa014†]

Mangusuwa mbïwap mï amun naman. \\
[ma-ngusuwa mbï-wap] [mï amun na-ma-n]\\
[3 sg.obj- poor here-be. pst] [3 sg.subj now detr- go- ipfv] \\
`The poor thing stayed here and today she’s leaving.’ [ulwa032_06:25]

Sentences ex:complex:24, ex:complex:25, and ex:complex:26 are all translated with ‘and’. Coordinated clauses can have concessive coordination concessive (i.e., ‘but’) senses as well. Again, this is achieved without any overt coordinating conjunction ex:complex:27.

[3 sg.subj neg thus Manu village 3sg.obj =be] [3sg.subj detr- go. pfv] \\

concessive coordination

Coordination of clauses is not, however, especially common: speakers generally prefer to mark one or more clauses as dependent ( sec:12.2 ).

complement clause

Ulwa makes prolific use of clause-linking, connecting dependent clause s to following independent clause s (or to further dependent clauses) with the verbal suffix -e ‘ dep ’, which is glossed here as “ dependent ”. The order of constituents in a subordinate clause is the same as is found in main clause s (i.e., SOV). Complement clauses (i.e., clausal object s) occur in the same position as nominal objects (i.e., between the subject and the verb of the matrix clause ). There are no complementizer s in Ulwa.

Subordinate clauses have the same **SOV** word order as main clauses, and complement clauses occur in the same position as nominal objects, between the subject and verb of the matrix clause. Ulwa has no complementizers.

The dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’ is a suffix that can affix to fully inflect ed verb forms (that is, to verbs with TAM suffix marking). Whether the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’ affixes to the imperfective suffix -e ‘ ipfv ’ is, however, an insoluble question, since a posited underlying form of /-e-e/ would reduce to [e]. In this grammar, verbs with the form [ stem ][e] are glossed sometimes as ‘[ stem ]- ipfv ’ and sometimes as ‘[ stem ]- dep ’, according to context. At times the decision is arbitrary. The glossing should never be taken to be a definitive statement on which of the two homophonous forms is being used. Moreover, in many instances it is possible that both forms are underlyingly present in the same verb form. The use of the dependent marker in Ulwa is not considered an indication of the prototypical clause chaining (or medial clause s) found in many languages of New Guinea, since the de\-pendent-marked verbs in these clauses do not have “more restricted structures”, nor do they indicate “ switch reference ”. This is, nevertheless, clearly a kindred phenomenon. See sec:12.4 for what may be a better candidate of clause chaining in Ulwa.

As just implied, the subject of the dependent clause may be the same as or different from the subject of a subsequent independent clause without any morphological indication one way or the other. When one clause is subordinated to another, it almost always precedes it. A subordinate clause marked by the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’ may bear one of a few semantic relations to the main clause on which it depends: causal ( sec:12.2.2 ), concessive ( sec:12.2.3 ), temporal ( sec:12.2.4 ), and so on. Proto-Keram probably contrasted two dependent marker s: *-a, which would have marked a sequential relationship to the following clause, and * -e, which would have marked a simultaneous relationship to the following clause. The Keram language Ambakich still retains the distinction. In Ulwa, however, this contrast has been lost: the sole dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’ can indicate either a sequential or a simultaneous temporal relationship, as well as other logical relationships between clauses.

summary:
The Ulwa dependent marker **-e** is a suffix that attaches to fully inflected verb forms, though its relation to the imperfective suffix **-e** is sometimes impossible to determine because the two forms are homophonous. The grammar therefore glosses forms ending in **[stem][e]** either as **-ipfv** or **-dep** depending on context, and in some cases both may be underlyingly present.

Ulwa subordinate clauses usually precede the main clause, and the subject of the subordinate clause may match or differ from that of the following independent clause without any special marking. The dependent marker can express several relations, including causal, concessive, temporal, sequential, and simultaneous ones; unlike prototypical clause chaining, it does not mark switch reference or more restricted clause structure.

Subordinate clauses marked with the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’ are used extensively in the rhetorical structure known as tail-head linkage, whereby the final clause of one sentence is more or less repeated at the start of the following sentence. In these structures, the final verb of the first sentence is fully repeated somewhere in the first clause of the second sentence (i.e., it has the same exact object marker and TAM suffix ); the addition of the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’, however, allows the clause with the repeated verb to serve as a transition into a new independent clause. In tail-head linkage constructions, it is possible for the entire pivot to be repeated exactly, as in ex:complex:65.

Min nay wambana ndutap. Min nay wambana ndutape wa namane.\\

`The two went and caught fish. After the two went and caught fish, [they] headed home.’ [ulwa011_00:34]

It is more common, however, for the recapitulatory clause to be a reduced form of its model, eliding, for example, the subject or one or more coordinated verb phrase s. Such reductions in tail-head linkage constructions may be seen in examples ex:complex:66 through ex:complex:70.

It is also common for seemingly independent clause s to receive the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’. In this way, when added almost as an afterthought, this suffix can serve a sort of coordinating function, equivalent almost to a conjunction ‘and’ in use. By affixing -e ‘ dep ’ to the end of a clause (and in so doing signaling that another clause is to follow), a speaker may have a better chance at holding the floor. Indeed, some speakers commonly insert the sound [-e] in the silence following a clause to signal that they are not yet done talking, as in examples ex:complex:72, ex:complex:73, and ex:complex:74.

Rays muku kot nïn ani lïp. E Dora lïmndï nala. \\

`The two brought it, went to a place, put it down, and rested. And then [they] got up again, got it, were getting it.’ The use of the noun pul ‘piece’ to mean ‘place’ may be calque d from TP hap ‘piece, place’. [ulwa035_04:20]

Ndï maka lop. E ndï we ndïmokop. E ndï mbïlop. \\

Thus this structure roughly means something like ‘that being [the case]’ and can, accordingly, function as a connector between clauses or as a floor-holding particle. Its use is illustrated in ex:complex:75, ex:complex:76, and ex:complex:77.

In addition to the dependent-marker suffix -e ‘ dep ’ and the afterthought-like forms [e] and [pe], there is a form we ‘(and) then’, which can connect clauses. It is often used in conditional statements, occurring between the verb of the apodosis (marked by the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’) and the start of the protasis ex:complex:78. Phonological ly (i.e., in terms of prosodic unit s), this word we ‘then’ belongs to the apodosis.

Ndï ita we unan matïna. \\

This form may occur in other sentence types besides just conditional sentence s, however. Sometimes it is not perfectly clear whether it is a separate lexeme (i.e., we ‘then’) or an elongated version of the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’.

The word we ‘(and) then’ also functions like a coordinator. It may be used to connect sentences in discourse, helping the speaker to floor-holding hold the floor. Examples ex:complex:79 and ex:complex:80 illustrate the use of we ‘then’ in connecting independent clause s.

In Ulwa, there is no overt morphological marker for relative clauses -- that is, there are no relative pronoun s or relativizer s, nor are there resumptive pronoun s or other means of overtly coreferencing an argument in the relative clause with an argument in the matrix clause. A relative clause immediately precedes the head noun of the matrix clause, and the verb in the relative clause is marked for TAM as any finite verb in a clause would be. Thus I analyze relative clauses as prenominal dependent clause s with unexpressed subjects. Relative clauses in Ulwa may thus be said to employ the gap strategy, since the syntactic spot where the head noun of the antecedent clause should be found in the relative clause (i.e., before the verb) is empty (i.e., there is no overt phonological form). The basic structure of Ulwa relative clauses is outlined in ex:complex:80a.

As an argument in the matrix clause, the head noun of the matrix clause may fulfill any grammatical relation -- that is, it may be a subject, an object, or an oblique. The noun phrase in the relative clause that refers to this antecedent, however, must be the grammatical subject of the clause. Thus, viewed crosslinguistically in terms of the hierarchy accessibility hierarchy ( ), Ulwa has a rather limited set of grammatically possible relative clause constructions, as only subjects can be relativize d.

There are no correlative relative clause s in Ulwa, nor are there adjoined relative clause s (i.e., non-adjacent relative clause s). In an alternative analysis relative clauses in Ulwa may be considered head-internal relative clause head-internal, with the head being expressed as a full NP only within the relative clause, namely postverbally. A schematization of the head-internal analysis is given in ex:syntax:278 in sec:13.7. In this analysis, relative clauses would exhibit a different word order from that found in most Ulwa clauses: whereas the word order of pragmatic ally neutral active voice active clauses is S(O)V ( sec:11.1 ), the word order of relative clauses would be (O)VS. While this analysis seems typologically unusual, it perhaps has some support when considered alongside Ulwa’s passive constructions ( sec:13.7 ). However, it does not seem best to analyze the head as being internal, since it takes grammatical marking according to its role in the matrix clause, not according to what its role would be within the embedded clause. For example, we find the object marker ma= ‘ 3sg.obj ’ as opposed to the subject marker mï ‘ 3sg.subj ’ in sentences such as ex:complex:82. Thus, it seems best to me to analyze relative clauses, like other subordinate clauses, as maintaining canonical S(O)V order and employing a gap strategy.

Example ex:complex:81 consists of a simple intransitive sentence. The word order is the canonical SV.

Itom ngata mï nip. \\
itom ngata mï ni-p\\
father grand 3sg.subj die- pfv \\
`The old man died.’ [elicited]

Example ex:complex:82 shows how the sentence given in ex:complex:81 might appear in a relative clause. Here, itom ngata ‘old man’ is both the subject of the relative clause and the object of the matrix clause. The brackets in ex:complex:82 enclose the relative clause. Thus, sentence ex:complex:82 is considered to contain a noun-modifying clause, the verb nipe ‘died’ thus constituting the entire relative clause, with a gap for the subject occurring immediately before the verb.

Nï nipe itom ngata makamp. \\
nï [ni-p-e] itom ngata ma=kamb-p\\
1 sg [die- pfv-dep] father grand 3 sg.obj =shun- pfv \\
`I avoided the old man who died.’ [elicited]

Note also that the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’ is employed on the verb in the dependent relative clause ( sec:12.2.1 ). This lends further support to the idea that the structure in question is indeed a clause.

A relative clause can also serve as the subject of a matrix clause, as in ex:complex:83.

Nipe itom ngata mï ankam anma. \\
[ni-p-e] itom ngata mï ankam anma\\
[die- pfv - dep] father grand 3sg.subj person good\\
`The old man who died is a good person.’ [elicited]

Note that verb phrase s that consist of discontinuous elements (i.e., separable verb s, sec:9.2.1 ) will surround the relative clause if the relative clause is the object of the verb phrase ex:complex:84.

Ndï lïmndï nipe itom ngata mala.\\
ndï lïmndï [ni-p-e] itom ngata ma=ala \\
3 pl eye [die- pfv-dep] father grand 3 sg.obj =see\\
`They saw the old man who died.’ [elicited]

Finally, it may be shown that, in addition to subjects and objects, relative clauses may function as oblique argument s within matrix clause s, such as objects of postposition s, as in ex:complex:85.

Damnda mï nipe itom ngata maya i. \\
Damnda mï [ni-p-e] itom ngata ma=iya i\\
[name] 3 sg.subj [die- pfv-dep] father grand 3 sg.obj =toward go. pfv \\
`Damnda went to the old man who died.’ [elicited]

Just like intransitive clauses, transitive clauses may function as relative clauses. Example ex:complex:86 illustrates a simple transitive sentence. The word order is SOV.
summary:
Ulwa relative clauses have no overt relative pronouns, relativizers, or resumptive pronouns; instead, the relative clause immediately precedes the head noun and the missing argument position inside the clause is left as a gap. The author therefore analyzes them as prenominal dependent clauses with canonical S(O)V order, and notes that only subjects can be relativized, even though the head noun in the matrix clause may be a subject, object, or oblique.  

The passage also argues against a head-internal analysis, since the head noun receives grammatical marking according to its role in the matrix clause, not its role in the relative clause. Relative clauses can function as subjects, objects, or oblique arguments in the matrix clause, and the dependent verb in the relative clause bears the dependent marker -e.

[name] 3 sg.subj [pig 3 sg.obj =hit- pfv-dep] person 3 sg.obj =toward go. pfv \\
`Sinda went to the person who killed the pig.’ [elicited]

It is possible for oblique s to occur within the dependent relative clause s as well, whether they contain a transitive verb ex:complex:90 or an intransitive verb ex:complex:91.

Mï lïmndï mananï lamndu masape ankam mala.\\
mï lïmndï [ mana=nï lamndu ma=asa-p-e] ankam ma=ala\\
3 sg.subj eye [spear= obl pig 3 sg.obj =hit- pfv-dep] person 3 sg.obj =see\\
`She saw the man who stabbed the pig with the spear.’ [elicited]

Mï lïmndï ankam ul natane yana mala.\\
mï lïmndï [ ankam ul na-ta-n-e] yana ma=ala\\
3 sg.subj eye [person with detr- say -ipfv-dep] woman 3sg.obj =see\\
`She saw the woman who is talking with the man.’ [elicited]

Relative clauses occur rarely in discourse, and some speakers (especially the younger ones) probably never employ them. It could the case that these fairly complex syntactic structures are being lost as the language experiences grammatical attrition due to rapid replacement by Tok Pisin, a language that also -- for many speakers -- has no formal structures for relativization (see sec:15). Nevertheless, relative clauses do occasionally occur in the speech of some older speakers. Sentences ex:complex:92 through ex:complex:96 provide examples of relative clauses taken from texts.

Ndï manji mawl anmbiye ndï kwa masap. \\
ndï [ma-nji ma=ul an-mbï-i-e] ndï kwa ma=asa-p\\
3 pl [3 sg.obj-poss 3 sg.obj =with out-here-go. pfv-dep] 3 pl one 3 sg.obj =hit- pfv \\
`They killed one [of] his [brothers] who came along with him.’ [ulwa001_12:39]

Awal men pe nji ndïkuklïp. \\
awal [ma=in p-e] nji ndï=kuk-lï-p\\
yesterday [3 sg.obj =in be -dep] thing 3 pl =gather-put- pfv \\
`Yesterday [we] gathered [our] things that were in it [= the house].’ [ulwa042_05:16]

Anga mape numïni mï angani mape. \\
[anga ma=p-e] numïni mï angani ma=p-e\\
[side 3 sg.obj =be -dep] ditch 3sg.subj behind 3sg.obj =be -ipfv\\
`The ditch that is on the other side [of the river] is behind it.’ [ulwa014†]

Nul mbiye yanat mambi umbenam nay. \\
[nï=ul mbï-i-e] yanat ma-ambi umbenam na-i\\
[1 sg =with here-go. pfv-dep] daughter 3 sg.obj-top morning detr-go. pfv \\
`As for the daughter who came with me, she left this morning.’ [ulwa032_11:01]

Apa mbïpe itom inom min luke nji ulwap. \\
[apa mbï-p-e] itom inom min luke nji ulwa=p\\
[house here-be -dep] father mother 3du too thing nothing= cop \\
`The two home-owners have nothing either.’ (Literally ‘The father and mother who are in the house here, too, have no things.’) [ulwa032_20:01]

One possible reason for the relative rarity of these constructions in discourse is that fact that the pragmatic function of relative clauses can be assumed by nominalization ( sec:12.3.1 ), of which speakers tend to make more frequent use. Relative clauses may have their historical origins in nominalized verb phrase s. The formal distinction between the two is slight, basically hinging on the presence (in nominalization ) versus the absence (in relativization ) of a final /-n/. It is thus possible that in some examples the sound has simply been elide d. Still, based on speaker perceptions and on the careful pronunciations of elicited sentences, these are treated (at least synchronically) as two separate structures: nominalized verb phrase s and relative clauses. Furthermore, speakers may employ paratactic relative clause s as an alternative to this more complicated syntactic structure ( sec:12.3.2 ).

The passage shows that this language forms relative clauses with a dependent verb suffix -e, and these clauses can function as objects, subjects, or oblique arguments in the matrix clause. Relative clauses may also contain oblique phrases, and examples are given with both transitive and intransitive verbs.  

Relative clauses are said to be rare in discourse, especially among younger speakers, possibly because Tok Pisin is replacing the language and because nominalization often serves the same pragmatic function. Examples such as ex:nouns:18 and ex:nouns:19 in sec:3.2 illustrate how nominalized verb phrase s may function similarly to relative clauses. Often, these nominalized forms are used with locative verb s, as in ex:complex:97.

The verb phrase that is nominalized may consist of more than one verb ex:complex:98. Only the final verb receives the nominalizing morphology.

There is yet another means of accomplishing the pragmatic task of narrowing the reference of a noun. In addition to relative clauses ( sec:12.3 ) and nominalized verb phrase s ( sec:12.3.1 ), speakers of Ulwa can make use of paratactic relative clauses ( ). In these constructions, there is no formal morphological or syntactic relativization; rather, what could otherwise be expressed as matrix clause s with embedded clause embedded relative clauses are here expressed by sets of two paratactically juxtaposed clauses. Sentences ex:complex:100 through ex:complex:103 provide examples of paratactic relative clauses. The clauses in each example are enclosed in brackets.

Tembi la ndï wa mbïp. \\
[tembi ala] [ndï wa mbï-p]\\
[bad pl.dist] [3pl village here-be]\\
`Those people here in the village are bad.’ (Literally ‘Those [people] are bad; they are here in the village.’) [ulwa032_47:06]

Ango mundu kom un mat nïnan! \\
[ango mundu kom] [un ma=tï nï=na-n]\\
[ neg food neg] [2pl 3sg.obj =take 1sg =give- pfv] \\
`That’s not food you gave me!’ (Literally ‘Not food; you gave it to me.’) [ulwa020_02:04]

Anda nji tembi wa mï unaniya wa ine. \\
[anda nji tembi wa] [mï unan=iya wa i-n-e]\\
[ sg.dist thing bad just] [3 sg.subj 1 pl.incl =toward village come- pfv-dep] \\
`That’s a bad thing that’s come to our village.’ (Literally ‘That is a bad thing; it has come to us, to the village.’ There is no prosodic break between the clauses.) [ulwa037_20:57]

Numbu anma nda u mole. \\
[numbu anma anda] [u ma=lo-e]\\
[garamut good sg.dist] [2sg 3sg.obj =cut- ipfv] \\
`That’s a good garamut drum that you’re carving.’ (Literally ‘That is a good garamut; you are carving it.’) [ulwa009_02:08]

These paratactic relative clauses are, for some speakers, the exclusive means of creating relative-clause-like structures -- that is, they lack the formal relative clauses described in sec:12.3. It is possible that paratactic relative clauses are a relatively recent syntactic innovation, having emerged as the formal relative clause structures have become obscure to younger speakers (see sec:15).

summary: Ulwa uses paratactic relative clauses as another way to narrow the reference of a noun, alongside ordinary relative clauses and nominalized verb phrases. In these constructions, there is no overt morphological or syntactic relativization; instead, the intended meaning is expressed by two juxtaposed clauses that together function like a relative clause. For some speakers these are the only relative-clause-like structures, and they may be a recent innovation as older formal relative clauses have become obscure to younger speakers.

Whereas dependent-marked clauses do not participate in prototypical clause-chaining structures, there is one verb, tï- ‘take’, which does appear to behave as a medial verb, albeit in a very restricted way. It may occur as the first of two verbs within a series of two clauses, taking its own object argument, but lacking TAM marking, as in ex:complex:104.

Un ango ame tï inde.\\
un ango ame tï inda-e \\
2 pl neg basket take walk- ipfv \\
`You don’t carry baskets around.’ [ulwa014_34:31]

It is rare for tï- ‘take’ to occur with other medial verb s (if it itself may be considered to be a medial verb ); rather, such “clause chains” formed with tï- ‘take’ are generally restricted to this verb plus one verb in an immediately following final clause. Often, tï- ‘take’ is phonological ly reduced to [t] in such constructions. The verb is perhaps in the diachronic process of grammaticalizing to become a postposition. The most common medial-clause use of tï- ‘take’ is found in ‘giving’ constructions, which typically use na- ‘give’ as the verb in the final clause (see sec:11.3 for examples as well as further discussion on other possible “ ditransitive ” constructions in the language). It may also be used with a motion verb (typically inda- ‘walk’) as the final verb, giving the meaning ‘carry’, as in ex:complex:104, and further illustrated by ex:complex:105 and ex:complex:106.

Nï ul unji alum nïpat ngat indape.\\
nï u-lo un-nji alum nïpat nga=tï inda-p-e\\
1 sg from-go 2 sg-poss child giant sg.prox =take walk- pfv-dep \\
`I carried that giant daughter of yours around.’ [ulwa032_17:07]

Apïn ngïl tembi nji ngala ndï ndït inde.\\
apïn ngïn tembi nji ngala ndï ndï=tï inda-e \\
fire cloud bad thing pl.prox 3 pl 3 pl =take walk- ipfv \\
`These marijuana cigarettes -- they carry them around.’ The speaker here pronounces apïn ngïn `smoke’ with a final [l], presumably a speech error. (Literally ‘these bad smoke things’) [ulwa037_21:52]

The medial verb tï- ‘take’ can also be used with a motion verb (typically ma- i- ‘go’) as the final verb to give the meaning ‘bring’, as in examples ex:complex:107, ex:complex:108, and ex:complex:109.

Nï ndït i.\\
nï ndï=tï i \\
1 sg 3pl= take go. pfv \\
`I brought them.’ [ulwa014_12:06]

Nï upin mat anmbi mat manane.\\
nï upin ma=tï an-mbï-i ma=tï ma=na-n-e\\
1 sg crowned.pigeon 3 sg.obj =take out-here-go. pfv 3 sg.obj =take 3 sg.obj =give- pfv-dep \\
`I brought the crowned pigeon out here and gave it to her.’ [ulwa037_03:51]

Uma ndït li unde. \\
uma ndï=tï li unda-e \\
bone 3 pl =take down go- ipfv \\
`[She] would bring [their] bones down.’ [ulwa020_00:13]

If the goal argument (the location to which something is brought) is encoded, then it is typically done so as the argument of a subsequent clause -- that is, not within a chained clause, but rather within another final clause following the chained group of medial clause and final clause, as in ex:complex:110.

Ndït i Wopata may.\\
ndï=tï i Wopata ma=i \\
3 pl =take go. pfv [place] 3 sg.obj =go. pfv \\
`I brought them [= fish] to Wopata.’ (Literally ‘I brought them [and I] went to Wopata.’) [ulwa014_29:41]

When the goal is functioning rather more adverb ially, as in ex:complex:109 (i.e., li ‘down’) or in ex:complex:111 (i.e., wa ‘village’), then it may be included once within a clause chain consisting of a medial clause and a final clause.

Mat wa ita una malan! \\
ma=tï wa i-ta unan ma=la-n\\
3 sg.obj =take village go. pfv-cond 1pl.incl 3sg.obj= eat- imp \\
`If [we] bring it [= a crocodile] home, we’ll eat it!’ [ulwa038_04:29]

The recipient argument (the person to whom something is brought) can be encoded in a postpositional phrase, either with a direction al postposition such as iya ‘toward’, as in ex:complex:112 and ex:complex:113, or with a benefactive postposition such as ala ‘for’ ex:complex:114 or nap ‘for’ ex:complex:115.

Inga la mat aniya i.\\
inga ala ma=tï an= iya i\\
affine pl.dist 3 sg.obj =take 1 pl.excl= toward go. pfv \\
`[My] in-laws brought it to us.’ [ulwa037_36:56]

Ndïtï wiya mana.\\
ndï=tï u= iya ma-na\\
3 pl =take 2 sg =toward go- irr \\
`[They] would bring them to you.’ [ulwa014_36:45]

Mala numan kot i.\\
ma= ala numan ko=tï i\\
3 sg.obj =for husband indf =take go. pfv \\
`[They] brought a husband for her.’ [ulwa019_00:53]

Ndï ndinap ndït nïnap iye.\\
ndï ndï=ina-p ndï=tï nï= nap i-e\\
3 pl 3 pl =get- pfv 3 pl =take 1 sg =for go. pfv-dep \\
`They got them and brought them for me.’ [ulwa014_47:24]

summary:
The passage says that dependent-marked clauses generally do not take part in normal clause-chaining structures, but the verb *tï-* ‘take’ behaves in a limited medial-verb way. It usually appears as the first verb in a two-clause chain without TAM marking and is mainly used in constructions meaning ‘carry’ or ‘bring,’ often with final verbs like *inda-* ‘walk’ or *ma-* ‘go’.  

When *tï-* is used this way, the goal is typically expressed in a following clause or, if more adverbial, within the same clause chain, while recipients are marked in postpositional phrases such as directional or benefactive phrases. The text also suggests that *tï-* may be grammaticalizing diachronically into a postposition.

This chapter covers an assortment of syntactic constructions, organized rather more by functional concerns than by syntactically motivated principles. Thus this chapter explains how a speaker of Ulwa may accomplish certain communicative goals, such as formulating question s, issuing command s, negation negating propositions, and reporting on the speech of others.

syntax|)
summary: This chapter presents a range of syntactic constructions organized mainly by communicative function rather than by syntactic theory. It explains how speakers of Ulwa can formulate questions, issue commands, negate propositions, and report the speech of others.

wh- question

There are, as in most languages, two basic types of question s in Ulwa: polar question s (‘yes/no’ questions) ( sec:13.1.1 ) and content question s ( wh- questions) ( sec:13.1.2 ).

syntax|)
summary: Ulwa has two basic types of questions, as is typical in many languages: polar questions, which are yes/no questions, and content questions, which are wh-questions. These are discussed separately in the grammar in sections 13.1.1 and 13.1.2.

Polar questions in Ulwa are identical in form to their declarative counterparts. They are recognizable, however, through pragmatic factors and through phonology ( intonation ). First, context often makes it apparent that a question, rather than a statement, is being formed by the speaker. Second, polar questions are identifiable through a rising intonation. The questions presented in ex:syntax:1 through ex:syntax:4, if given the right context and said without a rising intonation, could all also function as statements.

Itom mï awal tembi wap. \\
itom mï awal tembi wap\\
father 3sg.subj yesterday bad be. pst \\
(a) ‘Was father sick yesterday?’

(b) ‘Father was sick yesterday.’ [elicited]

U namap. \\
u na-ama-p\\
2sg detr -eat- pfv \\
(a) ‘Have you eaten?’

(b) ‘You’ve already eaten.’ [elicited]

Inom mï amun ya ute. \\
inom mï amun ya uta-e\\
mother 3 sg.subj now coconut grind- ipfv \\
(a) ‘Is mother grinding coconut now?’

(b) ‘Mother is grinding coconut now.’ [elicited]

Alum mï ikali ya ndïsina. \\
alum mï i-kali ya ndï=si-na\\
child 3sg.subj hand-send coconut 3pl= push- irr \\
(a) ‘Can the child catch the coconuts?’

(b) ‘The child can catch the coconuts.’ [elicited]

Perhaps especially in leading question s, Ulwa can employ the interjection s a ‘eh?’ or e ‘eh?’ as a tag word at the end of the interrogative sentence. These forms are common also in Tok Pisin, which possibly played a role in their use in Ulwa. These tag word s serve as an additional means of indicating that a sentence is a question, as seen in ex:syntax:5, ex:syntax:6, and ex:syntax:7.

Alo un apa map a?\\
ala=o un apa ma=p a \\
pl.dist=voc 2 pl house 3 sg.obj =be interj \\
‘Hey, you all -- are you home?’ [ulwa018_01:37]

Ngun andin ngun mundu ngunas a?\\
ngun andin ngun mundu ngun=asa a \\
2 du du.dist 2 du hunger 2 du =hit interj \\
`You two, you two over there -- you’re hungry, yeah?’ [ulwa041_01:09]

U ango anmbï mbi e?\\
u ango an-mbï mbï-i e \\
2 sg neg out-here out-go. pfv interj \\
`You didn’t come out, eh?’ [ulwa040_00:06]

There are not many examples of these tag interjection s in my corpus. Although examples ex:syntax:5 through ex:syntax:7 might suggest a contrast in polarity between the interjection s a ‘eh?’ and e ‘eh?’, I do not suspect that such a contrast exists.

Polar questions may be answered with full sentences, with paralinguistic gesture s, with general-purpose exclamation exclamatory interjection s (such as m ‘mhm’), or with the designated response interjection s ‘yes’ or ‘no’. The word iyo ‘yes’ (with the alternate form iya ‘yeah’) is used for the affirmative, and the word ase ‘no’ (with the alternate form asa ‘nah’) is used for the negative. To disagree with a negative proposition in a question, a speaker may answer ‘yes’. Thus, for example, the answer to ex:syntax:7 is provided in ex:syntax:8.

Iya nï awal mbi lïmndï tawatïp ndale. \\
iya nï awal mbï-i lïmndï tawatïp ndï=ala-e\\
yes 1 sg yesterday here-go. pfv eye child 3pl =see- dep \\
`Yes, I came out yesterday and watched the children.’ [ulwa040_00:08]

Here the responder answers ‘yes’ to mean: ‘No, I did come out.’

Content questions in Ulwa rely on several different wh- words, which are presented in ex:syntax:9. For more on interrogative pronoun s, see sec:6.5. There are no interrogative verb s in Ulwa.

Interrogative word s

( ango (luwa) ) \= (how many?)
kwa \> ‘who? [ sg]’ \\
kuma \> ‘who? [ nsg]’ \\
kwanji \> ‘whose? [ sg]’ \\
kumanji \> ‘whose? [nsg]’ \\
angos \> ‘what?’\\
ango \> ‘which?’\\
ango (luwa) \> ‘where?’\\
ango tem \> ‘when?’\\
angwena \> ‘why?’\\
anjika \> ‘how many?’\\
anjikaka \> ‘how?’

The interrogative pronoun angos ‘what?’ is discussed in sec:6.5. Examples ex:syntax:10 and ex:syntax:11 demonstrate its use in texts.

A nïnji nungol ala angos landa? \\
a nï-nji nungol ala angos la-nda\\
ah 1 sg-poss child pl.dist what eat- irr \\
`Ah, what will my children eat?’ [ulwa014_64:56]

U angos natan? \\
u angos na-ta-n\\
2 sg what detr -say- ipfv \\
`What are you saying?’ [ulwa014†]

As mentioned in sec:8.3.2, the question word s angos ‘what?’ and ango ‘which?’ likely derive from the negation marker ango ‘ neg ’. This may suggest that content questions in general may derive from polar question s (e.g., a question like ‘what will my children eat?’ in ex:syntax:10 would have its origin in something like ‘will my children not eat?’). Similarly, interrogative pronoun s like kwa ‘who? [ sg] ’ and kuma ‘who? [ nsg] ’ are colexified with indefinite pronoun s. Thus, content questions such as the one in ex:syntax:13 may thus derive from polar question s (i.e., ‘who is carrying it?’ < ‘is someone carrying it?’).

Sentences ex:syntax:12 and ex:syntax:13 provide examples of kwa ‘who? [ sg ]’ (further discussed in sec:6.5 ). This form is often shortened to [ko]. Whereas the form kwa ‘who? [ sg ]’ refers to exactly one referent, the form kuma ‘who? [ nsg] ’ refers to two or more referents. Thus the number distinction made in the words meaning ‘who?’ (or ‘whose?’) is a binary distinction of singular versus non-singular, as opposed to the three-way contrast of singular, dual, and plural that runs throughout many other paradigms in the language.

Kwa tïki man tïnangana? \\
kwa tïki ma=n tïnanga-na\\
one again 3 sg.obj=obl arise- irr \\
`Who will get it [= the school] up again?’ [ulwa014_54:01]

Ko mat inde? \\
ko ma=tï inda-e\\
one 3 sg.obj =take walk- ipfv \\
`Who is carrying it around?’ [ulwa037_17:22]

wh-movement
summary:
Ulwa polar questions are formally identical to declaratives and are distinguished mainly by context and rising intonation; some questions may also end with the tag interjections *sa* or *e*. They can be answered with full sentences, gestures, exclamations, or the dedicated words *iyo/iya* ‘yes’ and *ase/asa* ‘no’, and *yes* may be used to agree with a negative proposition.  

Ulwa content questions use a range of wh-words and have no interrogative verbs. The passage notes that some question words may historically derive from negation or indefinite forms, and that *kwa* ‘who? [sg]’ versus *kuma* ‘who? [nsg]’ show a singular vs. non-singular distinction rather than the language’s usual singular/dual/plural contrast.

text:
As mentioned in sec:11.1, there is no so-called wh -movement in Ulwa; all content questions are asked in-situ -- that is, with the questioned element occurring in the same place where it would occur in an equivalent declarative sentence. Thus, kwa kuma ‘who?’ or angos ‘what?’ occur in the subject position when the questioned element is the subject of a clause, and they occur in the object position when the questioned element is an object. Likewise, kwanji kumanji ‘whose?’ occurs immediately before the possessed NP, just as would any possessive pronoun possessive pronominal marker. Thus, for example, in ex:syntax:14, the ‘who(m)?’ element occurs in the position typically held by objects.

U man ko lïp sina? \\
u ma=n ko lï-p si-na\\
2 sg 3 sg.obj=obl one put- pfv push- irr \\
`Whom will you blame?’ (Literally ‘Onto whom will you push with it?’) [ulwa014†]

In questions of countable quantity, the question word anjika ‘how many?’ appears after the noun phrase whose quantity is the topic of questioning. This could be either a subject or an object (or even an oblique phrase ). The word anjika ‘how many?’ is thus syntactically identical to any modifying adjective and -- in particular -- to numeral s, which immediately follow the enumerated NP. Its use is exemplified in ex:syntax:15 and ex:syntax:16.

Wambana anjika inim mo man? \\
wambana anjika inim ma=u ma-n\\
fish how.many water 3sg.obj =from go- ipfv \\
`How many fish are swimming?’ [elicited]

U wambana anjika tïn? \\
U wambana anjika tï-n\\
2sg fish how.many take- pfv \\
`How many fish did you catch?’ [elicited]

yes/no question

It should be noted that questions of non-countable quantity -- that is, questions about mass noun s (i.e., ‘how much?’) -- are not asked with anjika ‘how many?’. Rather, such interrogative s can only be formed as ‘yes/no’ questions, in which an inquiry is made whether the amount in question is ‘big’ or ‘little’, as seen in examples ex:syntax:17, ex:syntax:18, and ex:syntax:19.

U inim ambi amap? \\
u inim ambi ama-p\\
2 sg water big eat- pfv \\
`How much water did you drink?’ (Literally ‘Did you drink big [i.e., much] water?’) [elicited]

U inim ilum amap? \\
u inim ilum ama-p\\
2 sg water little eat- pfv \\
`How much water did you drink?’ (Literally ‘Did you drink little water?’) [elicited]

Nungol mï inim ambi ame? \\
nungol mï inim ambi ama-e\\
child 3sg.subj water big eat- ipfv \\
`How much water does the child drink?’ (Literally ‘Does the child drink big [i.e., much] water?’) [elicited]

Other question word s, such as anjikaka ‘how?’ and angwena ‘why?’ cannot serve as either subject or object of a predicate. Accordingly, they may be considered oblique s. Their position in a clause is thus akin to the positioning of adverb s -- that is, following the subject (when expressed) and preceding the entire verb phrase, including the object of the verb if the verb is transitive, as seen with the form anjikaka ‘how?’ in ex:syntax:20 and ex:syntax:21.

U anjikaka apa maytap? \\
u anjikaka apa ma=ita-p\\
2sg how house 3sg.obj= build- pfv \\
`How did you build the house?’ [elicited]

Alimban mï anjikaka lamndu masap? \\
Alimban mï anjikaka lamndu ma=asa-p\\
[name] 3sg.subj how pig 3sg.obj =hit- pfv \\
`How did Alimban kill the pig?’ [elicited]

This is the same position as other oblique s, such as postpositional phrase s, as illustrated by ex:syntax:22, or oblique -marked NPs, as illustrated by ex:syntax:23 ( sec:11.4 ).

Alimban mï tïn mol lamndu masap.\\
Alimban mï tïn ma=ul lamndu ma=asa-p\\
[name] 3sg.subj dog 3sg= with pig 3sg.obj =hit- pfv \\
`Alimban killed the pig with the dog.’ [elicited]

Although glossed in ex:syntax:20 and ex:syntax:21 as a monomorphemic word, anjikaka ‘how?’ is actually analyzable as anjika-ka ‘how.many-let’. It may even be analyzable further (cf. the possible etymology of anjika ‘how many?’ presented in ex:otherwc:148 in
sec:8.3.2 ). In other words, the final element is taken to be the perfective / imperfective form of the irregular verb ka- ‘let, leave, allow’ ( sec:9.2.3 ). Though perhaps having undergone a process of grammaticalization and now often analyzed simply as ‘how?’, the word’s verbal morphology is apparent in sentences such as ex:syntax:24 through ex:syntax:29, which reflect the irrealis form laka(na) ‘let [ irr ]’ of the verb.

Itom mï anjikalaka apa maytana? \\
itom mï anjika- la-ka apa ma=ita-na\\
father 3 sg.subj how.many- irr -let house 3sg.obj =build- irr \\

child 3 pl how.many- irr -let fish 3 pl =grind- irr \\
`How will the boys catch the fish?’ [elicited]

Nga kwa anjikalakana mane? \\
nga kwa anjika- la-ka-na ma-n-e\\
sg.prox one how.many- irr -let- irr go- ipfv-dep \\
`What is this one going to do?’ [ulwa001_05:53]

U manï anjikalakana?\\
u ma=nï anjika- la-ka-na \\
2 sg 3 sg.obj=obl how.many- irr- let- irr \\
`What will you do with it?’ [elicited]

itom mï mana ma=nï anjika- la-ka-na \\

2 sg 3 pl =take walk- cond 3 pl=obl how.many- irr -let- irr \\
`What will you do with them if you carry them around?’ [ulwa014_14:06]

Note that these irrealis -marked forms of this question word often convey a sense other than strictly ‘how?’, as examples ex:syntax:26 through ex:syntax:29, which are translated as ‘what will [someone] do?’. The irrealis examples notwithstanding, elsewhere throughout this grammar the form anjikaka ‘how?’ is glossed simply as ‘how?’, without being analyzed as being polymorphemic.

idiom
summary:
Ulwa content questions do not involve wh-movement; instead, questioned elements remain in the same syntactic position they would occupy in a declarative sentence. The language uses in-situ question words such as kwa kuma/angos for subjects or objects, kwanji kumanji for possessors, anjika ‘how many?’ after the noun phrase it modifies, and anjikaka/angwena as oblique-like forms placed like adverbs before the verb phrase.  

For non-countable quantity, Ulwa does not use anjika ‘how many?’ but forms yes/no questions contrasting ‘big’ and ‘little’ amounts. The word anjikaka ‘how?’ is also analyzed as historically polymorphemic, with a final element related to the verb ka- ‘let, leave, allow,’ and its irrealis forms can mean more like ‘what will [someone] do?’ than strictly ‘how?’.

text:
Idiomatically, anjika ‘how many?’ can also be used to ask a question somewhat akin to English ‘what happened to [someone]?’, or ‘what’s up with [someone]?’, as seen in ex:syntax:30.

Mï nan mat a u anjika?\\
mï na=n ma=ta a u anjika \\
3sg.subj talk= obl 3 sg.obj =say ay 2 sg how.many\\
‘He said to her: “Ay, what happened to you?”’ [ulwa001_15:48]

As mentioned in the discussion of interrogative pronoun s ( sec:6.5 ), questions of ‘which?’ are formed with ango ‘which?’, homophonous with the negative marker and likely derived from it. The two differ, however, in terms of syntactic position: whereas the negative marker typically follows the grammatical subject, the question word ‘which?’ precedes the NP it modifies (whether subject, object, or oblique ). Sentences ex:syntax:31, ex:syntax:32, and ex:syntax:33 provide additional examples of ango ‘which?’ as it is used in questions.

Ango wa makape wombïn? \\
ango wa maka=p-e wombïn\\
which village thus= cop-dep work\\
`Which village has work like this?’ [ulwa014_61:04]

U ango tïlwa u mbi? \\
u ango tïlwa u mbï-i\\
2 sg which road from here-go. pfv \\
`Along which road have you come here?’ [ulwa037_29:44]

Mbïpïta ango ini mawat pïta? \\
mbï-p-ta ango ini ma=wat p-ta\\
here-be -cond which ground 3 sg.obj =atop be -cond\\
`If [they] stay, which ground will they live on?’ [ulwa014_21:01]

The interrogative word angos ‘what?’ may be used in a similar fashion, modifying an NP (by preceding it) to ask ‘what kind of?’ or ‘what sort of?’, as in ex:syntax:34 and ex:syntax:35.

Ayndin nï angos na ukïna? \\
Ayndin nï angos na u=kï-na\\
[name] 1 sg what talk 2 sg =say- irr \\
`Ayndin, what should I say to you?’ (Literally ‘what talk?’) [ulwa037_00:01]

Una wandam mawap angos wombïn ninda? \\
unan wandam ma=wap angos wombïn=n ni-nda\\
1 pl.incl jungle 3 sg.obj =be. pst what work =obl act- irr \\
`[When] we are in the jungle, what [sort of] work will [we] do?’ [ulwa030_01:08]

Questions of time are asked by combining ango ‘which?’ with tem ‘time’, the latter word borrow ed from Tok Pisin taim ‘time, when’. Thus, quite transparently, temporal questions in Ulwa are rooted in a phrase meaning ‘which time?’. This phrase occurs in the canonical position for temporal adverb s (e.g., umbe ‘tomorrow’, amun ‘now’, etc.). In other words, ango tem ‘when?’ occurs immediately following the subject NP, as illustrated by ex:syntax:36, whose answer is given in ex:syntax:37.

Kapos mï ango tem lamndu masap? \\
Kapos mï ango tem lamndu ma=asa-p\\
[name] 3sg.subj which time pig 3sg.obj =hit- pfv \\
`When did Kapos kill the pig?’ ( tem < TP taim ‘time’) [elicited]

Kapos mï awal lamndu masap. \\
Kapos mï awal lamndu ma=asa-p\\
[name] 3sg.subj yesterday pig 3sg.obj= hit- pfv \\
`Kapos killed the pig yesterday.’ [elicited]

Sentence ex:syntax:38 and ex:syntax:39 provide additional examples of ango tem ‘when?’.

Itom mï ango tem utam mamap? \\
itom mï ango tem utam ma=ama-p\\
father 3sg.subj which time yam 3 sg.obj= eat- pfv \\
`When did father eat the yam?’ ( tem < TP taim ‘time’) [elicited]

Ango tem man ninda?\\
ango tem ma=n ni-nda\\
which time 3 sg.obj=obl act- irr \\
`When will [we] do it?’ ( tem < TP taim ‘time’) [ulwa031_01:27]

Alternatively, the phrase ango tem ‘which time?’ (i.e., ‘when?’) can take the oblique marker =n ‘ obl ’, thus forming a phase meaning ‘with which time?’ (i.e., ‘at which time?’), as in ex:syntax:40 and ex:syntax:41.

Kapos mï ango temnï lamndu masap? \\
Kapos mï ango tem=nï lamndu ma=asa-p\\
[name] 3sg.subj which time= obl pig 3sg.obj =hit- pfv \\
`When did Kapos kill the pig?’ ( tem < TP taim ‘time’) [elicited]

Ango temnï natana?\\
ango tem=nï na-ta-na\\
which time= obl detr -say- irr \\
`When will the meeting start?’ (Literally ‘[They] will at which time talk?’) ( tem < TP taim ‘time’) [elicited]

Spatial questions are also formed with the question word ango ‘which?’. Unlike temporal questions, however, ango ‘which?’ usually occurs without overtly modifying any noun, such as, for example, a word meaning ‘place’. That is, when taken alone, ango ‘which?’ is understood to mean ‘which location?’. Again, the spatial question word (or, possibly, abbreviated phrase) occurs in the same position as spatial modifiers in indicative clauses, as illustrated by the pair of examples ex:syntax:42 and ex:syntax:43.

Ankam mï ango i? \\
ankam mï ango i\\
person 3sg.subj which go. pfv \\
`Where did the person go?’ [elicited]

Ankam mï ngaya i. \\
ankam mï ngaya i\\
person 3sg.subj far go. pfv \\
`The person went far away.’ [elicited]

Motion verbs in Ulwa can be transitive, taking a goal argument as their direct object. Thus, in questions of ‘where to?’ or ‘whither?’, the question word ango ‘which?’ occurs in object position, as illustrated by the pair of examples ex:syntax:44 and ex:syntax:45.

Tangin mï ango i? \\
Tangin mï ango i\\
[name] 3sg.subj which go. pfv \\
`Where did Tangin go?’ [elicited]

Tangin mï wa may. \\
Tangin mï wa ma=i\\
[name] 3sg.subj village 3sg.obj= =go. pfv \\
`Tangin went to the village.’ [elicited]

As the object of the verb i ‘go. pfv ’, the noun wa ‘village’ can be indexed with the object marker ma= ‘ 3sg.obj ’ in ex:syntax:45. Critically, however, the object marker is not permitted in questions such as in ex:syntax:44. Its inclusion would render an interpretation of [ango] as ‘ neg ’ rather than as ‘which?’, as illustrated by ex:syntax:46.

Tangin mï ango may. \\
Tangin mï ango ma=i\\
[name] 3sg.subj neg 3sg.obj= go. pfv \\
(a) ‘Tangin did not go [there].’

(b) * ‘Where did Tangin go?’ [elicited]

The source of motion (i.e., origin ), on the other hand, can be indicated as the object of the postposition u ‘from’. Thus, in questions of ‘where from?’ or ‘whence?’, the question word ango ‘which?’ occurs as the object of the postposition u ‘from’, as seen in the pair of sentences ex:syntax:47 and ex:syntax:48.
summary: The passage explains how Ulwa uses **ango** ‘which?’ in several wh-questions: by itself it can mean ‘where?’ or be used in object position for ‘where to?’, while **ango tem** ‘which time?’ asks ‘when?’, with an optional oblique form **ango tem=nï**. It also notes that **angos** ‘what?’ can modify a noun to mean ‘what kind of?’, and that **anjika** ‘how many?’ can idiomatically mean something like ‘what happened to [someone]?’ or ‘what’s up with [someone]?’.

text:
U ango u mbi? \\
u ango u mbï-i\\
2sg which from here-go. pfv \\
`Where did you come from?’ [elicited]

Nï wandam u mbi. \\
nï wandam u mbï-i\\
1sg jungle from here-go. pfv \\
`I came from the jungle.’ [elicited]

Indications that ango ‘where?’ is elliptical for ‘which place?’ come from sentences such as ex:syntax:49, which contains the entire phrase ango luwa ‘which place?’. This lengthier method of asking ‘where?’, however, seems to be relatively uncommon.

Popo ndï un ango luwa pe.\\
popo ndï u=n ango luwa p-e\\
papaya 3 pl 2sg=obl which place be -ipfv\\
`Where are your papayas?’ (Literally ‘The papayas for you are at which place?’; popo < TP popo ‘papaya’) [ulwa014_07:36]

It may be noted that something of the negative sense of [ango] is perhaps preserved in example ex:syntax:49, since this is a rhetorical question meant to imply ‘you have no papayas’. Sentence ex:syntax:50 is another example in which the full phrase ango luwa ‘which place?’ occurs.

Ngun ango luwa wap?\\
ngun ango luwa wap\\
2 du which place be. pst \\
`Where were you?’ (Literally ‘You were at which place?’) [ulwa014_40:07]

As a modifying element, the ango ‘which?’ component of the abbreviated phrase ‘which place?’ can receive the copular enclitic or be followed by a locative verb, thereby serving as the predicate of its own clause, as in examples ex:syntax:51, ex:syntax:52, and ex:syntax:53.

Unan angop?\\
unan ango= p \\
1pl.incl which= cop \\
`Where are we?’ (Literally ‘We are [at] which [place]?’) [elicited]

U ango wap?\\
u ango wap \\
2sg which be. pst \\
`Where were you?’ [elicited]

Yanapi mï angopïna?\\
Yanapi mï ango= p-na \\
[name] 3sg.subj which= cop - irr \\
`Where will Yanapi be?’ [elicited]

Such clauses with verbalized ‘where?’ constructions can combine with other clauses, as in the question in ex:syntax:54.

Itom mï angope lamndu masap? \\
itom mï ango= p-e lamndu ma=asa-p\\
father 3sg.subj which= cop-dep pig 3sg.obj =hit- pfv \\
`Where did father kill the pig?’ Note that the verbalized ango ‘which?’ now functions as the linking element between two clauses, and accordingly receives both the copular enclitic =p ‘ cop ’ and the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’. (Literally something like ‘Father killed the pig, having been where?’) [elicited]

In a similar sentence, but with irrealis modal ity, the verb in each of the two clauses would be marked for irrealis or conditional mood ex:syntax:55.

Itom mï angopïta lamndu mawalinda? \\
itom mï ango= p-ta lamndu ma=wali-nda\\
father 3sg.subj which= cop - cond pig 3sg.obj =hit- irr \\
`Where will father kill the pig?’ (Literally ‘Father will kill the pig if [he] is where?’) [elicited]

Finally, ‘why’ questions are formed with the question word angwena ‘why?’. Although this is pronounced as a single word, it, too, likely derives from a phrase containing ango ‘which?’. The second element probably derives from na ‘talk, speech, story, message, thought, reason, language’, here having the sense of ‘reason’ (i.e., ‘[for] what reason?’). It is unclear why the form is pronounced as [angwena] as opposed to the expected †[angona], but the pronunciation may have changed due to a folk etymological association with ina ‘liver’, the seat of reasoning and emotion in the Ulwa conception of the human body. This form also appears in words such as inakawana- ‘think’ (see sec:9.2.1 for a proposed etymology). Laycock1971a field notes seem to indicate that the Yaul dialect form is angola ‘why?’ (Appendix sec:app.g ), thereby supporting the etymology of *ango ‘which?’ + *la ‘talk, reason’. The question s in ex:syntax:56 through ex:syntax:59 all contain angwena ‘why?’.

u angwena mbï-i\\
2sg why here-go. pfv \\
`Why did you come here?’ [elicited]

Itom mï angwena apa maytap? \\
itom mï angwena apa ma=ita-p\\
father 3 sg.subj why house 3 sg.obj =build- pfv \\
`Why did father build the house?’ [elicited]

mï ndï=n angwena ndï=tï inda-e\\
3 sg.subj 3 pl=obl why 3 pl =take walk- ipfv \\

summary: The passage argues that the common question word **ango ‘where?’** is likely elliptical for **ango luwa ‘which place?’**, though the longer form is relatively rare. It shows that the abbreviated form can be verbalized with copular or locative markers and used in larger clauses, while **angwena ‘why?’** is probably another compound based on **ango ‘which?’** plus a word meaning ‘reason/talk,’ possibly influenced by folk etymology and dialect variation.

Ulwa interrogative constructions have the productive ability to question multiple things simultaneously. Like English constructions such as who gave what to whom?, Ulwa constructions may inquire into multiple unknowns. An example of an Ulwa multiple- question construction is given in ex:syntax:60.

Ango luwa angos nji ndïlanda? \\
ango luwa angos nji ndï=la-nda\\
which place what thing 3 pl =eat- irr \\
`Where will [we] find something to eat?’ (Literally ‘[We] will eat what things [at] which place?’) [ulwa032_07:52]

Whereas English constructions like who gave what to whom? are mostly limited to situations in which it is assumed by the asker that each question component has a known referent, Ulwa multiple- question constructions are more flexible. Thus, for example, the two question s ‘where will we find food?’ and ‘what food will we find?’ may be combined into something like ‘where will we find what food?’, a sentence that would stretch the capacities of English multiple- question constructions. Examples ex:syntax:61, Admittedly, this sample sentence is not a prototypical multiple- question construction, since one of the two questioned elements is perhaps more properly considered an indefinite pronoun ( sec:6.4 ) as opposed to a wh- word. An alternative analysis of these multiple question s would be that these are sets of conjoined phrases with no overt conjunction (e.g., ‘at what place and what thing will we eat?’, ‘from which place and what thing can we two get for them?’, etc.). ex:syntax:62, and ex:syntax:63 illustrate more multiple- question constructions of this type.

U ango luwa angos matïn?\\
u ango luwa angos ma=tï-na\\
2 sg which place what 3 sg.obj =take- irr \\
`Where will you get something?’ [ulwa032_12:10]

Ngan ndandï ango luwa u angos tïna? \\
ngan ndï=andï ango luwa u angos tï-na\\
1 du.excl 3 pl =for which place from what take- irr \\
`From which place can we two get what for them?’ [ulwa032_19:58]

E ngusuwa ko angwena angos mundu wananda nat? \\
e ngusuwa ko angwena angos mundu wana-nda na-ta\\
ay poor just why what food cook- irr detr -say\\
`Ay, why did that poor thing say that he would cook whatever kind of food?’ (Literally ‘Why did the poor thing say that [he] would cook what food?’) [ulwa014_15:28]

Multiple question s can also be expressed in what are clearly multiple clauses. In ex:syntax:64, the conditional form -ta ‘ cond ’ marks the end of the first clause – that is, the protasis.

Ndï ango luwa wandam luta angos mundu malan? \\
ndï ango luwa wandam lo-ta angos mundu ma=la-n[da]\\
3 pl which place jungle go- cond what food 3 sg.obj =eat- irr \\

summary: Ulwa interrogative constructions can productively ask about multiple unknowns at once, similar to English questions like *who gave what to whom?*, but they are more flexible in allowing combinations such as “where will we find what food?” The passage notes that these forms may involve wh- words or an indefinite pronoun, and some analysts treat them as conjoined phrases without overt conjunction. Multiple questions can also appear across clauses, as in a conditional construction where one clause asks where they will go and the next asks what they will eat.

Questions often serve rhetorical purposes – that is, a speaker may not be actually requesting information, but rather may be making an argument (usually anticipating a negative response to the rhetorical question ). Example ex:syntax:65 illustrates how these may be made in Ulwa.

Ndï nji ndïwatlunda? \\
ndï nji ndï=wat-lo-nda\\
3 pl thing 3 pl= atop-cut- irr \\
`Will they clear the things?’ (The anticipated response is: ‘No, they will not.’) [ulwa014_53:02]

Rhetorical questions can be either polar question s or content question s. In polar rhetorical questions, the anticipated response is ‘no’; in content rhetorical questions, the anticipated response is ‘nothing’, ‘nowhere’, ‘nobody’, and so on. Example ex:syntax:66 contains first a polar question, and then a content question.

U ko wandam nji ndï ango luwa pe? U ko lïmndï ndala?\\
u ko wandam nji ndï ango luwa p-e u ko lïmndï ndï=ala\\
2 sg just jungle thing 3 pl which place be -dep 2sg just eye 3 pl =see\\
`Where are your jungle properties? Do you see them?’ [ulwa032_39:45]

The first question is literally ‘Your jungle things have which place?’ The anticipated response to it is: ‘No place’. The anticipated response to the second question is: ‘No’. Example ex:syntax:66 also illustrates the use of the modal adverb ko ‘just’, which may be used for emphasis in rhetorical questions.

summary: Questions can be used rhetorically, not to request information but to make an argument, often by expecting a negative answer. The passage notes that rhetorical questions in Ulwa may be either polar questions, which anticipate “no,” or content questions, which anticipate answers like “nothing,” “nowhere,” or “nobody.” It also shows that the modal adverb *ko* ‘just’ can be used for emphasis in such rhetorical questions.

Commands (or requests) are, generally, built around an imperative form of a verb ( sec:4.7 ). Imperative sentences may contain an expressed subject (typically a second person pronoun ), but, as in all sentence types, it is possible for the subject to be omitted. Examples ex:syntax:67 through ex:syntax:71 illustrate how second person pronoun s may be included in imperative sentences.

U nul man! \\
u nï=ul ma- n \\
2 sg 1 sg =with go- imp \\
`Go with me!’ (said to one person) [ulwa014_70:49]

Ngun naman! \\
ngun na-ma- n \\
2 du detr- go- imp \\
`Go!’ (said to two people) [ulwa001_09:46]

U ikali ngasin! \\
u i-kali nga=si- n \\
2 sg hand-send sg.prox =push- imp \\
`Hold this!’ (said to one person) [ulwa014_62:22]

U manji ndï nan makïn! \\
u ma-nji ndï na=n ma=kï- n \\
2 sg 3 sg.obj-poss 3 pl talk= obl 3 sg.obj =say- imp \\
`Tell her about her [sago palms]!’ (said to one person) [ulwa037_42:10]

Un maya wa nayn! \\
un ma=iya wa na-i- n \\
2 pl 3 sg.obj= toward village detr- come- imp \\
`Come home to her!’ (said to multiple people) [ulwa032_04:30]

In the imperative sentences shown in ex:syntax:72, ex:syntax:73, and ex:syntax:74, the second person subject is not expressed.

Amun man! \\
amun ma- n \\
now go- imp \\
`Go now!’ [elicited]

Unji mat indan! \\
u-nji ma=tï inda- n \\
2 sg-poss 3sg.obj= take walk- imp \\
`Carry your [child] around!’ [ulwa032_17:15]

Unji al kwa ndawa ka lowon! \\
u-nji al kwa anda-awa ka lo-wo- n \\
2 sg-poss net one sg.dist-int in irr- sleep- imp \\
`Sleep in that other mosquito net of yours!’ [ulwa011_01:42]

Third person imperative s (or jussive s) are also possible. These are no different from prototypical second person imperatives: they, too, contain a verb with the imperative suffix; the only difference is that the command is issued to a third person referent. Sentences ex:syntax:75, ex:syntax:76, and ex:syntax:77 are examples of third person imperative s in Ulwa.

Mï lan! \\
mï la- n \\
3sg.subj eat- imp \\
`Let him eat!’ [elicited]

Ndï wutïnin! \\
ndï wutï-ni- n \\
3pl leg-beat- imp \\
`Let them dance!’ [elicited]

Kalingana kalilïta mï man! \\
Kalingana kali-lï-ta mï ma- n \\
[name] send-put -cond 3 sg.subj go- imp \\
`Send Kalingana and he’ll go!’ (Literally ‘If [you] send Kalingana, let him go!’) [ulwa018_01:00]

First person imperative s (or hortative s) are possible as well, but only for non-singular inclusive forms. That is, at least one addressee must be included in the exhortation. Sentences ex:syntax:78, ex:syntax:79, and ex:syntax:80 are examples of first person imperative s in Ulwa.

Ngunan lan! \\
ngunan la- n \\
1 du.incl eat- imp \\
`Let’s eat!’ [elicited]

Unan ndïlan! \\
unan ndï=la- n \\
1 pl.incl 3pl =eat- imp \\
`Let’s eat them!’ [ulwa037_45:40]

Una man! \\
unan ma- n \\
1 pl.incl go- imp \\
`Let’s go!’ [ulwa014_66:54]

Indeed, the only referents that cannot be the subjects of imperative s are first person non- inclusive forms -- that is, first person singular, first person dual exclusive, and first person plural exclusive, as illustrated by the ungrammatical sentences ex:syntax:81 and ex:syntax:82. Similar constructions containing these pronominal forms, however, can be created with the irrealis suffix, as illustrated by sentences ex:syntax:83 and ex:syntax:84.

Nï lan! \\
nï la -n\\
1sg eat- imp \\
`Let me eat!’ [elicited]

An lan! \\
an la- n \\
1pl.excl eat- imp \\
`Let’s eat!’ [elicited]

Nï landa.\\
nï la- nda \\
1sg eat- irr \\
`I should eat.’ [elicited]

An landa.\\
an la- nda \\
1pl.excl eat- irr \\
`We should eat.’ [elicited]

The issue is, however, complicated, since, in casual speech, speakers commonly drop verbal endings, especially of irrealis verb forms. Thus, among the collected texts there are examples of irrealis clauses with, for example, 1 sg subjects that do appear to employ the imperative suffix -n ` imp ’, as in ex:syntax:85. I consider it more likely, however, that this alveolar nasal represents an abbreviated form of the irrealis suffix -na -nda ` irr ’.

Nï ma ndïn lun.\\
nï ma ndï=n lo- n[da] \\
1 sg go 3 pl=obl cut- irr \\
`I will go and plant them.’ [ulwa014_08:10]

Prohibition s (i.e., negative command s) are treated separately from true imperative s, not only since they require a special word, wana wanap ‘ proh’, but also because they do not permit the imperative suffix. Prohibition s may be issued to any referent, including first person non- inclusive forms (see sec:13.2.4 for examples).

summary: The passage explains that Ulwa commands are typically formed with a verb in the imperative suffix -n, and may optionally include an expressed second-person subject; it also shows that third-person imperatives and first-person inclusive hortatives are possible. First-person non-inclusive subjects are not allowed in true imperatives, though similar meanings can be expressed with the irrealis suffix, and prohibitions are separate because they use a special negative marker and do not take the imperative suffix.

The fact that the irrealis suffix can encode deontic modality ( sec:4.6 ) -- and, specifically, a directive mood -- means that it may function very much like an imperative suffix. Indeed, it is possible that the imperative suffix derives historically from the irrealis suffix -- that is, as an apocope apocopated version, which could be expected to occur in emphatic direct address.

Thus, some clauses containing irrealis verbs may be functionally equivalent to imperative s, and they may therefore be translated as such in English, as in the first translation of examples ex:syntax:86, ex:syntax:87, and ex:syntax:88.

U landa! \\
u la- nda \\
2 sg eat- irr \\
(a) ‘Eat!’

(b) ‘You must eat.’ [elicited]

Asa u mat nïnanda! \\
asa u ma=tï nï=na- nda \\
no 2 sg 3 sg.obj =take 1sg =give- irr \\
(a) ‘No, give it to me!’

(b) ‘No, you should give it to me.’ [ulwa032_28:41]

Kïkal misimisi ngawananda! \\
kïkal misimisi nga=wana- nda \\
ear story sg.prox =feel- irr \\
(a) ‘Listen to this story!’

(b) ‘[You] must/should listen to this story.’

(c) ‘Would that [you] were listening to this story!’ [elicited]

This use of the irrealis suffix also applies to third person imperative s ex:syntax:89 and first person imperative s, whether dual ex:syntax:90 or plural ex:syntax:91.

Some clauses with irrealis verbs are therefore translated as imperatives or related commands in English, and this use applies not only to second person forms but also to third person and first person imperative constructions.

Generally, no distinction is made between commands and requests -- that is, there is no common formulaic expression formulaic question form (as in, for example, English can you please pass the salt? ) to signal a gentle request as opposed to a stern command. Typically, intonation and context alone define an imperative form as serving the pragmatic functions of either command or request. There are, however, two other formal devices for indicating requests as opposed to commands: the adverb kop ‘please’ and the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’ ( sec:13.2.3 ). Since these devices are softer than commands made with only the imperative verb form, they may be considered akin to requests.

The modal adverb kop ‘please’ ( sec:8.2.5 ) may be used to soften a command, as seen in sentences ex:syntax:92 and ex:syntax:93, which contain imperative verb forms ( sec:4.7 ).

summary: In this language, commands and requests are generally not formally distinguished: the same imperative form is usually interpreted as either one depending on intonation and context. However, requests can be softened by the modal adverb **kop** ‘please’ and by the conditional suffix **-ta**, which make the utterance less forceful than a plain command.

Another method of softening a command is using a conditional verb form – that is, one with the ending -ta ‘ cond ’ ( sec:4.12, sec:13.5 ), as illustrated by ex:syntax:94.

Nï umbe Supam ul mata mï maya ata mana. \\
nï umbe Supam ul ma- ta mï ma=iya ata ma-na\\
1sg tomorrow [name] with go- cond 3 sg.subj 3sg.obj =toward up go- irr \\
`I’ll go with Supam tomorrow and she’ll climb it [= a tree].’ [ulwa001_01:14]

In the story from which sentence ex:syntax:94 is taken, a mother is addressing her children, including Supam. While the literal meaning of the first clause is ‘if I go with Supam …’, it has the pragmatic value of ‘Supam, you shall go with me …!’ This imperative use of a typically dependent conditional clause may thus be taken as an example of insubordination. Further examples of conditional sentence s functioning as softened commands are given in ex:syntax:95, ex:syntax:96, and ex:syntax:97.

Nïlakata nï mawl malanda! \\
nï=la-ka- ta nï ma=ul ma=la-nda\\
1sg = irr- let- cond 1sg 3 sg.obj =with 3 sg.obj =eat- irr \\
`Let me eat with him!’ (Literally ‘If [you] let me, I will eat with him.’) [ulwa001_06:11]

Yena ngalat ndïnata ndï ndul lowope lunda! \\

`Give them these women, and they, having slept with them, will go!’ (Literally ‘If [you] give them these women, they, having slept with them, will go.’) [ulwa002_06:04]

Kwa nïnji mol niya wa ita nï ko lïmndï mandïn. \\
kwa nï-nji ma=ul nï=iya wa i- ta nï ko lïmndï ma=andï-na\\

`If [you] come home to me with my [cousin], I will see her.’ (i.e., ‘Please bring my cousin to me so that I can see her!’) [ulwa037_46:36]

The conditional form may also be used with first person commands (i.e., exhortation s, sec:13.2 ). Often, only the protasis (marked with the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’) is expressed, leaving the apodosis only implied, as in ex:syntax:98.

Unan na kali wa alan lïta! \\
unan na kali wa ala=n lï- ta \\
1 pl.incl talk send village pl.dist=obl put -cond\\
`Let’s send a message to those villages!’ (Literally ‘If we send a message to those villages …’) [ulwa001_15:22]

The modal adverb kop ‘please’ may be used in conjunction with the conditional verb form ex:syntax:99.

Kop ma wa na ndïtata mata! \\
kop ma wa na ndï=ta- ta ma-ta\\
please go just talk 3 pl =say- cond go- cond \\
`Please, just go and tell stories!’ (Literally ‘If [you] please just go and say the talks, [it] will go.’) [ulwa014†]

The form kop ‘please’ may be shortened to [ko], as in ex:syntax:100 and ex:syntax:101.

summary: The passage explains that the conditional suffix **-ta** can be used to soften commands, often with a literal meaning like “if I/you …” but a pragmatic force of a request or order. In some cases, the conditional clause stands alone with the apodosis left unspoken, especially in first-person exhortations, and it can be combined with the modal adverb **kop** ‘please’ (or shortened **ko**) to make requests even more polite.

Negative commands are formed with the prohibitive marker wana ‘proh ’ or wanap ‘proh ’, which occurs along with an irrealis verb form (and not with an imperative verb form, sec:8.3.1 ). The prohibitive marker occurs in the same position as the standard negator ango ‘neg ’, which is used to negate, for example, declarative statements. In other words, the prohibitive marker follows the subject and precedes the verb phrase, including any expressed object in transitive clauses. As in positive commands, it is common for the second person subject of negative commands to be omitted, as in ex:syntax:102 and ex:syntax:103.

Wana nunu nji tï ip lïp mana! \\
wana nunu nji tï ip lï-p ma-na\\
proh every thing take nose put- pfv go- irr \\
`Don’t go destroying everything!’ (Literally ‘Don’t go, having put nose to everything!’) [ulwa014†]

Angani i wanap makape na! \\
angani i wanap maka=p-e na\\
behind go. pfv proh thus= cop-dep talk\\
`Later, when [you] have come, do not [make] talk like this!’ [ulwa014†]

Prohibitions, however, are not limited to second person forms, but may apply to any person or number, as seen in examples ex:syntax:104 through ex:syntax:109.

(U) wana nuwalinda! \\
(u) wana nï=wali-nda\\
( 2sg) proh 1sg= hit- irr \\
`Don’t hit me!’ (commanded to one person) [elicited]

(Un) wana nïnji utam malanda! \\
(un) wana nï-nji utam ma=la-nda\\
( 2pl) proh 1sg-poss yam 3sg.obj= eat- irr \\
`Don’t eat my yam!’ (commanded to more than two people) [elicited]

Mï wana landa! \\
mï wana la-nda\\
3sg.subj proh eat- irr \\
`Don’t let him eat!’ [elicited]

Unan wana mana! \\
unan wana ma-na\\
1pl.incl proh go- irr \\
`Let’s not go!’ [elicited]

An wana nakïna! \\
an wana na-kï-na\\
1pl.excl proh detr- say- irr \\
`We shouldn’t talk.’ [elicited]

Nï wana mana! \\
nï wana ma-na\\
1sg proh go- irr \\
`I shouldn’t go.’ [elicited]

Prohibitions may include the speculative suffix -t ‘ spec ’ on the irrealis verb form ( sec:4.11 ), as in examples ex:syntax:110 through ex:syntax:115.

Tarambi wana apka nïklop ma ngaya manat!\\
Tarambi wana apka nï=klop ma ngaya ma-na- t \\
[name] proh very 1 sg =cross go far go- irr-spec \\
`Tarambi, don’t go completely bypass me and go far away!’ [ulwa014†]

Wana ndïwalindat!\\
wana ndï=wali-nda- t \\
proh 3 pl =hit- irr-spec \\
`Don’t shoot them!’ [ulwa037_47:35]

Wanap mbïpïnate!\\
wanap mbï-p-na- t -e\\
proh here-be- irr-spec-dep \\
`Don’t stay here!’ [ulwa001_01:40]

Wana ata ma Kambaramba manat!\\
wana ata ma Kambaramba ma-na- t \\
proh up go [place] go- irr-spec \\
`Don’t go up to Kambaramba [village]!’ [ulwa014†]

Inim wana malakanat ko man ambi ndalan!\\
inim wana ma=la-ka-na- t ko ma=n ambi anda=la-n\\
water proh 3 sg.obj = irr -let- irr-spec just 3 sg.obj=obl big sg.dist =eat- imp \\
`Water -- don’t avoid it; drink a lot of it!’ [ulwa014†]

Wana imba pïta niya mbundanat!\\
wana imba p-ta nï=iya mbï-unda-na- t \\
proh night be -cond 1 sg =toward here-go- irr-spec \\
`Don’t come around here to me at night!’ (Literally ‘Don’t, when it is night, come around here to me!’) [ulwa014_14:22]

Example ex:syntax:115 also illustrates the use of the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’ ( sec:4.12 ). Although here it is used to show an actual condition (along with the speculative suffix on the final irrealis -marked verb), it may also be used idiom atically in prohibitions, presumably to present an implied apodosis (i.e., ‘or else …!’), as in ex:syntax:116 and ex:syntax:117.

Wana mapta! \\
wana ma=p- ta \\
proh 3sg.obj =be -cond\\
`Don’t live there!’ [ulwa014†]

Wana mbundata inim lata makapta! \\
wana mbï-unda -ta inim la-ta maka=p- ta \\
proh here-go- cond water eat -cond thus= cop-cond \\
`Don’t come around here and drink beer like that!’ [ulwa014†]

The prohibitive marker wana wanap ‘proh ’ probably originated as the verb wana- ‘hear’, likely originally occurring sentence-finally, but later being reanalyzed as a negative marker (as opposed to a verb) and thus migrating to the canonical sentence position for negator s. See for discussion of a similar grammaticalization process in Pondi.

summary: Negative commands, or prohibitions, are formed with the marker *wana* or *wanap*, which occurs with an irrealis verb form rather than an imperative form and occupies the same position as the ordinary negator *ango*. The second-person subject is often omitted, but prohibitions can also apply to other persons or numbers, and the verb may additionally take the speculative suffix *-t* and sometimes the conditional suffix *-ta*. The passage also suggests that *wana/wanap* originated as the verb *wana-* ‘hear’ and was later reanalyzed as a negative marker.

This section concerns sentences that exhibit negative polarity. There is no verbal morphology in Ulwa used to indicate polarity, whether positive or negative. Although sentences with negative polarity contain propositions concerning events or states that are contrary to perceived reality, they need not be marked as being irrealis through verbal morphology. Indeed, negative sentences may reflect the same basic three-way TAM distinction that occurs in positive sentences ( sec:4.2 ). The marking of negative sentences can differ depending on the type of predication: verbal ( sec:13.3.1 ) or non-verbal non-verbal predication ( sec:13.3.2 ).

summary: Ulwa has no verbal morphology specifically for indicating positive or negative polarity, and negative sentences are not required to be marked as irrealis. Even though negative clauses express propositions contrary to perceived reality, they can still show the same basic three-way TAM distinction found in positive sentences. The way negation is marked depends on whether the predication is verbal or non-verbal.
