Negative declarative sentences in Ulwa are typically readily identifiable by the negator word ango ‘ neg’ (‘no, not’), which comes immediately after the subject NP (or, potentially, after other postnominal modifying elements, such as temporal adverb s). Only when a subject NP is omitted can the negator occur clause-initially. Examples ex:syntax:118 and ex:syntax:119 illustrate the variable ordering of ango ‘ neg ’ with other adverb ial-like words.

Kolpe mï amun ango apa mayte. \\
Kolpe mï amun ango apa ma=ita-e\\
[name] 3sg.subj now neg house 3sg.obj =build- ipfv \\
`Kolpe is not building the house now.’ [elicited]

Kolpe mï ango amun apa mayte. \\
Kolpe mï ango amun apa ma=ita-e\\
[name] 3sg.subj neg now house 3sg.obj =build- ipfv \\
`Kolpe is not building the house now.’ [elicited]

Sentences ex:syntax:120 through ex:syntax:135 provide examples of negative constructions in Ulwa, all of which use the form ango ‘ neg ’. Many of these would be translated in English (or many other languages) variously (e.g., with words such as ‘no one’, ‘not … anything’, ‘nothing’, etc.). Where relevant, parallel positive - polarity sentences are provided to illustrate contrasts.

Constructions that negate non-verbal predicate s occasionally work the same as those that negate verbal predicate s -- that is, non-verbal negation may be expressed simply by means of the negator ango ‘ neg ’ (see sec:10.2 for non-verbal predication ). Both classificatory predication classificatory ex:syntax:136 and possessive predication possessive ex:syntax:137 predication can be expressed with zero copula. In both of these examples, negation is accomplished by means of ango ‘ neg ’ alone.

Kolpe mï ango yana. \\
Kolpe mï ango yana\\
[name] 3sg.subj neg woman\\
`Kolpe is not a woman.’ [elicited]

Nambi ango wandam ambi. \\
nï-ambi ango wandam ambi\\
1 sg-top neg jungle big\\
`As for me, I don’t have a big garden.’ [ulwa037_50:05]

Both attributive predication attributive ex:syntax:138 and classificatory predication classificatory ex:syntax:139 predication can, alternatively, be expressed with the copular enclitic =p ‘ cop ’. Here, too, negation is marked by ango ‘ neg’.

Ango anmap. \\
ango anma=p\\
neg good= cop \\
`[It] is not good.’ [ulwa001_09:18]

U Ango ulum ulwape. \\
u ango ulum ulwa=p-e\\
2 sg neg palm nothing= cop-dep \\
`You had no lack of sago palms.’ This sentence offers a nice example of litotes. [ulwa014_50:02]

More commonly, however, non-verbal negation is accomplished by means of a clause-final negator, either me ‘ neg’ or kom ‘ neg’ (sometimes kome ‘ neg ’, perhaps reflecting the dependent marker -e ‘ dep ’). Typically, the clause-final negator occurs in conjunction with the general negator ango ‘ neg’ in its typical post-subject clause position. Thus non-verbal negation in Ulwa is generally accomplished by means of a discontinuous structure (cf. French ne … pas ). The discontinuous structure ango … me ‘ neg ’ can be used to negate different kinds of non-verbal predication non-verbal predicate s: equative predication equative ex:syntax:140, attributive predication attributive ex:syntax:141, identificational predication identificational ex:syntax:142, existential predication existential ex:syntax:143, and classificatory predication classificatory ex:syntax:144; as well as different kinds of possessive predication, as in ex:syntax:145 and ex:syntax:146.

Nï ango unji itom me.\\
nï ango un-nji itom me \\
1 sg neg 2pl-poss father neg \\
‘I am not your father.’ [ulwa009_02:55]

Way ango ambi me.\\
way ango ambi me \\
turtle neg big neg \\
`The turtle wasn’t big.’ [ulwa006_00:02]

Ango Taw me.\\
ango Taw me \\
neg [place] neg \\
`[It] is not Taw.’ [ulwa014_25:06]

ipka ango wambana ambi me \\
before neg fish big neg \\
`Before, there weren’t any big fish.’ [ulwa014_69:19]

Ango nu luwa me.\\
ango nu luwa me \\
neg close place neg \\
`[It] was not a close place.’ [ulwa031_04:53]

Unanambi ango unanji amba me.\\
unan-ambi ango unan-nji amba me \\

ango u-nji me \\
neg 2 sg-poss neg \\

Sentence ex:syntax:147 offers an example of the discontinuous negator ango … me ‘ neg ’ being used with a nominalized verb phrase.

Mï ango nan nïkapen me.\\
mï ango na=n nï=kï-p-en me \\
3 sg.subj neg talk= obl 1sg =say- pfv-nmlz neg \\
`She didn’t reply to me.’ (Literally ‘She was not a having-spoken-to-me [person].’) [ulwa032_21:36]

It is interesting to note that there are also examples of clauses with nominalized verb phrase s in which ango ‘ neg ’ is used without any clause-final negator. The distinction between the presence and absence of such clause-final negator could reflect a possible difference in scope for the negator ango ‘ neg’: the presence of the clause-final negator me ‘ neg’ (or kom ‘ neg’ ) would thus suggest that the non-verbal predicate (resulting from a deverbalization deverbalized verb) is being negated; and the absence of the clause-final negator would suggest that the verb itself has been negated (before being deverbalized ). For example, ex:syntax:148 contains me ‘neg’, whereas ex:syntax:149 lacks it.

Nambi ango alanji wandam unden me.\\
nï-ambi ango ala-nji wandam unda- en me \\
1 sg-top neg pl.dist-poss jungle go- nmlz neg \\
`As for me, I’m not one to go around in other people’s jungles.’ [ulwa037_41:09]

Nambi ango ndiya mawnden.\\
nï-ambi ango ndï=iya ma=unda- en \\
1 sg-top neg 3 pl =toward 3 sg.obj =go- nmlz \\
`As for me, I don’t go around to them there.’ (Literally ‘As for me, I am not a to-them-there goer.’) [ulwa037_63:56]

Perhaps ex:syntax:148 could thus be translated as something like ‘I am not a going-around-in-other-people’s-jungles person’, whereas ex:syntax:149 could be translated as something like ‘I am a not-going-around-to-them-there person’. Negative scope is discussed further in sec:13.3.4. Alternatively, it is possible that the absence of clause-final negator s with nominalized verb phrase s simply reflects a more general optionality of such marking.

This discontinuous pattern negates a range of non-verbal predicates, including equative, attributive, identificational, existential, classificatory, and possessive clauses, and can also occur with nominalized verb phrases and relative clauses. The text notes that **me** and **kom** appear to be interchangeable, with no clear difference in meaning or use identified.

text:
Sometimes when non-verbal predication non-verbal predicate s are negated, the clause-final negator is used alone -- that is, the only negative element in the sentence is me ‘ neg’ or kom ‘ neg’, without ango ‘ neg’ being used at all. This may resemble Jespersen’s Cycle, a syntactic change grammatical change whereby a preverbal negative marker is replaced by a postverbal negative marker via a stage of two-part negation (again, as in French). However, if in fact different diachronic stages are represented by the presence or absence of preverbal or postverbal negator s, then their relative chronologies are not readily discernible. Discontinuous negation discontinuous negator is prevalent throughout the Keram family, although the morphology associated with it is perhaps not reconstructible. Given the rather rigid verb-final nature of these languages, the clause-final negator may have more likely emerged via grammaticalization of an older verb form. The particular history of this grammatical structure remains unknown. Example ex:syntax:163 illustrates the peculiar behavior of kalam ‘knowledge, knowledgeable’, a loan verb from Waran that has taken on nominal/adjectival adjective features ( sec:5.4 ). Here it is first verbalized with the copular enclitic =p ‘ cop’, before receiving the nominalizing suffix -en ‘ nmlz’. Finally, this nominalize d form is negated with the non-verbal negator me ‘ neg’.

Finally, it must be noted here that there are also instances in which me ‘ neg ’ is used alone without any apparent negative sense. Such uses seem more common with adjective s designating the greatness of someone or something, as in ex:syntax:165 and ex:syntax:166.

E an namndu nïpat me! \\

Perhaps sentences such as ex:syntax:165 and ex:syntax:166 should be taken to mean, for example, ‘not [merely] giant, [but rather] really, really giant’. Alternatively, they could perhaps be irony ironical statements.

The passage describes non-verbal negation in Keram languages, where clause-final negators like **me** and **kom/kome** can occur alone without the preverbal negator **ango**, sometimes resembling Jespersen’s Cycle. An interesting fact about Ulwa negation concerns the scope of the negator. The tendency in Ulwa is to place ango ‘ neg ’ within the first clause of multiclausal construction s, even when the scope of negation is smaller than the whole series of clauses. In other words, a subsequent clause or clausal element may be negated, without any negation implied concerning the clause in which ango ‘ neg ’ occurs, as illustrated in examples ex:syntax:168 through ex:syntax:170.

An ango apa mbïlop mbïwap. \\
an ango apa mbï-lo-p mbï-wap\\
1 pl.excl neg house here-go- pfv here-be. pst \\
`We came home, but didn’t stay.’ (Literally ‘We did not come home and stay.’) [ulwa032_33:21]

Ango ulum ale we wandam pen. \\
ango ulum ale-e we wandam p-en\\
neg palm scrape- dep sago jungle be -nmlz\\
`When [they] scrape sago palms, the sago starch is not [left behind] in the jungle.’ (Literally ‘[It is] not [the case that], having scraped sago palms, the sago starch is [left behind] in the jungle.’) [ulwa014_60:03]

Ango mat mïnjikan kïna: … \\
ango ma=tï mïnjika=n kï-na\\
neg 3sg.obj =take speech= obl say- irr \\
`Having gotten it, [they] wouldn’t say [the following]: …’ (Literally ‘[It is] not [the case that they] get it and would say [the following]: …’) [ulwa032_46:52]

This rather early placement of ango ‘ neg ’ occurs in conditional statements as well -- that is, the negator may occur within the protasis, even when the verbal element to be negated belongs in the apodosis. In each of the conditional statements in ex:syntax:171, ex:syntax:172, and ex:syntax:173, ango ‘ neg ’ occurs within the protasis.

Ango maka apwanam mapta inim landa. \\
ango maka apwanam ma=p-ta inim la-nda\\
neg thus side.of.house 3 sg.obj =be -cond water eat- irr \\
`As long as [she] is staying at the side of the house, [a recent mother] may not drink water.’ [ulwa014_36:12]

Ango mat ita nduwe malanda. \\
ango ma=tï i-ta ndï-we ma=la-nda\\
neg 3sg.obj =take go. pfv-cond 3pl-part.int 3sg.obj =eat- irr \\
`If [he] brings it, they will not eat it alone.’ [ulwa014_64:59]

Ango amunpïta ikali masinate. \\
ango amun=p-ta i-kali ma=si-na-t-e\\
neg now= cop-cond hand-send 3sg.obj =push- irr-spec-dep \\
`If [a baby] is still very young, [then fathers] will not hold it.’ [ulwa014_37:45]

In the two conditional prohibitive statements given in ex:syntax:174 and ex:syntax:175, the negative marker wana ‘ proh’ occurs in the protasis, even though the negation properly occurs in the apodosis.

It is relatively uncommon to answer ‘yes’ or ‘no’ to question s in Ulwa: rather, interlocutors tend to respond with full answers or paralinguistic gesture s (such as head movements) or interjection s (such as m ‘hm!’). It is nevertheless possible to use the word ase ‘no’ (sometimes realized as [asa]), whether as a response to a question, or as a simple denial (without any question necessarily having been posed). Sentences ex:syntax:176 through ex:syntax:179 provide examples of its use.

Ndï man nan nït ase.\\
ndï ma=n na=n nï=ta ase \\
3 pl 3 sg.obj=obl talk= obl 1sg= say no\\
`They told me “no”.’ [ulwa014_20:39]

Ase unan tïngïnpe. \\
ase unan tïngïn=p-e\\
no 1 pl.incl many= cop-dep\\
`No, we are many [now].’ [ulwa014_64:27]

Nï ango wa mbïpta ul wombïn ninda. Ase nï umbe un ka wandam namana. \\
nï ango wa mbï-p-ta u=ul wombïn=n ni-nda ase nï umbe u=n ka wandam na-ma-na\\
1 sg neg village here-be -cond 2sg= with work= obl act- irr no 1 sg tomorrow 2 sg=obl let jungle detr- go- irr \\
`I won’t stay in the village and work with you. No, tomorrow I’ll leave you and go to the jungle.’ [ulwa031_00:12]

Asa mï mïnjikan ngunankap: … \\
asa mï mïnjika=n ngunan=kï-p\\
no 3 sg.subj speech= obl 1 du.incl =say- pfv \\
`No, he said the following to us: …’ [ulwa014_23:38]

The word ulwa ‘nothing’, or a verbalized form ulwa=p ‘there is nothing’, may also be used as a negative response word, particularly when declining a request for a physical item. This may be compared with the Tok Pisin word nogat ‘no’ which derives from no gat ‘there is not [something/anything]’.

However, the word *ase* ‘no’ (also realized as *asa*) can be used as a response or as a standalone denial, and *ulwa* ‘nothing’ or *ulwa=p* ‘there is nothing’ may also serve as a negative response, especially when refusing a request for a physical object.

In Ulwa, direct discourse is constructed around at least two separate clauses: one containing the quoted utterance (typically the second clause) and one reporting who uttered it (typically the first clause). Direct discourse constructions are thus of the form: ‘speaker says/said: “[what that person says/said]”’, as in ex:syntax:179a.

Nï mat ndï amun up. \\
nï ma=ta ndï amun u-p\\
1 sg 3 sg.obj =say 3 pl now put- pfv \\
`I said: “They’ve only now planted (them).”’ (Literally ‘I said it...’) [ulwa014_10:29]

Direct discourse constructions are generally formed with one of two mostly synonymous verbs, either ta- ‘say’ or kï- ‘say’. The basic three-way TAM paradigms for these verbs (as well as the imperative and conditional forms) are presented in tab:syntax:13.

The verb ta- ‘say’ often occurs in a reduced ( defective ) form [t], although only when permitted by the phonotactics of the utterance in which it occurs. The verb ka- ‘say’, however, never occurs reduced as †[k] (indeed, word-final [k] is illicit, sec:2.1.1 ). The conditional form for kï- ‘say’ may be built alternatively from the perfective form kap ‘say [ pfv ]’, which exhibits vowel lowering ( sec:4.2 ). There is no attested conditional form of ta- ‘say’ built from its perfective form (i.e., †[tapta] does not occur).

summary: In Ulwa, direct discourse consists of at least two clauses: one reporting who spoke and one containing the quoted speech, typically following the reporting clause. This construction usually uses one of two near-synonymous verbs meaning ‘say,’ ta- or kï-, with ta- sometimes appearing in a reduced form [t], while kï- never reduces to [k]. The two verbs also differ in their conditional forms: kï- can form a conditional from kap ‘say [pfv],’ but no conditional formed from the perfective of ta- is attested.

It is, however, much more common for the verb of speaking to be transitive, taking as the object either the thing said or the person addressed. In examples ex:syntax:183 through ex:syntax:186, the object of the verb is the thing said. Note that the detransitivizing marker na- ‘detr’ is not present in these transitive clauses. The noun na ‘talk’, however, may occur.

Min na kuma tap.\\
min na kuma ta -p\\
3 du talk some say- pfv \\
`The two planned something.’ (Literally ‘The two said some talks.’) [ulwa014_03:37]

Nï ango na tïngïn tana.\\
nï ango na tïngïn ta -na\\
1 sg neg talk many say- irr \\
`I won’t tell many stories.’ [ulwa024_01:55]

Nï mol na ndïtane.\\
nï ma=ul na ndï= ta -n-e\\
1 sg 3 sg.obj =with talk 3 pl =say- ipfv-dep \\
`I was telling the stories with him.’ [ulwa014_40:12]

Ndï ndïnap atwana kïna.\\
ndï ndï=nap atwana kï -na\\
3 pl 3 pl= for question say- irr \\
`They will ask about them.’ [ulwa032_52:41]

Example ex:syntax:186 illustrates how reported question s can be expressed: namely, one uses the verb phrase ‘say a question’, where ‘question’ is the object of the verb of speaking.

Often, the verb of speaking takes as an object the thing said, without there being much semantic value to this object. That is, the object (always a bare 3sg object-marker clitic ) functions as an expletive, as in examples ex:syntax:187 through ex:syntax:191.

Nï mat a! \\
nï ma=ta a\\
1 sg 3sg.obj= say ah\\
`I said, “ah!”’ (Literally ‘I said it: “Ah!”’) [ulwa014_70:46]

Mï mate ankam alanji ala! \\
mï ma=ta -e ankam ala-nji ala\\
3 sg.subj 3sg.obj =say- dep person pl.dist-poss pl.dist \\
`He said it [that he would kill their pigs], but those are other people’s [pigs]!’ [ulwa014_27:04]

Mï ambïwana mat a nï ta tata tïn mol li ina mane. \\
mï ambï=wana ma=ta a nï ta tata tï-n ma=ul li i-na ma-n-e\\
3 sg.subj sg.refl= feel 3 sg.obj= say ah 1 sg already papa take- pfv 3 sg.obj =with down come- irr go- ipfv-dep \\
`It thought to itself and said: “Ah! I’m already able to get papa and come down with him.”’ [ulwa006_02:22]

Makape mï i. \\
ma=kï-p -e mï i\\
3 sg.obj =say- pfv-dep 3 sg.subj go. pfv \\
`Having spoken, he went.’ [ulwa039_00:28]

Nï lïmndï minlïpe mat: … \\
nï lïmndï min=lï-p-e ma=ta \\
1 sg eye 3 du =put- pfv-dep 3sg.obj =say\\
`I saw the two of them and said: …’ [ulwa014_42:15]

As illustrated by examples such as ex:syntax:191, among others, it is common for verbs of speaking (or at least the verb ta- ‘say’) to be defective -- that is, the verb stem is often left unmarked for TAM (and loses its stem -final vowel ), thus being pronounced as just [t]. This occurs especially in situations in which the object of speech is an expletive (or dummy ) object.

The role of the object of the transitive verb of speaking, however, need not be the thing spoken, but may instead be the person addressed, as in ex:syntax:192.

Nï nan mat nï ango makïke lunda. \\
nï na=n ma= ta nï ango ma=kïke lo-nda\\
1 sg talk= obl 3 sg.obj =say 1sg neg 3sg.obj= throw go- irr \\
`I told her: “I won’t sell it.”’ [ulwa042_01:46]

In such constructions, the word na ‘talk’ is often present before the object marker. This word may or may not be followed by the oblique marker =n ‘ obl ’. When this marker is present, then the construction is analyzed as a clause that consists of a transitive verb taking the person addressed as its direct object and an oblique phrase composed of the word na ‘talk’ plus the oblique marker (i.e., literally ‘tell [someone] with/by means of speech/talk’). In examples ex:syntax:193 through ex:syntax:199, the verbs ta- ‘say’ and kï- ‘say’ are used transitive ly, taking as an object the person addressed. The verb phrase follows the oblique phrase na=n ‘with talk’.

Nï nan ndït nga unji.\\
nï na=n ndï= ta nga un-nji\\
1 sg talk= obl 3 pl =say sg.prox 2pl-poss \\
`I said to them: “This is yours.”’ [ulwa014_06:44]

Nïnji yanat mï nan ndïkap: … \\
nï-nji yanat mï na=n ndï= kï-p \\
1 sg-poss daughter 3sg.subj talk= obl 3pl= say- pfv \\
`My daughter told them: …’ [ulwa032_22:49]

Nï ine Tarambi nan nït: …\\
nï i-n-e Tarambi na=n nï= ta \\
1sg come- pfv-dep [name] talk= obl 1 sg =say\\
`When I came, Tarambi told me: …’ [ulwa014†]

An nan amblakap: …\\
an na=n ambla= kï-p \\
1 pl.excl talk= obl pl.refl =say- pfv \\
`We said to each other: …’ [ulwa032_24:57]

Nï angos nan ukïn?\\
nï angos na=n u= kï -na\\
1 sg what talk= obl 2 sg =say- irr \\
`What should I tell you?’ [ulwa037_16:20]

Nan nungolke ngalakapta ndï kalampïn! \\
na=n nungolke ngala= kï-p -ta ndï kalam=p-na\\
talk= obl child pl.prox =say- pfv-cond 3pl knowledge= cop - irr \\
`Tell these children so that they’ll know!’ (Literally ‘If [you] tell these children with speech, they will know.’) [ulwa006_07:23]

Mï nan minte ngun naman!\\
mï na=n min= ta -e ngun na-ma-n\\
3 sg.subj talk= obl 3 du =say- dep 2du detr- go- imp \\
`He told the two of them: “Go!”’ [ulwa001_09:45]

Dependent marking dependent marker is not necessary in such reported speech constructions, although it may be possible, as in ex:syntax:199.

Since the word na ‘talk’ functions as the head noun of its own oblique phrase in these constructions, it is possible for it to be modified by an adjective ex:syntax:200.

The passage explains that verbs of speaking are often transitive in reported speech, either taking the thing said as their object or, less often, the person addressed. When the thing said is the object, the object is frequently a bare 3sg clitic with little semantic content, functioning as an expletive, and the verb stem may be defective by losing TAM marking.

When the person addressed is the object, the construction often includes na ‘talk’, sometimes with the oblique marker =n, so that the phrase can be analyzed as ‘tell [someone] with/by means of speech.’ In these reported-speech constructions, dependent marking is not required, and na ‘talk’ can itself be modified as the head of an oblique phrase.

When the oblique marker is absent, on the other hand, then the construction is analyzed as a compound verb compound verb phrase in which the nominal element occurs before the object (that is, they are separable verb constructions; see sec:9.2.1 ). In certain situations, however, it is impossible to tell whether the form [na] contains the enclitic =n ‘ obl ’ or not: if [na] is followed by a word that begins with /n-/ or /nd-/, then the sequence /nn/ -- if ever present -- would degeminate to [n]. In examples ex:syntax:201 through ex:syntax:206, the verbs ta- ‘say’ and kï- ‘say’ are used transitive ly, taking as an object the person addressed. Although the word na ‘talk’ is present, it does not take the oblique marker =n ` obl ’. Accordingly, these sentences are interpreted as containing compound verb phrase s, in which the nominal component is separate from the verb stem, occurring before the object.

Nï na makïna ase. \\
nï na ma= kï -na ase\\

The literal meaning of these constructions could be rendered as ‘tell [someone] with it’ (with ‘speech’ understood as the antecedent of ‘it’). A topic spoken about can be referred to as a phrase consisting of the topic, possession possessive marking, and the word na ‘talk’ (literally something like ‘X’s story’, where X can be any kind of referent: a person, thing, or concept). Various means of indicating possession can be used in such constructions: the possessive suffix -nji ‘ poss’ ex:syntax:212, the oblique enclitic =n ‘ obl’ ex:syntax:213, or a non-subject pronominal ex:syntax:214 or deictic ex:syntax:215 form.

Manji na latane.\\

`[We] were talking about her.’ (Literally ‘were saying those talks of her’) [ulwa037_00:19]

`When I was talking about the land, where were you, [people from] Wore?’ [ulwa014_22:43]

Nï amun maka lamndu wonmbi ma na tana manen.\\

1 sg now thus pig tusk 3 sg.obj talk say- irr go- ipfv-nmlz \\
`Now I’m thus going to tell the story of the boar tusk.’ [ulwa016_00:03]

Sande anda=n apa anda na ta-e\\
Sunday sg.dist=obl house sg.dist talk say- dep \\
`Last Sunday, [he] was talking about that church.’ ( Sande = TP) [ulwa014_26:07]

If there is a person addressed in such constructions, then this person typically occurs as the direct object of the verb of speaking and the topic is included as an oblique phrase marked by =n ‘ obl ’ following the word na ‘talk’, as in ex:syntax:216, ex:syntax:217, and ex:syntax:218. The possession possessive marker does not seem to be necessary.

Ndï isi nan antane.\\
ndï isi na=n an=ta-n-e\\
3 pl salt talk= obl 1 pl.excl =say- ipfv-dep \\
`They were asking us about salt.’ [ulwa032_27:51]

Ndunduma nan nïte nï mat: …\\

summary:
The passage describes a construction for reported speech or topics of conversation in which the topic is expressed as a phrase with the noun *na* ‘talk’ plus possessive marking, literally meaning something like “X’s story.” Possession can be marked in several ways, including the possessive suffix *-nji*, the oblique enclitic *=n*, or non-subject pronominal/deictic forms.

When a person is explicitly addressed, that person usually appears as the direct object of the verb of speaking, while the topic follows *na* as an oblique phrase marked by *=n*. In these cases, the possessive marker on the topic phrase is not required.

In casual speech, the verb of speaking is sometimes omitted, presumably implied by the word na ‘talk’ plus the oblique marker =n ‘ obl ’ (or by the expletive oblique phrase ma=n ‘with it’), as in ex:syntax:219 and ex:syntax:220.

Nï nan: … \\
nï na=n \\
1 sg talk= obl \\
`I said: …’ [ulwa014†]

Nï wolka man Carobim u nul man! \\
nï wolka ma=n Carobim u nï=ul ma-n\\
1 sg again 3 sg.obj=obl [name] 2 sg 1 sg =with go- imp \\
`I in turn [told] Carobim: “Go with me!”’ [ulwa014_70:48]

Sometimes speech is reported without any word of speaking at all to signal the quotation -- that is, there is neither the verb ta- ‘say’ or kï- ‘say’ nor the noun na ‘talk’ or an expletive in its place. Such quotations are often signaled by intonation or by paralinguistic sound s or paralinguistic gesture gestures. Often they follow a phrase of ‘seeing’, which may be used idiom atically to signal thought or reflection, as in ex:syntax:221 and ex:syntax:222.

Nï lïmndï ndala ungusuwata wombïn ambi nda.\\
nï lïmndï ndï=ala un-ngusuwata wombïn ambi anda\\
1 sg eye 3 pl =see 2 pl- poor work big sg.dist \\
`I saw them [and said:] “You poor things – that’s big work.”’ [ulwa014_59:50]

Itom ndï lïmndï anala a anji nungol ala ambi nape.\\
itom ndï lïmndï an=ala a an-nji nungol ala ambi na-p-e\\
father 3 pl eye 1pl.excl =see ah 1 pl.excl-poss child pl.dist big detr- be -dep\\
`[Our] fathers saw us [and said:] “Ah! Our sons have gotten big.”’ [ulwa013_04:54]

As illustrated by example ex:syntax:222, the exclamation a ‘ah!’ often signals speech as well ( sec:8.3.3 ). It typically belongs at the end of a prosodic unit, with the rest of the quoted speech continuing at the start of the subsequent prosodic unit.

When recounting stories, people may also omit a verb of speaking to make the action livelier ex:syntax:223.

Ne may tata! \\
na-i ma=i tata\\
detr- go. pfv 3sg.obj =go. pfv papa\\
`[He] went, went to him [and said:] “Papa!”’ [ulwa009_02:06]

Also, when conversations are recounted, the back-and-forth between two or more quoted speakers need not contain verbs of speaking between each turn, as in ex:syntax:224.

Nï atwana mat a un ango luwa? An ma we ndatïna le. Ande nol! \\
nï atwana ma=ta a un ango luwa an ma we anda=tï-na lo-e ande na-lo\\
1 sg question 3 sg.obj =say ah 2 pl which place 1 pl.excl go sago sg.dist =take- irr go- dep ok detr- go\\
`I asked her: “Ah! Where are you [going]?” [And she said:] “We’re going to get sago starch.” [And I said:] “All right, go!”’ [ulwa037_63:00]

The word mïnja ‘speech’ often appears in clauses introducing reported speech. Much like na ‘talk’, it may be used with an oblique marker along with a verb of speaking. It may serve a discourse- deictic function, pointing to what has just been reported or to what is about to be reported (i.e., ‘[someone] said this’), as in examples ex:syntax:225, ex:syntax:226, and ex:syntax:227.

Nï mïnjan ndït mambinalakan! \\

1 sg speech= obl 3 pl =say 3 sg.obj-top =detr-irr- let- imp \\
`I told them: “Leave it alone!”’ [ulwa037_07:09]

Ndï mïnjan ke: Mï unanï wa mbïpe.\\
ndï mïnja=n kï -e mï unan=nï wa mbï-p-e\\
3 pl speech= obl say- dep 3sg.subj 1pl.incl=obl village here-be -ipfv\\
`They’re saying this: “It’s here in the village with us.”’ [ulwa037_17:18]

Thomas mï na nïte nï mïnjan mat: …\\
Thomas mï na nï=ta-e nï mïnja=n ma= ta \\
[name] 3 sg.subj talk 1 sg =say- dep 1sg speech= obl 3 sg.obj =say\\
`When Thomas told me, I said to him: …’ [ulwa037_05:54]

Frequently, however, the word mïnja ‘speech’ occurs in a more elliptical construction, in which it takes oblique marking but where there is no expressed verb, as in ex:syntax:228 and ex:syntax:229.

The passage describes several ways reported speech can be introduced without an explicit verb of saying. In casual speech, the verb may be omitted and replaced by na ‘talk’ or the oblique phrase ma=n, and quotations can also appear with no speech verb at all, often signaled by intonation, gestures, or by a preceding phrase of ‘seeing’ used idiomatically for thought or reflection.

When speech is reported indirectly, two clauses are employed: a matrix clause containing the verb of speaking and a dependent clause containing the reported speech. The dependent clause, which consists of the indirect speech, is embedded within the matrix clause. Embedded dependent clause s of indirect discourse maintain Ulwa’s canonical S(O)V word order. As in any clause, the subject of the embedded clause may be omitted; this may be especially common when the subject of the embedded clause matches that of the matrix clause (e.g., ‘he i said that he i …’). In ex:syntax:232, the form [na] (which is not necessarily required in such constructions) is analyzed as the detransitivizing marker na- ‘ detr ’.

Alma mï Guren mï apa maytape natap.\\
Alma mï [Guren mï apa ma=ita-p-e] na- ta -p\\
[name] 3sg.subj [[name] 3 sg.subj house 3 sg.obj =build- pfv-dep] detr- say- pfv \\
`Alma said that Guren built the house.’ [elicited]

The verb in the embedded clause may be marked for irrealis mood if the reported statement refers to something that has not necessarily already transpired, as in ex:syntax:233 and ex:syntax:234.

Mï mol malanda nate. \\
mï [ma=ul ma=la- nda ] na-ta-e\\
3 sg.subj [3 sg.obj =with 3 sg.obj =eat- irr] detr- say- dep \\
`She said that [she] would eat with him.’ [ulwa001_06:05]

Ndï i mana nakap. \\
ndï i [ma- na ] na-kï-p\\
3 pl go. pfv [go- irr] detr- say- pfv \\
`They came and talked about going.’ [ulwa001_18:26]

Example ex:syntax:235 suggests that it may also be possible for the embedded clause of indirect discourse to be embedded within a noun phrase head ed by the word na ‘talk’. In this analysis, the literal rendering of this sentence would be something like ‘yesterday, Dorothy told me would-sell-it talk’.

Dorothy awal makïke lunda na nïte. \\
Dorothy awal [ma=kïke lo- nda na] nï=ta-e\\
[name] yesterday [3 sg.obj =throw go- irr talk] 1sg =say- dep \\
`Yesterday, Dorothy told me that [she] would sell it.’ [ulwa042_01:45]

A reflexive pronoun may be used within the embedded clause of speech to refer to the speaker, which is the subject of the matrix clause. See examples ex:pron:23, ex:pron:24, and ex:pron:25 in sec:6.3 for illustrations of how binding principles apply within indirect discourse. This only seems to occur when the pronoun referring to the speaker in the embedded clause has a role other than subject; otherwise, no pronoun is used at all. There is no designated logophoric pronoun in Ulwa.

Often a verb of speaking is used to refer to thinking (or other non-vocal events), as in examples ex:syntax:236, ex:syntax:237, and ex:syntax:238. This use seems to be more common with the verb kï- ‘say’ than with the verb ta- ‘say’, with which it is otherwise mostly synonymous. Note that there is no overt complementizer used in complements of verbs of thinking.

Alma mï Guren mï apa mayte nakap.\\
Alma mï [Guren mï apa ma=ita-e] na- kï-p \\
[name] 3 sg.subj [[name] 3 sg.subj house 3 sg.obj =build- dep] detr- say- pfv \\
`Alma thought that Guren was building the house.’ [elicited]

Nï anmbï ina nakap.\\
nï [an-mbï i-na] na- kï-p \\
1 sg [out-here come- irr] detr- say- pfv \\
`I thought about coming out here.’ (i.e., ‘I thought that [I] would come out here.’) [ulwa040_00:55]

Im maya ata mana nakap.\\
[im ma=iya ata ma-na] na- kï-p \\
[tree 3 sg.obj= toward up go- irr] detr- say- pfv \\
`[He] thought about going up a tree.’ (i.e., ‘[He] thought that [he] would go up a tree.’) [ulwa035_02:17]

In sentence ex:syntax:239, the verb of speaking kï- ‘say’ is assisted by the form wana- ‘feel’, creating a compound surrounding the embedded clause of indirect speech or thought, thus functioning as a discontinuous compound verb form ( sec:9.2.1 ).

Subjects in the embedded clause may be omitted, especially when they are the same as the matrix subject, and the embedded verb may take irrealis marking when the reported event is not yet realized. The passage also notes that speech verbs can report thoughts or other non-vocal events, that there is no overt complementizer in such complements, and that Ulwa lacks a dedicated logophoric pronoun.

A basic conditional statement in Ulwa consists of two clauses, the first (the protasis ) expressing the condition, and the second (the apodosis ) expressing the consequence. There are variations to this pattern, though, such as sentences that include more than one protasis, sentences that include more than one apodosis, and sentences in which the result clause is not a statement, but rather a question or a command. An example of a simple conditional sentence is given in ex:syntax:240.

Inim lopota nï mana. \\
inim lopo- ta nï ma-na\\
water rain- cond 1sg go- irr \\
`If it rains, I’ll go.’ [elicited]

In the prototypical conditional sentence, the verb in the protasis is marked with the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’, whether affixed to the full perfective form of the verb or to the verb stem ( sec:4.12 ). The verb in the apodosis is always marked as irrealis. This verb may additionally receive the suffix -ta ‘ cond ’, but only when built from the irrealis form of the verb. That is, the verb in the apodosis cannot be in any way perfective-marked or imperfective-marked. Thus, conditional sentences in Ulwa are taken always to be hypothetical condition hypothetical. For implicative condition s (or factual condition s), Ulwa does not employ the suffix -ta ‘ cond ’, and thus, on grammatical grounds, these are not taken to be conditional sentence s. Proclamations such as ‘if it rains, the ground gets wet’ would not be expressed as conditions in Ulwa; instead, a speaker would likely connect two clauses by subordinating one to the other and employing the dependent marker on the first clause (i.e., ‘[when] it rains, the ground gets wet’).

Conditional clauses in Ulwa can variously be translated in English with ‘if’, ‘when’, ‘whenever’, ‘once’, ‘lest’, ‘even if’, or ‘even though’, depending on the context and intended meaning of the utterance. Sentences ex:syntax:241, ex:syntax:242, and ex:syntax:243 are all translated with ‘if’. The protasis always precedes the apodosis in an Ulwa conditional sentence.

U atwana nïkïta nï utana. \\
u atwana nï=kï- ta nï u=ta-na\\
2 sg question 1 sg =say -cond 1sg 2sg =say- irr \\
`If you ask me, I’ll tell you.’ [elicited]

Itom mï mbita unan landa. \\
itom mï mbï-i- ta unan la-nda\\
father 3sg.subj here-go. pfv-cond 1 pl.incl eat- irr \\
`If father comes, we’ll eat.’ [elicited]

Mï anmapïta we ande ndï wolka mol nena. \\
mï anma=p- ta we ande ndï wolka ma=ul na-i-na\\
3 sg.subj good= cop-cond then ok 3pl again 3 sg.obj =with detr- come- irr \\
`If he is well, then, OK, they would come back with him.’ This example also illustrates how conditional sentence s may contain the subordinator we ‘then’ to connect the two clauses ( sec:12.2.7 ). [ulwa029_10:14]

The conditional sentence s given in ex:syntax:244, ex:syntax:245, and ex:syntax:246 are better translated with ‘when’.

Nï anganika ma maya mata ngan lowonda. \\
nï anganika ma ma=iya ma- ta ngan lo-wo-nda\\
1 sg after go 3 sg.obj =toward go- cond 1 du.excl irr- sleep- irr \\
`When I later go, go to her, we two will sleep.’ [ulwa032_18:45]

We mï akïnakapïta u mankapta mï anmapïna. \\
we mï akïnaka=p-ta u ma=nïkï-p- ta mï anma=p-na\\
sago 3 sg.subj young= cop - cond 2 sg 3 sg.obj =dig- pfv-cond 3 sg.subj good= cop - irr \\
`When the sago starch is fresh, [then] when you prepare it, it will be good.’ [ulwa014_60:23]

Ndïnkïta ndul wa undana mane. \\
ndï=nïkï- ta ndï=ul wa unda-na ma-n-e\\
3 pl =dig- irr-cond 3 pl =with village go- irr go- ipfv-dep \\
`When we have butchered them, we’re going to go home with them.’ [ulwa038_03:18]

As illustrated by ex:syntax:243, the conditional marker -ta ‘ cond ’ may follow the copular enclitic =p ‘ cop ’ ( sec:10.2 ). Sentence ex:syntax:247 also contains a copular enclitic, as well as a periphrastic ‘going’ verb in the apodosis in lieu of a simple irrealis verb.

Tembipïta ndï mo ina mane.\\
tembi=p- ta ndï ma=u i-na ma-n-e \\
bad= cop-cond 3pl 3sg.obj= from come- irr go- ipfv-dep \\
`Whenever [people] were sick, they were going to come from there.’ [ulwa029_09:50]

The use of periphrastic ‘going’ verbs in an apodosis is further illustrated by sentence ex:syntax:248, which also illustrates some of the complexity that is possible among conditional sentence s in Ulwa. It is not uncommon for either the protasis or the apodosis (or both) to be multiclausal. Whereas the protasis in ex:syntax:248 is monoclausal construction monoclausal (consisting of just a single verb, marked with the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’), the apodosis is multiclausal (consisting of first a perfective-marked verb and then a periphrastic construction that gives the entire multiclausal apodosis its irrealis mood ). Note that it is rare for the dependent-marker suffix to occur within conditional clauses, even within multiclausal apodosis apodoses or protasis protases -- that is, it does not occur anywhere except at the very end of the apodosis, as in ex:syntax:248. These clauses are thus considered to be coordinate structures ( sec:12.1 ). The perfective-marked verb in this example can thus be considered an irrealis perfective ( sec:4.9 ); and the periphrastic construction (technically an irrealis -marked verb plus an imperfective-marked verb) can thus be considered the requisite irrealis construction of the apodosis.

Nduwe unïn anmbïlumopta un nul ndinap ndulunda mane.\\
ndï=we un=ïn an-mbï-lumo-p-ta un nï=ul ndï=ina-p ndï=u-lo-nda ma-n-e \\
3 pl =cut 2 pl=obl out-here-put- pfv-cond 2pl 1sg= with 3 pl =get- pfv 3 pl =from-cut- irr go- ipfv-dep \\
`Once [I] have cut them [= tobacco leaves] out for you, you, having gotten them with me, are going to peel them.’ [ulwa042_03:44]

Like example ex:syntax:248, example ex:syntax:249 illustrates an irrealis perfective in the apodosis, here morphological ly clearer since the form of the verb is lamap ‘eat [ irr/pfv ]’ (cf. sec:4.9 ).

summary:
Ulwa conditional sentences typically consist of a protasis marked with the conditional suffix **-ta** and an apodosis marked **irrealis**; the protasis always precedes the apodosis. These conditionals are generally hypothetical rather than factual, and in some contexts the forms may be translated as “if,” “when,” “whenever,” or similar expressions depending on meaning.

The language allows variation such as multiple protases or apodoses, multiclausal clauses, and result clauses that are questions or commands. The text also notes that the conditional marker can follow a copular enclitic, that the apodosis may use periphrastic “going” constructions, and that dependent markers rarely appear inside conditional clauses except at the end of the apodosis.

U mat ita nï malamap wa mana.\\
u ma=tï i-ta nï ma=la-ama-p wa ma-na \\
2 sg 3 sg.obj =take go. pfv-cond 1sg 3 sg.obj = irr -eat- pfv village go- irr \\
`If you bring it, I’ll eat it and go home.’ [ulwa032_28:45]

In addition to exhibiting a multiclausal apodosis, sentence ex:syntax:249 exemplifies a protasis that contains two verbs. The first verb tï- ‘take’, however, is often defective and semantic ally closely connected to the following verb (often ma- i- ‘go’ or na- ‘give’), so this is perhaps not the clearest example of multiple clauses. In the conditional sentence s given in ex:syntax:250 and ex:syntax:251, the verb tï- ‘take’ is used both in the protasis and in the apodosis.

Olsem u ngalat nïnata nï nïnji ngalat unanda. \\
olsem u ngala= tï nï=na-ta nï nï-nji ngala= tï u=na-nda\\
thus 2sg pl.prox =take 1 sg =give- cond 1sg 1sg-poss pl.prox =take 2 sg =give- irr \\
`So if you give these to me, I’ll give mine to you.’ ( olsem = TP) [ulwa029_09:25]

Nï ko nji tï unata u ko nji tï nïnanda. \\
nï ko nji tï u=na-ta u ko nji tï nï=na-nda\\
1 sg just thing take 2 sg =give- cond 2sg just thing take 1 sg =give- irr \\
`If I give you something, you should give me something.’ [ulwa032_28:01]

In sentence ex:syntax:252, the verb tï- ‘take’ is indeed marked for TAM (here, perfective ).

Kalam ngatïn mol luta ngaya ndapïna. \\
kalam nga= tï-n ma=ul lo-ta ngaya anda=p-na\\
knowledge sg.prox =take- pfv 3 sg.obj =with go- cond far sg.dist =be- irr \\
`If he gets this knowledge and goes around with it, he will be far away.’ [ulwa014_73:58]

Notably, there is no conditional marking on the first verb in the protasis, even though it is not defective here. There are, however, instances in which multiple verbs in the protasis may be marked with the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’. In such sentences, it can be assumed that each verb represents a condition that must be met for the state or event in the apodosis to be or occur. Often these are best translated in English with a single clause, often with a single verb. The Ulwa sentence, however, contains multiple verbs in the protasis that may constitute either a single clause with multiple verb phrase s or a multiclausal protasis, as in ex:syntax:253. This sentence has two verbs marked with the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’ in the protasis (literally ‘if you are just here and if [you] eat food …’). Note that a simple irrealis stem of ama- ‘eat’ (i.e., [la-]) is employed, and not an irrealis perfective compound stem (i.e., not †/la-ama-/). This is because the hypothetical event in the protasis is not perfective – that is, the event need not have been completed for the situation in the apodosis to be true.

U kwa mapta mundu lata tamndï ko mundu ndïwalin. \\
u kwa ma=p- ta mundu la- ta tamndï ko mundu ndï=wali-n[da]\\
2 sg just 3 sg.obj =be -cond food eat -cond owner just hunger 3 pl =hit- irr \\
`If you just eat the food there, the owners will go hungry.’ [ulwa032_13:30]

Note, however, that verbs in the protasis clause or clauses should properly be marked as conditional only if the apodosis is in fact contingent on them. Thus, in sentence ex:syntax:254, the first verb (in fact a verbalized noun) receives no conditional suffix, but rather is dependent-marked.

Nungolkepe nï mandïm sata mï nït awi lïp nul wandam mana. \\
nungolke=p- e nï ma=andïm sa-ta mï nï=tï awi lï-p nï=ul wandam ma-na\\
child= cop-dep 1sg 3sg.obj= for cry -cond 3sg.subj 1sg= take shoulder put- pfv 1sg= with jungle go- irr \\
`When [I] was a child and I would cry for him [= my father], he would put me on his shoulder and go with me to the jungle.’ [ulwa033_01:47]

The protasis may have any number of conditional ly marked verbs, however. Sentence ex:syntax:255 contains three.

Mambilakata mankïta keka itïm nomopta una wo lolop wa pïn. \\
ma-ambi=la-ka- ta ma=nïkï- ta keka itïm na-lumo-p- ta unan wa lolop wa p-na\\
3 sg.obj-top = irr- let- cond 3sg.obj =dig- cond completely trash detr- put- pfv-cond 1pl.incl just just village be- irr \\
`If [we] abandon it, cut it [out], and throw [it] completely in the trash, [then] we will just stay [fine here] in the village.’ [ulwa037_07:19]

It is also possible for the conditional suffix to appear on one or more verbs in the apodosis. I suspect that this is a form of overextension, marking a clause as conditional simply because it is connected to a conditional clause. This may be seen in examples ex:syntax:256 and ex:syntax:257.

Nditapta kalam mï natïnangata.\\
ndï=ita-p- ta kalam mï na-tïnanga- ta \\
3 pl =build- pfv-cond knowledge 3 sg.subj detr -arise- cond \\
`When [they] build them [= school buildings], knowledge will increase.’ [ulwa014_26:35]

U mat nonal luwa malta mï lowop tembipïta.\\
u ma=tï nonal luwa ma=lï- ta mï lo-wo-p tembi=p- ta \\
2 sg 3sg.obj =take wind place 3 sg.obj =put- irr-cond 3 sg.subj irr -sleep- irr bad= cop-cond\\
`If you put it out in the open air, it will go bad overnight.’ [ulwa014_64:39]

Since clauses in the apodosis may also be marked with the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’, it is sometimes not entirely clear whether a clause belongs to the protasis or to the apodosis – that is, in instances in which a conditional sentence contains more than two clauses. Sentence ex:syntax:258 illustrates this possible ambiguity.

Mat ndïnata ndï mankïta malanda. \\
ma=tï ndï=na- ta ndï ma=nïkï- ta ma=la-nda\\
3 sg.obj =take 3 pl =give- cond 3 pl 3sg.obj= dig- cond 3sg =eat- irr \\
(a) ‘If [she] gives it to them, then they will prepare it and eat it.’

(b) ‘If [she] gives it to them, and if they prepare it, then [they] will eat it.’ [ulwa014_40:35]
summary: The passage describes Ulwa conditional constructions in which the protasis may contain multiple verbs, sometimes with only one or some verbs marked by the conditional suffix -ta. The verbs in the protasis can represent one condition or several separate conditions, and the same conditional marking may sometimes appear on verbs in the apodosis as well. In some cases, this creates ambiguity about how the clauses are grouped, especially when more than two clauses are involved.

text:
While many conditional sentence s have statements as apodosis apodoses, it is also possible for a conditional sentence to have a question or a command as the apodosis. In example ex:syntax:259, the apodosis takes the form of a question.

Nï mamata olsem ko kwa mbïpïta lïmndï ndutata ay nïkïta ndul landa? \\
nï ma=ma- ta olsem ko kwa mbï-p- ta lïmndï ndï=uta- ta ay nïkï- ta ndï=ul la-nda\\
1 sg 3 sg.obj =go- cond thus just one here-be -cond eye 3 pl =grind -cond sago dig- cond 3 pl =with eat- irr \\
`If I were to go there, who would stay here, watch after them, prepare sago, and eat with them?’ ( olsem = TP) [ulwa027_00:27]

Note the extensive use of conditional -marked verbs throughout example ex:syntax:259; indeed, every verb except the final irrealis verb in the apodosis exhibits the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’. Example ex:syntax:260 also has a question for its apodosis. Here, only one verb is marked with the suffix -ta ‘ cond ’.

Un nambï kenmbupïta un anjikaka imbamka lunda? \\
un nambï kenmbu=p- ta un anjikaka imbam-ka lo-nda\\
2 pl skin heavy= cop-cond 2 pl how run-let go- irr \\
`But if your body is heavy, how can you run around?’ [ulwa032_34:46]

It is possible for the question word to occur in the protasis even when (at least in the English translation) the interrogative would be expected to occur in the apodosis, as is the case in ex:syntax:261. This may have something to do with the placement and scope of the negator ango ‘ neg ’ in multiclausal construction s ( sec:13.3.3 ), since the question word s are etymologically related to ango ‘ neg ’.

Una ango luwa pïta inim malanda? \\
unan ango luwa p-ta inim ma=la-nda\\
1 pl.incl neg place be -cond water 3 sg.obj =eat- irr \\
`Where will we drink water?’ (Literally ‘We, if at which place, will drink water?’) [ulwa029_03:26]

It is also common for apodosis apodoses to take the form of imperative s. In fact, conditional constructions often serve the pragmatic function of softening a request or command ( sec:13.2 ), as seen in ex:syntax:262.

Un ma ya koya ata ma maynapta nditap ndïtïl nap ndït ita una ndutata inim uta ndïlan! \\
un ma ya ko=iya ata ma ma=ina-p- ta ndï=ita-p ndï=tïl na-p ndï=tï i- ta unan ndï=uta- ta inim u-ta ndï=la-n\\
2pl go coconut indf= toward up go 3 sg.obj =get- pfv-cond 3 pl =build- pfv 3pl =husk detr- be 3 pl =take go. pfv-cond 1 pl.incl 3pl= grind -cond water put -cond 3pl =eat- imp \\
`If you go, go up a coconut tree, and get it, [and] if [you] tie them [= the coconuts], husk them, and bring them, [then] we will grind them into water and eat them!’ [ulwa018_00:35]

Although presented as a series of conditions, the first clauses in sentence ex:syntax:262 are pragmatic ally tantamount to a request (i.e., ‘please get coconuts so that we may grind them and eat them’). Note also how the conditional form -ta ‘ cond ’ occurs in (what is translated here as) the apodosis. Another example of a conditional form used in a command is given in ex:syntax:263.

Un keka nul ndïn umop ulwap ndïwat itapta we un nol! \\
un keka nï=ul ndï=n lumo-p ulwa=p ndï=wat ita-p- ta we un na-lo\\
2 pl completely 1 sg =with 3 pl=obl put- pfv nothing= cop 3 pl =atop build- pfv-cond then 2 pl detr- go\\
`If you plant all of them [= the tobacco seedlings] with me and cover them [with leaves], then you [may] go!’ [ulwa040_01:15]

Sometimes, even without an imperative form, a conditional sentence can serve pragmatic ally as a request (see sec:13.2.3 ).

In some instances, the use of the conditional in imperative s may be seen as necessary to clarify a sequence of tasks that the speaker wishes the interlocutor to undertake, as in ex:syntax:264.

Inim ngan apïn ta we inim ngan ndanan! \\
inim nga=n apïn [lï]- ta we inim nga=n ndï=ana-n\\
water sg.prox=obl fire put- cond then water sg.prox=obl 3pl =scrub- imp \\
`Put this water on the fire, and then scrub with this water!’ [ulwa014_50:35]

Finally, in prohibition s, the conditional suffix -ta ‘ cond ’ may be employed without any following apodosis, as in ex:syntax:265. This may be considered a form of ellipsis. Alternatively, it could be the case that the suffix here is related to the speculative suffix -t ‘ spec ’ ( sec:4.11 ), which is also often used in negative command s.

Wanap nji ndïn umopta! \\
wanap nji ndï=n lumo-p- ta \\
proh thing 3 pl=obl put- pfv-cond \\
`Don’t grow things!’ [ulwa014_08:15]

See sec:13.2.4 and sec:13.3.2 for more on prohibition s.

summary: The passage shows that conditional sentences in this language do not always have statements as apodoses: the apodosis may also be a question or a command. It notes that conditional marking with -ta often appears throughout such clauses, including in questions, requests, imperatives, and even prohibitions, where the conditional can function pragmatically to soften or sequence commands, and in some cases may occur without an explicit apodosis.

Counterfactual sentences in Ulwa generally employ a verb with irrealis marking, as illustrated by ex:syntax:266.

Apïn kali malnda inim ngalope nï makam. \\
apïn kali ma=lï -nda inim nga=lo-p-e nï ma=kamb\\
fire send 3 sg.obj =put- irr water sg.prox =cut- pfv-dep 1 sg 3 sg.obj =shun\\
`[I] would have burned it, but this rain came, so I didn’t want to.’ [ulwa037_50:25]

The irrealis mood is a natural resource for designating counterfactual statements. While one prolific use of the irrealis mood is to mark future states or events, which are in a sense always counterfactual, the irrealis mood can also be applied to hypothetical states or events in present or past time that are known not to be true. Sentence ex:syntax:267 posits a hypothetical event in the past that is known not to have occurred. In this sentence, an irrealis form is used. This may be contrasted with the perfective forms used in the second clause to mark what was known to have occurred.

Wa mbïpïna Kowe awa mangusuwa asape mï i. \\
wa mbï-p- na Kowe awa ma-ngusuwa asa-p-e mï i\\
village here-be- irr [name] int 3 sg.obj- poor hit- pfv-dep 3 sg.subj go. pfv \\
‘[Kïtalwe] would have stayed in the village, but Kowe himself hit the poor thing [= Kïtalwe] and he [= Kïtalwe] left.’ [ulwa037_46:06]

Counterfactual statements are frequently used in conditional sentence s, presenting hypothetical states or events, whether in the past or in the present. Examples ex:syntax:268 and ex:syntax:269 illustrate counterfactual conditional statements referring to past time.

Nï ndïn ndul sita ndï ango uta tï nïnanda.\\
nï ndï=n ndï=ul si- ta ndï ango uta tï nï=na- nda \\
1 sg 3 pl=obl 3 pl =with push -cond 3pl neg bird take 1 sg =give- irr \\
‘If I had shown them [= the birds] to them, I would not have been able to take the birds for myself.’ [ulwa032_56:25]

U uk undana nakïta u ilum atnï wambana mokona.\\
u uk unda-na na-kï- ta u ilum at=nï wambana moko- na \\
2 sg hook go- irr detr- say -cond 2sg little fight= obl fish take- irr \\
`If you had thought of fishing, you would have gotten many fish.’ (Literally ‘would have taken with little fight’; uk = TP huk ) [ulwa032_22:59]

Examples ex:syntax:270 and ex:syntax:271 illustrate counterfactual conditional statements referring to present time.

counterfactual|)

Ndï ndandïlaluta ndalin. Ndï ango ndale. \\
ndï ndï=andïla-lo- ta ndï=ali- n[da] ndï ango ndï=ali-e\\
3 pl 3pl= await-go- irr-cond 3 pl =scrape- irr 3pl neg 3pl =scrape- ipfv \\
`If they looked for them, they would scrape them. But they don’t scrape them.’ [ulwa032_38:31]

A! Ala num tï mbïlta nï mbu wonlakana.\\
a ala num tï mbï-lï- ta nï mbï-u won- la -ka- na \\
ah pl.dist canoe take here-put- cond 1sg here-from cut- irr -let- irr \\
`Ah! If only those folks had a canoe here, I would cross from there.’ [ulwa037_02:50]
summary: In Ulwa, counterfactual sentences generally use verbs marked with the irrealis mood, which can refer to hypothetical situations in the future, present, or past that are known not to be true. The passage also shows that counterfactual conditionals commonly use this irrealis marking, with past-time examples contrasting irrealis forms in the unrealized clause and perfective forms in the clause describing what actually happened.

Syntactically, passive sentences are remarkable in Ulwa, since they do not comply with the canonical verb-final clause structure. Despite their crosslinguistically unusual formation (in that they rely solely on the manipulation of word order ), these constructions in Ulwa are considered here to be passive, since they satisfy common criteria for defining passives (see; ).

active voice Active sentences in Ulwa have a fairly rigid SOV constituent order ( sec:11.1 ), as in ex:syntax:272. In passive sentences, on the other hand, the verb occupies a different position: it precedes the subject, as in ex:syntax:273.

Yeta mï lamndu masap.\\
yeta mï lamndu ma=asa-p \\
man 3 sg.subj pig 3 sg.obj= hit- pfv \\
`The man killed the pig.’ [elicited]

Asape lamndu mï. \\
asa-p-e lamndu mï\\
hit- pfv-dep pig 3 sg.subj \\
`The pig was killed.’ [elicited]

Likewise, in the active-voice sentence in ex:syntax:274, the word order is SOV, whereas in the passive- voice sentence in ex:syntax:275, the word order is VS. The subject argument in the passive sentence corresponds to the object argument of its active voice active equivalent.

Inom utam nduwanap.\\
inom utam ndï=wana-p \\
mother yam 3 pl= cook- pfv \\
`Mother cooked the yams.’ [elicited]

Wanape utam ndï. \\
wana-p-e utam ndï\\
cook- pfv-dep yam 3 pl \\
`The yams were cooked.’ [elicited]

As the grammatical subject in the passive sentence, the postverbal patient -like argument is the only obligatory argument of the verb. As the subject, it is marked not with the object marker but with the subject marker. Although these markers are usually homophonous, there is a distinction in the 3 sg form: mï ‘3 sg.subj’ for subjects and ma= ‘3 sg.obj’ for non-subject s ( sec:7.2, sec:11.2 ). Crucially, as in example ex:syntax:273, the form [mï] (and not †[ma]) follows the subject of the passive clause. Furthermore, the verb in the passive sentence does not permit an object-marker proclitic, since the semantic patient (the object of the equivalent active voice active sentence) has been promoted to the role of subject. The difference in word order between active-voice and passive-voice clauses is presented in ex:syntax:275a.

Basic constituent order of active and passive clauses
basic constituent order
tabbing
(Passive- voice clauses ( intransitive ):) \= (SOV) \= ((APV))
Intransitive active-voice clauses: \> SV \> \\
Transitive active-voice clauses: \> SOV \> (APV)\\
Passive-voice clauses ( intransitive ): \> VS \> (VP)

The verb in the passive clause generally requires the suffix - e ‘ dep ’. The form [-e] serves several functions in Ulwa. Although it is glossed here as ‘ dep ’ (i.e., “ dependent ”), these passive sentences are analyzed as being independent, since they serve as complete sentences, without needing any additional clause, stated or implied. Although not functioning synchronically as dependent clause s, these passive sentences may have developed diachronically from a type of dependent clause, namely, relative clause s. Since relative clause s in Ulwa employ a gap strategy gapping strategy, they leave themselves open to reanalysis as head-internal relative clause s with inverted word order ( sec:12.3 ). For example, a set of matrix clause and relative clause as in ex:syntax:276 (with the subject “gapped”) could be reanalyzed as the structure presented in ex:syntax:277 (with inverted word order ).

embedded clause
head-internal relative clause

Gapping strategy analysis of relative clauses\\
[S[_ iOV]O iV]\\
the gap “_” represents the S of the embedded relative clause \\
the gap is co-indexed with the O (external head ) of the matrix clause

Head-internal analysis of relative clauses\\
[S[OVS/O]V]\\
“S/O” is the S of the relative clause \\
“S/O” is also the O (internal head ) of the matrix clause

Perhaps examples such as ex:syntax:273 and ex:syntax:275 could be analyzed as relative clause s. For example, sentence ex:syntax:275 could actually mean something like ‘the yams that were cooked’. However, since these examples are all fully capable of serving as independent sentences, not dependent on any other clause, they are analyzed here as indeed passive sentences and not as relative clause s.

The suffix -e ‘ dep ’ does not appear, at least not overtly, in irrealis - mood passives. Since the irrealis suffix invariably ends in [-a], and a phonological rule would syncopate a following /e/, it is, however, possible that there is an underlying suffix /-e/ even in these irrealis - mood passives. Sentence ex:syntax:278 provides an example of an irrealis - mood passive sentence.

Umbe walinda lamndu. \\
umbe wali- nda lamndu\\
tomorrow hit- irr pig\\
`The pig will be killed tomorrow.’ [elicited]

When passive clauses contain discontinuous verb forms ( sec:9.2.1 ), the entire verbal unit occurs prenominally, as in ex:syntax:279.

Lïmndï ale ankam.\\
lïmndï ala-e ankam\\
eye see- dep person\\
`The man was seen.’ [elicited]

Sentences ex:syntax:280 and ex:syntax:281, which are examples of simple passive sentences taken from texts, reveal some of the pragmatic functions of passive sentences. In sentence ex:syntax:280, the speaker is introducing a new topic and placing emphasis on the action (the killing of pigs) and not on the agent s of this action. In sentence ex:syntax:281, the role of the agent (the people who eat food in the dry season) is negligible; rather, the important point is -- quite impersonally -- that the dry season is a time when there is plenty food.

Asape nungol! \\
asa-p-e nungol\\
hit- pfv-dep child\\
`Piglets were killed!’ (Literally ‘Children [i.e., offspring of pigs] were killed!’) [ulwa014_47:11]

Ane se ame mundu. \\
ane sa-e ama-e mundu\\
sun cry- dep eat- dep food\\
`When the sun is shining, food is eaten.’ (i.e., the dry season is a good time for finding food) [ulwa041_02:10]

summary:
Ulwa passive clauses differ from the language’s normal SOV active order because the verb appears before the subject, yielding VS order, and the former object becomes the subject. The passive subject is marked with the subject marker rather than an object marker, and the verb typically takes the suffix -e, though this suffix is not overt in irrealis passives.  

Although these constructions have sometimes been analyzed as relative clauses because of the suffix -e and their unusual order, they are treated here as true passives since they function as independent clauses. The passage also notes that passives are used to foreground the event or patient rather than the agent.

text:
Although the agent of a passive sentence need not be expressed, it can be included as an oblique phrase. In active voice active sentences, oblique s (such as temporal adverb s) occur either in clause-initial position or immediately before the verb phrase -- that is, before the verb in intransitive clauses, and before the object of the verb in transitive clauses. Likewise, the agent oblique phrase, if included, appears at the beginning of the passive clause, immediately before the verb. The oblique marker =n ‘ obl ’ ( sec:11.4.1 ) is used to identify the agent of passive verbs, as in sentences ex:syntax:282, ex:syntax:283, and ex:syntax:284.

Ankamnï toplïpe mana. \\
ankam=nï top-lï-p-e mana\\
person= obl throw-put- pfv-dep spear\\
`The spear was thrown by the man.’ [elicited]

Ndïn asape lamndu. \\
ndï=n asa-p-e lamndu\\
3 pl=obl hit- pfv-dep pig\\
`The pig was killed by them.’ [elicited]

Nungolnï lukawtim mape nga. \\
nungol=nï lukawtim ma=p-e nga\\
child= obl look.after 3sg.obj= be -dep sg.prox \\
`This one was looked after by [my] son.’ ( lukawtim = TP lukautim ) [ulwa014_03:20]

It should be noted that passive sentences are very rare in Ulwa discourse. I suspect that they are being lost as the language experiences grammatical attrition in the face of obsolescence (see sec:15). In many situations in which one might expect to find a passive construction (i.e., situations in which the role of the agent of a transitive sentence is to be downplayed), alternative structures are often used. For example, some speakers use impersonal construction s. Since a pronominal subject can be omitted, it is possible to say something along the lines of ‘[they] did something’, in which the non-specific subject ‘they’ is unstated altogether, as in ex:syntax:285 and ex:syntax:286.

Nip malpe. \\
ni-p ma=lï-p-e\\
die- pfv 3 sg.obj =put- pfv-dep \\
`[He] died and [they] buried him.’ [ulwa037_45:52]

Lungum anda matï Tapon nana. \\
lungum anda ma=tï Tapon na-na\\
long.spear sg.dist 3sg.obj= take [name] give- pfv \\
`[They] gave a long spear to Tapon.’ [ulwa003_00:32]

Although often not necessary to convey information, passive clauses fulfill a very useful role in discourse, since they enable certain relative clause constructions that would otherwise be impossible. In relative clause constructions, only the subject argument is accessible to being relativize d ( sec:12.3 ). An antecedent noun phrase cannot serve as the direct object of the relative clause. Therefore, although it would be possible directly to translate into Ulwa a sentence like ‘Ginam saw the man who killed the pig’, it would not be possible directly to translate into Ulwa a sentence like ‘Ginam saw the pig that the man killed’.

Passivization, however, which can promote a direct object to subject, provides a means for conveying the meaning of a sentence like ‘Ginam saw the pig that the man killed’, changing the sentence, as it were, to a sentence like ‘Ginam saw the pig that was killed by the man.’ The sentence in Ulwa would appear as in ex:syntax:287.

Ginam lïmndï ankamnï asape lamndu mala. \\
Ginam lïmndï [ankam=nï asa-p-e] lamndu ma=ala\\
[name] eye [person= obl hit- pfv-dep] pig 3 sg.obj =see\\
`Ginam saw the pig that the man killed.’ (Literally ‘Ginam saw the pig that was killed by the man.’) [elicited]

It is a rather straightforward process to have the head noun in an independent clause, such as lam ‘meat’ in ex:syntax:288 or ex:syntax:289, function as the subject of a relative clause, as in ex:syntax:290.

Inom mï lam mawanap.\\
inom mï lam ma=wana-p\\
mother 3 sg.subj meat 3 sg.obj =cook- pfv \\
`Mother cooked the meat.’ [elicited]

Lam mï nungol masap.\\
lam mï nungol ma=asa-p\\
meat 3 sg.subj child 3 sg.obj =hit- pfv \\
`The meat killed the child.’ (i.e., it poisoned him and he died) [elicited]

Inom mï nungol masape lam mawanap.\\
inom mï [nungol ma=asa-p-e] lam ma=wana-p\\
mother 3 sg.subj [child 3 sg.obj =hit- pfv-dep] meat 3sg.obj =cook- pfv \\
`Mother cooked the meat that killed the child.’ [elicited]

It is not, however, possible, for the head noun in the matrix clause to correspond to a direct object in the relative clause. Thus, lam ‘meat’ in ex:syntax:291 cannot be relativize d. However, a comparable meaning can be conveyed by using a passive construction in the relative clause, as in ex:syntax:292.

Nungol mï lam mamap.\\
nungol mï lam ma=ama-p\\
[name] 3 sg.subj meat 3sg.obj =eat- pfv \\
`The child ate the meat.’ [elicited]

Inom mï nungolnï amape lam mawanap.\\
inom mï [nungol=nï ama-p-e] lam ma=wana-p\\
mother 3sg.subj [child= obl eat- pfv-dep] meat 3sg.obj =cook- pfv \\
`Mother cooked the meat that the child ate.’ (Literally ‘Mother cooked the meat that was eaten by the child.’) [elicited]

It is perhaps due to this usefulness that the passive voice does still appear in discourse, often in other complex constructions that employ relative clause s, like in ex:syntax:293.

U ko nananï nïwat lape mïnda ngawonp. \\
u ko nana=nï nï=wat la-p-e mïnda nga=won-p-e\\
2 sg just mama= obl 1 sg= atop plant- pfv-dep banana sg.prox =cut- pfv-dep \\
`You just cut this banana tree that was planted above me by mama.’ [ulwa001_02:32]

In many contexts speakers instead use impersonal constructions, but passives remain important because they allow relative clause formation when the direct object must be relativized, making sentences possible that otherwise could not be directly expressed.

Passive sentences ( sec:13.7 ) can be thought of as reducing the valency of a verb. Since their active voice active, transitive equivalents have two core argument s (a subject and a direct object ), whereas they themselves have only one argument (a patient -like subject), the valency of the verb is considered to be decreased. This section is concerned with other means of reducing valency or decreasing transitivity.

There are no formal properties, such as phonological differences, by which transitivity classes may be differentiated in Ulwa. That is, there are no formal distinctions between verbs that typically exhibit semantic properties associated with high transitivity and verbs that typically exhibit semantic properties associated with low transitivity. I follow here a scalar definition of “ transitivity ”, based on semantic properties including telicity, punctuality, volitionality of the agent, and affectedness of the patient, among others ( ). Therefore, semantic ally, transitivity is taken to be a property of an entire clause. Syntactically, on the other hand, I understand a transitive clause (as opposed to an intransitive clause) as being “a construction with two syntactically privileged arguments”.

In examining the degree to which verbs may be ambitransitive in Ulwa, we may consider both A-lability and P-lability. Here I follow, for example,, in differentiating two varieties of ambitransitivity or lability. In A-lability (i.e., agent -preserving lability ), the S argument of the intransitive use of the verb is semantic ally the same as the A argument of the transitive. In P-lability (i.e., patient -preserving lability ), on the other hand, the S argument of the intransitive use of the verb is semantic ally the same as the P argument of the transitive.

In considering A-lability, we may note that it seems that essentially any verb in Ulwa may occur without an expressed object. Although this could be taken to suggest that there exist no truly transitive verbs in Ulwa, an alternative view would be that at least some instances in which a putatively ambitransitive verb occurs without an overtly expressed object are examples of object deletion indefinite object deletion ( ). For example, the verb ama- ‘eat’ may occur either with ex:syntax:294 or without ex:syntax:295 an expressed object; when no object is stated, however, it could be argued that there is an indefinite object (i.e., ‘food’) that has simply been deleted. Crosslinguistically, the verb ‘eat’ often behaves idiosyncratically in terms of transitivity. Thus, it should perhaps not be taken as indicating too much about transitivity in the language in general. Nevertheless, Ulwa may here be contrasted with other Keram languages, such as Mwakai and Ap Ma, in which the semantic ally light noun si ‘things’ (in both languages) is commonly used as the object of the verb ‘eat’ when no particular food is being specified. Thus, in contrast to its sister languages, Ulwa -- or at least the Manu dialect of Ulwa -- seems to have an ambitransitive verb meaning ‘eat’. In the Maruat-Dimiri-Yaul dialect, on the other hand, ‘eat’ generally takes the object mundï ‘food’, when no particular food is being specified. Although contrasts such as the one exemplified by ex:syntax:294 and ex:syntax:295 suggest the possible ambitransitivity (namely, A-lability ) of the verb ‘eat’, it is common in the Manu dialect for the detransitivizing prefix na- ‘detr’ to occur with ‘eat’ when no particular food is being specified ( sec:13.8.2 ).

Nï ta lamndu amap. \\
nï ta lamndu ama-p\\
1 sg already pig eat- pfv \\
`I have already eaten pork.’ [elicited]

Nï ta amap. \\
nï ta ama-p\\
1 sg already eat- pfv \\
`I have already eaten.’ [elicited]

Next, we may consider P-lability. Ulwa does not have a class of patient - preserving lability labile verbs. Verbal notions such as ‘break’ and ‘burn’, which are crosslinguistically more likely to be expressed with P-labile verbs, occur in Ulwa as pairs of unrelated verbs (i.e., ‘break [ transitive ]’ vs. ‘break [ intransitive ]’ and ‘burn [ transitive ]’ vs. ‘burn [ intransitive ]’). In the terms of, Ulwa could be said to have an indeterminate valence orientation “indeterminate” valence orientation, since the correspondences between “plain” and “induced” verbs are generally of the suppletive variety ex:syntax:295a.

There are, for example, several ways of encoding ‘breaking’ events in Ulwa, but none of them instantiates P-lability. The verbs a- ‘break’, kol- ‘break, split’, kot- ‘break, bear’, and kun- ‘break, break off’ are all transitive, with the P argument referring to that which is broken; the verbs nungun u- ‘break ( intransitive )’ and tukul- ‘break ( intransitive )’, on the other hand, are both intransitive, with the S argument referring to that which is broken. Sentence ex:syntax:296 exemplifies the use of the intransitive verb tukul- ‘break’.

Amun nïnji maka palapal min mï maka tukulp.\\
amun nï-nji maka palapal min mï maka tukul -p\\
now 1 sg-poss thus decoration? band 3 sg.subj thus break- pfv \\
`Now, my, like, shell armband has broken like this.’ ( palapal < TP balbal palpal ‘Indian coral tree’?) [ulwa015_00:59]

Example ex:syntax:296 may be compared with example ex:otherwc:105 in sec:8.2.3, which illustrates the use of the intransitive verb nungun u- ‘break’.

Although tukul- ‘break’ may be etymologically related to kol- ‘break’, kot- ‘break’, or kun- ‘break’, it is not synchronically derived by any process (i.e., there is no known prefix †/tu-/). At any rate, the transitive verb a- ‘break’ is not related to any of these forms, whether diachronically or synchronically. An example of this transitive verb is given in ex:syntax:297, which may be compared with example ex:det:133 in sec:7.3 and example ex:det:199 in sec:7.5, which contain similar uses of this verb.

May mïnkïn map \\

3 sg.obj =go. pfv sago.species 3 sg.obj =break- pfv \\
`[We] went there and broke a sago palm.’ [ulwa037_03:43]
summary: The passage argues that Ulwa has no formal, phonological way of distinguishing transitivity classes; instead, transitivity is treated semantically as a property of the clause and syntactically as a construction with two privileged arguments. It then shows that while some verbs, such as *eat*, can appear without an overt object and may be analyzed as ambitransitive in the A-labile sense, Ulwa lacks P-labile verbs, since notions like ‘break’ and ‘burn’ are expressed by separate transitive and intransitive verbs rather than by a single patient-preserving verb.

The verb kot- ‘break’ often seems to exhibit ambitransitivity, namely when it has the secondary meaning ‘bear, give birth’. This, however, is indicative of A-lability, not lability P-lability.

Like ‘break’, the verbal notion of ‘burn’ in Ulwa is encoded with different verbs for transitive and intransitive meanings. The intransitive verb is wo- ‘burn, blaze’, which does not take an object. Transitive constructions, on the other hand, are formed with the phrase apïn=n ama- ‘eat with fire’, with the A argument referring to the person setting fire to something and the P argument referring to that which is burned ( apïn ‘fire’ occurs in an oblique phrase ) ex:syntax:297a.

Nï apïn im ngamap.\\
nï apïn=n im nga= ama -p\\
1 sg fire= obl tree sg.prox =eat- pfv \\
`I burned this tree.’ (Literally ‘I ate this tree with fire.’) [elicited]

Alternatively, apïn ‘fire’ can itself be the A argument (i.e., subject), with the P argument referring to that which is burned (i.e., ‘fire eats [something]’); since there is no animate agent here (the fire is the subject), this construction has, at least semantic ally, something like an intransitive meaning, although syntactically it is transitive ex:syntax:297b.

Apïn mï amun im ndame.\\
apïn mï amun im ndï= ama -e\\
fire 3 sg.subj now tree 3 pl =eat- ipfv \\
`The trees are burning now.’ (Literally ‘Fire is now eating the trees.’) [elicited]

Finally, although potentially any verb may be used without an overtly stated object, there are some prototypically low- transitivity verbs that never occur with an object, such as ‘die’. It would thus not be unreasonable to consider such verbs to be intransitive. There is no class of ditransitive verbs in Ulwa ( sec:11.3 ).

There is an important bound morpheme in Ulwa that serves a number of grammatical functions, often with nuances that are difficult to explain, but whose basic function seems to be to reduce the transitivity of verbs. This is the verbal prefix na- ‘ detr’ (i.e., “ detransitivizer ”). Reasons for treating the detransitivizing form na- ‘detr’ as a prefix rather than a clitic include the fact that it only occurs before verbs and the fact that object-marker proclitic s may precede it. It may be seen in sentence ex:syntax:297c.

Ndï naytap.\\
ndï na -ita-p\\
3 pl detr -build- pfv \\
`They built [something].’ [ulwa014_26:43]

In Ulwa, there are not strong distributional or structural differences between what may be thought of as transitive and intransitive verbs. Many verbs with meanings that are often considered prototypically intransitive can, in Ulwa, have direct object s and, as such, may be marked with object-marker proclitic s. For example, the verb ma- i- ‘go’ can function simply as an intransitive verb, requiring no object ex:syntax:298.

Nï i.\\
nï i \\
1 sg go. pfv \\
`I went.’ [ulwa014_12:42]

As an intransitive verb, ma- i- ‘go’ may accept a postpositional phrase to demarcate a goal argument ex:syntax:299.

Nï ndiya i.\\
nï ndï= iya i \\
1 sg 3 pl =toward go. pfv \\
`I went to them.’ [ulwa014_05:39]

Alternatively, ma- i- ‘go’ can function as a transitive verb, with the goal argument as its object. As an object, the goal argument can, accordingly, receive object marking ex:syntax:300.

Nï Kumba may.\\
nï Kumba ma=i \\
1 sg Bun 3 sg.obj =go. pfv \\
`I went to Bun [village].’ [ulwa032_00:16]

As a transitive verb, ma- i- ‘go’ may take an object even without an object-marker proclitic ex:syntax:301.

Mï i wandam iye.\\
mï i wandam i -e\\
3 sg.subj go. pfv jungle go. pfv-dep \\
`She went, went to the jungle.’ [ulwa001_00:42]

Furthermore, as a transitive verb, ma- i- ‘go’ can even have both a direct object and a postpositional phrase marking an additional destination (i.e., goal ), as in ex:syntax:302. Thus the verb ma- i- ‘go’ may be considered transitive (or at least capable of being transitive ), taking as its direct object a goal argument. Even when there is no expressed object, the claim can be made that the verb is still transitive, only that the direct object has been left unexpressed.

Nï maya wa may.\\
nï ma= iya wa ma=i \\
1 sg 3 sg.obj =toward village 3 sg.obj =go. pfv \\
`I went to him in the village.’ [ulwa037_37:38]

Although it is possible for the verb ma- i- ‘go’ to function as an intransitive verb without any special marking, it very commonly receives the detransitivizing prefix na- ‘detr’, which seems to serve the primary purpose of reducing transitivity, in this case changing the verb’s meaning from something perhaps better glossed as ‘go to’ to something meaning simply ‘go’, as in ex:syntax:303 and ex:syntax:304.

Ndï nay.\\
ndï na -i\\
3 pl detr- go. pfv \\
`They went.’ [ulwa032_31:28]

Mangusuwata namana.\\
ma-ngusuwata na -ma-na\\
3 sg.obj- poor detr- go- irr \\
`The poor thing will be going.’ [ulwa037_59:19]

This same prefix is seen on the verb ‘go’ also when a single argument is expressed in a postpositional phrase (i.e., the goal is not expressed as the direct object of the verb), as in ex:syntax:305.

Mï maya nay.\\
mï ma=iya na -i\\
3 sg.subj 3 sg.obj =toward detr- go. pfv \\
`He went to her.’ [ulwa009_02:26]

The same prefix na- ‘ detr’ can occur with other verbs, also marking them as intransitive. In example ex:syntax:306, the verb ama- la- ‘eat’ is transitive (i.e., it has an overt object). This sentence may be compared with examples ex:syntax:307 and ex:syntax:308, in which the same verb is intransitive, in these examples being marked with the prefix na- ‘detr’.

Tïn mï utam mamap.\\

dog 3 sg.subj yam 3 sg.obj =eat- pfv \\
`The dog ate the yam.’ [elicited]

Nï ta namap.\\
nï ta na -ama-p\\
1 sg already detr -eat- pfv \\
`I’ve already eaten.’ [elicited]

Ndul nalanda! \\

3 pl =with detr- eat- irr \\
`[Let’s] eat with them!’ [ulwa029_04:11]

As a verbal affix that allows an otherwise transitive verb to lose its direct object argument, the prefix na- ‘detr’ could theoretically be described as an antipassive morpheme, even though this term is not commonly used in descriptions of languages with nominative-accusative morphosyntactic alignment, such as Ulwa. See for discussion of antipassive s in nominative-accusative nominative-accusative alignment languages.

The morpheme na- ‘detr’ is often better described as reducing the transitivity of a verb rather than changing its valency. In example ex:syntax:309, the object of the verb is technically the question word angos ‘what?’. However, given the fact that the event that the verb is encoding is far from being prototypically transitive (i.e., the situation is non-punctual, irrealis, etc.), it is not surprising that the detransitivizing prefix na- ‘detr’ is employed.

Una angos nalanda?\\
unan angos na -la-nda\\
1 pl.incl what detr -eat- irr \\
`What shall we eat?’ [ulwa040_00:46]

Examples ex:syntax:310 and ex:syntax:311 illustrate how the verb ita- ‘build’ can likewise be detransitivized with the prefix na- ‘detr’. In example ex:syntax:310, the verb is transitive and receives the object marker ma= ‘3 sg.obj ’; in example ex:syntax:311, the verb is intransitive, and receives the detransitivizing prefix na- ‘detr’.

summary: Ulwa has a verbal prefix na- ‘detr’ that functions to reduce the transitivity of verbs, and it is treated as a prefix because it appears only before verbs and can follow object-marker proclitics. The language shows little sharp difference between transitive and intransitive verbs: even verbs like ‘go’ and ‘eat’ can occur with or without direct objects, and na- often marks a more intransitive or less transitive use. Although na- could be described as antipassive in effect, the passage emphasizes that it is better understood as a detransitivizer than as a simple valency-changing morpheme.
